boundaries in the region intentionally unclear, which enabled all sides to construct
their own image of what had been surrendered or gained (in the case of France and
Britain) or how far to allow European powers to extend into Indigenous territory
(in the case of the Wabanaki). Though neither the French nor the English could
control the region, both wanted to. The projects undertaken after 1713, which in-
cluded new pales within the British geographic fiction of Nova Scotia, economic
growth, and increased attention to Indigenous inhabitants, demonstrated that
“Nova Scotia or Acadia” was increasingly important to European officials. These
competing imperial ideas, however, remained firmly within the lived reality of
Indigenous homelands.
   From the fall of Port Royal in 1710 to the conclusion of British-Wabanaki trea-
ties in 1726, European powers worked to marshal geographic evidence that could
anticipate an Acadia or Nova Scotia that did not yet exist. The primary task was
determining what had been won or lost, but in the face of Indigenous territorial
control neither British nor French officials could assert authority over more than the
forts they inhabited. French Acadians remained in their small villages and slowly
expanded along the coast, surrounded by marshlands and the fields of wheat they
created by stealing land back from the Bay of Fundy tides. The Mi’kmaq moni-
tored these settlements and British forts and launched attacks when necessary,
though Indigenous groups were excluded from the official discussions over their
territory taking place in administrative offices on the other side of the Atlantic. As
the Wabanaki were increasingly drawn into territorial conflicts, British and French
officials employed a wide array of geographic strategies to defend or expand their
limited holdings in the northeast. The British hoped that military efforts would
facilitate the extension of their influence beyond their forts and provide for British
settlements that would help bring the idea of Nova Scotia closer to reality; French
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                           47


officials relied on their Indigenous allies to resist English expansion, including
efforts to push north from Boston into the Dawnland and Wulstukwik. During
this era, however, Nova Scotia and Acadia remained imperial fictions, competing
against each other for control over a handful of villages, trading posts, and forts.
   Though it was little more than an idea expressed in maps and surveys, Nova
Scotia was a local and an Atlantic concern after 1710. As British administrators es-
tablished a small site of authority at Port Royal, economic factors drew attention to
other regions. Canso, a valuable fishing outpost strategically located at the north-
east end of the peninsula, quickly emerged as a site of intense competition that
required imperial consideration. Though production at Canso paled in comparison
to the Newfoundland fishery – the entire operation consisted of only a few wooden
buildings scattered across a collection of small islands with beaches suitable for
drying cod – the outpost was the most valuable resource in Nova Scotia into the
1730s and thus merited attention from administrators in Europe. Official nego-
tiations over the boundaries and possession of Canso (which hinted at the larger
unanswered questions about the size and possession of Acadia) took place in Paris
in 1720 but quickly collapsed under geographic misinformation and claims of car-
tographic forgery. This effort had a parallel among local officials in Nova Scotia,
who also attempted to resolve the Canso dispute with maps only to discover that
extant evidence failed to make a convincing argument for either side.
   Officials realized that more, new, and better maps were required to assert a con-
vincing claim over even a small outcropping of rocks along the coast and thus this
period witnessed a great desire for maps, though requests for new information
largely outstripped either French or British capabilities to produce useful knowl-
edge. The example of the schooner William Augustus, used for a brief British sur-
vey of the coast before being requisitioned for more practical duties, demonstrates
the real world obstacles to undertaking mapping projects. Yet these challenges on
the ground certainly didn’t end the desire for more maps. What becomes obvious
during this era is that the distance between Nova Scotia and Britain, and equally
between Acadia and France, required local and imperial strategies that weren’t
always effectively coordinated or carried out. Context and contingency drove lo-
cal development, while officials in Britain and France struggled to understand
the physical and temporal differences between what they saw on paper and what
they could build on the ground.
   The Wabanaki withstood British efforts to create Nova Scotia and French efforts
to define Indigenous land as Acadia. Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, Passamaquoddy,
and Abenaki groups held the balance of power and adjusted to new British tenants
in the region relatively well. After the fall of Port Royal, Indigenous forces contin-
ued to attack British ships, resist British territorial expansion, and fight alongside
French forces when their interests intersected, which they often did. By the early
1720s, the Wabanki had to respond to territorial encroachment by launching at-
tacks and border raids in what became known as Dummer’s War. The treaties
struck in the 1720s between the British and Indigenous groups to end that conflict
demonstrate the territorial strength of Indigenous nations. These agreements were
not land surrenders, but rather recognitions of a new order that required treaties of
“peace and friendship.” Land was a major concern, and boundaries were the topic
of much debate at the treaty negotiations. The result was Wabanaki recognition
48                             Homelands and Empires


of various British pales and an agreement on terms for future expansion. These
agreements were undoubtedly rife with misunderstanding (genuine and deliber-
ate), but the treaties established a framework meant to enable coexistence in a ter-
ritory that remained dominated by Indigenous nations.

                                      •••
British forces under Francis Nicholson attacked Port Royal in October 1710 as
a consolation prize. The War of the Spanish Succession was raging in Europe
and, consequently, in North America, and the British sought to strike at the heart
of France’s American empire. New England forces had tried and failed to take
Acadia twice in 1707 but remained hopeful that the French fort would fall. In
1708, Samuel Vetch outlined a grander design against French Canada in his essay
“Canada Survey’d.” Vetch was the son of a Scottish minister and had been edu-
cated in Utrecht. He fought for William of Orange in 1688 and eventually made
his way to North America in 1700. That year, his marriage to Margaret Livingston,
the daughter of Robert Livingston, a prominent New York merchant and member
of the New York council, secured him a comfortable life in New York with society
connections, and Vetch quickly parlayed his position into a successful but illicit
trade with Canada. By 1705 he was in Boston working with Governor Dudley on
prisoner exchanges, a job that required frequent travel along the craggy and wood-
ed coastline that ran along the edges of the Dawnland; through the high tides in
the Bay of Fundy and across marshlands that led to Port Royal; and down the St
Lawrence, with its dangerous currents threatening to smash ships into the rocks,
towards Quebec.1 These trips served as a geography class. On a return to Britain in
1708 he presented “Canada Survey’d” to Queen Anne and received her approval
to launch an attack on Canada. With the aid of Francis Nicholson, a colonial gov-
ernor whose military and political acumen enabled him to bridge the upheaval
of the Glorious Revolution and serve in North America under both James II and
William of Orange, Vetch organized troops – which included volunteer forces from
the colonies and about 450 Iroquois – and prepared for the campaign.2 Their attack
depended on the support of British naval ships, so Vetch and Nicholson waited.
The summer months passed with no sign of British ships. By October 1709, Vetch
and Nicholson learned that Queen Anne had diverted the fleet to Portugal.
   To save the expedition, Nicholson returned to London and won the approv-
al of a smaller attack against Acadia in Mi’kma’ki. Much to Vetch’s frustration,
Nicholson was put in charge of the smaller attack and Vetch was to serve under
him. Forces left from Boston in September 1710. The crumbling sodden fort at Port
Royal stood little chance of resisting the British. Acadia’s governor, Subercase, sur-
rendered after only a few days of fighting and thus fared only slightly better than
de Menneval had twenty years earlier.3 The fort was renamed Annapolis Royal
and garrisoned with British soldiers, but little else in the region changed. John
G. Reid and others have investigated the impact of the capture of Port Royal and
questioned the implications of the “conquest,” suggesting that both Acadian and
Indigenous inhabitants responded in 1710 as they had several times previously.4
Yet other historians continue to argue that after 1710, “suddenly and silently, the
Acadians assented to their fate, while their new British masters looked upon them
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          49


with disdain and suspicion.”5 On the contrary, the Mi’kmaq remained the domi-
nant force and the Acadians responded to the British presence in measured and
deliberate ways.
   Nicholson, emboldened by his victory against the French pale in Mi’kma’ki, re-
turned to London to push for a new commitment to Vetch’s larger plan to attack
Quebec. He recruited four “Indian Kings” to travel to England with him, meet
with the Queen, and demonstrate Iroquois support for a larger expedition. The
“kings” were far from royalty. Young men all of them, none commanded more
than a dozen men and only one could loosely be considered a sachem among his
people. But they were willing to go and would have to suffice. The kings toured
London’s narrow streets, met with Queen Anne and, through an interpreter who
spoke on their behalf, expressed their desire to contribute to an attack against
Canada. This diplomatic mission also served to excite Londoners. Britons within
and without London read about the kings’ activities, and some were lucky enough
to see them in the flesh. At a performance of Macbeth attended by the kings, the
audience so desired to gawk at the young Iroquois men that the play was inter-
rupted to remove the putative royals from their box seats and place them on the
stage. Those in attendance could then easily shift their gaze from Shakespeare’s
dark tragedy about regicide to the play’s Indigenous audience. The stage was full
of men pretending to be kings.6
   Nicholson’s push succeeded in gaining official and public support for a new
campaign, but the attack was a disaster. In August of 1711, Admiral Hovenden
Walker – lacking reliable charts and capable navigators – sailed down the noto-
riously difficult St Lawrence towards the citadel fortress at Quebec. Well before
reaching their destination the fleet was swallowed into a thick fog, resulting in the
wreck of eight ships and the loss of 889 seamen. The remaining ships were rescued
with much effort, and after consultation with locally sourced pilots the decision
was made to return to England. Walker’s fortunes refused to improve. While at
anchor at Spithead, his ship Edgar exploded and the admiral (who had just enough
luck to be onshore at the time) lost all his papers. Though he was never repri-
manded for the debacle in the St Lawrence, without his official records Walker was
unable to account fully for his actions.7 New Englanders, facing a loss of their own,
were forced to come to terms with a second failed attempt on Quebec.
   The expedition to Canada, though an unquestionable failure, was part of the
larger “Grand Design” meant to remove the French from North America. The ini-
tial victory won for Britain a crumbling fort on the shores of what is now the Anna­
polis Basin; the subsequent defeat left eight naval ships at the bottom of the St
Lawrence River. What could account for such a dismal showing? Rumours quickly
circulated around the British Atlantic, and blame came to rest on the shoulders
of allegedly apathetic New Englanders and their greedy merchants. The entire
venture needed a defender, and it found one in Jeremiah Dummer. The grandson
of an assistant in the Massachusetts Bay Colony and one of Harvard College’s
brightest graduates, Dummer seemed destined for great things. After graduating
from Harvard in 1699, his interest in French, mathematics, and travel took him to
Leiden and Utrecht where he earned a doctorate for submitting no fewer than four
theses. After an unsuccessful attempt at securing a professorship in philology at
Harvard – despite being championed by Increase Mather, who declared him the
50                              Homelands and Empires


best scholar of his time – Dummer returned to London and soon became a colonial
agent. He maintained rooms at the Middle Temple and fell within the influential
orbit of the Board of Trade, so it is not surprising that Dummer, the well-connected
New Englander, provided answers when questions were raised about the failed
expedition against Canada.8
   Dummer emphasized the importance of thinking geographically when con-
structing an imperial fiction. In A Letter to a Noble Lord Concerning the Late Expedition
to Canada (1712), Dummer offered an explanation for Walker’s failure while simul-
taneously emphasizing the success of Nicholson’s campaign against Port Royal.
The short pamphlet took as its objective answering three questions. First, what was
Canada’s value and was it worth the effort to capture it? Second, was the expedi-
tion well planned? And third, were New Englanders to blame for the failure? Were
Canada an isolated geographic entity, according to Dummer, it would be almost
worthless. “Canada then is a poor country,” he wrote, “and in itself little valuable.”
Anyone who has spent a winter in Montreal or Quebec City can attest to Dummer’s
general conclusion: “being subject to winds that blow from vast lakes above a thou-
sand leagues westerly make it extremely cold and barren.” But what made Canada
barren also made it economically attractive, especially were it peopled by British
subjects who would be forced to rely on English manufactures because they could
produce so little locally.9
   Beyond a potential addition to Britain’s mercantilist project, Canada was a
strategically valuable territory. “The situation of that country gives the people
an opportunity to invade all the British colonies when-ever they please,” Dum-
mer warned, before listing each British colony that lay susceptible to French and
Indigenous attacks: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecti-
cut, New York, the Jerseys, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Virginia.10 What made
these threats especially dangerous was France’s alliance with Indigenous groups
stretching from the Great Lakes to Louisiana. Flipping the Black Legend on its
head, Dummer compared Indigenous brutalities against the English to Spain’s
treatment of Indigenous peoples in South America. Unable to bring himself to
describe the atrocities suffered by English women and children at the hands of
France’s Indigenous allies, Dummer laments, “I believe your Lordship never met
with any thing like it in history, unless you have seen the account which Bar-
tholomeo de las Casas has given the world.”11 Indigenous groups sympathetic to
the French were “blindly bigoted to [French] superstitions,” converted, as many
had been, to the Catholic faith, and “lived in a vast wilderness” to which they
could retreat after launching raids.12 Summarizing the first pages of his pamphlet,
Dummer mused rhetorically: if selling manufactures, securing trade with Indig-
enous peoples and ending their raids against the English, and protecting the fish-
ery are worthwhile endeavours, then capturing Canada is well worth the effort.13
   The conclusion of Dummer’s pamphlet returned to the theme of supporting the
imperial fiction of Nova Scotia to protect against the French. Dummer dismissed
the rumours that New Englanders didn’t care much for the expedition and that
greedy merchants, whose interests lay in maintaining illicit trade with the French,
failed to support the mission. He argued that no assembly would sacrifice the hon-
our of its colony to satisfy a handful of smugglers.14 On a positive note, however,
the successful conquest of Port Royal outweighed the failure to capture Quebec
                               Mapping the Spoils of Peace                                   51


due to Nova Scotia’s strategic geography. The English might have equal title to
Canada and Nova Scotia according to the rights of discovery,

  But I must beg leave to say, that in point of interest the latter is of more consequence
  to the crown than the former. For when that is in the French hands, it’s a bridle to the
  eastern parts of New-England, where the tall pines grow, which are yearly brought
  home in the mast-fleet, and indeed where there is such a vast quantity of naval stores
  of all sorts, as is not to be found in any part of the New World.15

As a defence of the failed campaign against Canada, Dummer reminded his read-
ers that Nova Scotia itself was worth the effort; New England had been freed from
the restrictive French presence in the northeast and could now extend English
settlement from Boston to Annapolis Royal, or so he hoped.

                                        •••
Officials who met to end the War of the Spanish Succession can be forgiven for
leaving unanswered certain questions regarding Acadia. The war was a thor-
oughly European affair and the northeast of North America was peripheral. New
Englanders thought it was important, as did officials at Quebec. But in the larger
scheme, Port Royal simply didn’t rate. Though the French were willing to sur-
render their imagined Acadia, it wasn’t worth the effort of defining exactly what
Acadia was or, more important, where it ended. Instead, the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht
ceded the region according to its “ancient limits,” but the two sides had different
ideas of where those limits lay. France’s secretary of state for the Marine, Jérôme
de Phélypeaux, comte de Pontchartrain (son of Louis Phélypeaux), provided the
French commissioners sent to negotiate the treaty with a memorial outlining his
thoughts on the matter, including the importance of reserving the fishery for
France and establishing the New England-Acadia boundary at the Kennebec Riv-
er.16 Both sides made demands about Acadia’s limits, but in the end it was decided
that a commission would settle the matter at a later date.17 While reserving this
discussion may have facilitated reaching a peace in 1713, inaction on determining
Acadia’s boundaries set the stage for a geographic and cartographic battle that
would test the limits of diplomacy in Europe and of peace in the northeast.
   This was a contest for which the French were well prepared, as French officials
were not new to the practice of using maps and geographic reports to trans-
form their collection of overseas pales into a coherent, though imaginary, colony.
Completely ignoring Indigenous homelands allowed diplomats in Europe to pit
one imperial fiction against another. The uncertainty surrounding Acadia’s limits
during and after the Treaty of Utrecht opened the door for offensive and defensive
cartographic strategies. In 1713 Pontchartrain wrote to Governor Vaudreuil and
Intendant Bégon at Quebec asking them to marshal evidence that would restrict
the Acadian boundaries. Writing from Versailles, and likely with a map of the re-
gion nearby, the minister included what he thought the boundaries should be and
asked that a map be prepared and sent to France to emphasize those limits.18 That
was an offensive strategy. Intendant Bégon’s reply to Pontchartrain offered a de-
fence against English claims to Wabanaki homelands from Beaubassin to Kaskébé
52                               Homelands and Empires

(present-day Portland, Maine) by referring to the ancient maps of England, France,
and Holland that mark only peninsular Nova Scotia with the name Acadia (fig-
ure 2.1) Moreover, Père Aubery, the Jesuit missionary stationed with the Eastern
Abenaki, created a map informed by the Treaty of Ryswick that set the boundary
between New England and New France at the St George River.19 The western coast
of the Baie Française (Bay of Fundy), he argued, was New France and not Acadia.
   The undefined limits set by the Treaty of Utrecht were bound to conflict with
France’s rich cartographic materials. Though the limits of Acadia were never de-
fined, the treaty did set concrete geographic limits for commercial activities and as-
signed certain territories based on their location. French ships were allowed to fish
along the French shore in Newfoundland but could not travel within thirty leagues
east of Sable island, a treeless sandbar that many ships saw too late to prevent them
                            Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          53


from being wrecked; the British gained title over Acadia and its dependencies,
while the French retained Cape Breton and islands in the mouth of the Gulf of
St Lawrence, a vague distinction – and one that could be read differently in the
French and Latin versions of the Treaty – that soon caused confusion.20 In 1713,
the duc de Villiers received a memoir expressing confusion over Nova Scotia’s
limits as suggested by the Treaty. There were two major concerns: first, the French
would be prevented from fishing in waters from Sable Island to the southwest tip
of Nova Scotia and thirty leagues from shore; second, the southern limits of Acadia
as listed in Article XII were unclear and did not correspond to those indicated on
French maps. Moreover, the memoir’s author was suspicious that the British were
conveniently adjusting their maps to correspond to their desired location of Sable
Island to exclude France from the region’s fishery.21 Accusations of cartographic
impropriety would increase over the following decades as Britain and France em-
ployed geographic evidence to support their respective imperial fictions.
   A major source of confusion between British and French depictions of Nova
Scotia/Acadia were the various geographic histories of the region. Both imperial
forces were willing to ignore Mi’kma’ki as an Indigenous homeland, but even this
exclusion only reduced the complexity by one third. How could the English prov-
ince of Nova Scotia superimpose itself on a French Acadia with fluid boundaries
that had been claimed as different regions dating back to the contests between
La Tour and d’Aulnay in the seventeenth century? That internal competition was
resolved only when d’Aulnay died from exposure after his canoe capsized and
La Tour hastily married his widow.22 A 1713 French memoir on what had been
surrendered at Utrecht argued that there was a western and eastern Acadia, and
that the confusion lay in determining the limits of the western region, which the
British called Nova Scotia because it was north of New England, as Scotland is
to England.23 The author argued that it would be possible to grant this part of
“western” Acadia to the British (including sections of both Wulstukwik and the
Dawnland) “by giving to this large region natural boundaries that will prevent
any future dispute between the two nations.”24 The eastern limit would be the
Baie Française (Bay of Fundy), the northern limit would be the Saint John River.
Lands through which rivers ran into the Saint John would be British, while lands
through which rivers ran into the St Lawrence would remain with France, as
would “eastern” or peninsular Acadia. The author’s desire to retain the penin-
sula was justified because France needed access to the fishery and to the Gulf
of St Lawrence to reach New France. The French could temper this demand by
destroying Port Royal and promising to build no new forts on the Bay’s coast.25
No mention was made of how best to convince the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy,
and Wulstukwiuk of the merits of this plan.
   British officials in Nova Scotia were initially less concerned with Nova Scotia’s
boundaries than afraid that they would quickly lose what little authority they had
had in the region since 1710. From the time that Britain captured Port Royal there
was a fear that the French and Indigenous peoples would combine forces and
retake the post, and local officials and military officers outlined these concerns
to imperial administrators.26 This concern was more than paranoia. In 1711, hav-
ing returned to France after surrendering Acadia, Subercase wrote to the minister
of the Marine informing him that he had spent his time studying maps of Port
54                                 Homelands and Empires


Royal and its surroundings to develop a plan for retaking Acadia. Subercase be-
lieved that time was of the essence, noting that the English inability to win over
the French inhabitants and the Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk would facilitate his
plans.27 Yet the French would have more time than originally anticipated. Nova
Scotia’s governor complained in 1720 that his authority did not extend “beyond
cannon reach of this fort.”28
   On the other hand, the British commissioners in the months leading up to the
Treaty of Utrecht were more concerned with determining the boundaries of Nova
Scotia than with bolstering the crumbling fort. In 1712, the Board of Trade argued
that Cape Breton should be included in any negotiation over Nova Scotia as it had
always been considered part of that province. The year before, French authorities
seemed unsure of Cape Breton’s status as part of Acadia. In a memorial outlining
how to retake Acadia, the region’s limits were initially described as including
Cape Breton until an editor’s pen crossed out that claim.29 The British Board of
Trade outlined clearly what it believed Nova Scotia’s boundaries to be: the region
included what the French called Acadia, with its boundaries being the St Croix to
the west, north towards the St Lawrence River, and east to the Atlantic Ocean. It
was to be described as such to avoid future disputes.30 At this stage the Board of
Trade had few maps to support its claims, but it found other sources to support
this idea of the colony. Of particular importance were the passes that Subercase
granted to inhabitants as France’s governor in Acadia. By these passes he claimed
authority over Acadia, Cape Breton, and all lands adjacent from Cape Rosier to
the Kennebec River.31 These passes helped demonstrate to the British how local
French authorities facilitated travel within their putative colony and imagined it
as more than the sum of its parts. But more evidence was necessary to counter
France’s numerous maps.
   In the first half of the eighteenth century, the French were far superior to the
British in the production of maps and charts. While the Board of Trade searched
near and far for reliable maps of North America, French officials had at their dis-
posal a network of geographers, engravers, and printers who increasingly worked
within a few blocks of each other in Paris.32 France had established educational
and military infrastructures to train and employ geographers, whereas British
schools, though they taught elements of geography, provided no real assistance
in producing or distributing maps.33 Yet Britain was not entirely devoid of capa-
ble geographers and the Board of Trade managed to secure geographic descrip-
tions and maps of Nova Scotia after the fall of Port Royal. In 1710, Massachusetts
privateer-turned-cartographer-turned naval commander Cyprian Southack, who
witnessed his first naval battle at the ripe old age of ten, wrote a memorandum in
which he outlined the boundaries of Nova Scotia as he interpreted them: starting
at the St George River in the Dawnland and cutting through the thickly forested
interior to the Gaspé, down through the narrow Gut of Canso and around the
eastern coast of the peninsula.34 Around the time of this memorandum a map of
Annapolis Royal was sent to the Board of Trade. The map was entitled

     PLAN of Annapolis Royall Fort the principall place of strength in Nova Scotia in
     America, its situation is upon a tongue of land formed on the North East Side by the
     river Dauphin, and on the south east by a large morras in 44 degrees 25 minutes North
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                            55


  Latitude surrendered to her majesties armes under the command of the Honourable
  Collonel Francis Nicholson after eight days Siege in October 1710.35

The title provided British officials with a geographic description of Annapolis.
The image itself featured an imposing fort and the location of settlers’ houses and
fields (figure 2.2). As the Board would soon learn, the fort at Annapolis was crum-
bling and in desperate need of repair.
   In 1714, Nova Scotia’s governor, Samuel Vetch, who had returned to London,
provided a slightly more detailed account of the British possessions in America
that depended on employing geographic descriptions for imperial purposes.
Vetch claimed that British territory on the eastern coast began at the Gut of Canso,
which separated Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, and extended to the limits between
South Carolina and St Augustine. The region behind this stretch of land had no
real boundaries and was currently the site of several French forts.36 Vetch sug-
gested that “it would very much contribute not only to the peace and posterity but
true interest and honour of Great Brittain to have those limits advantageously ad-
justed,” presumably by mapping the region to support imperial territorial claims
in lands belonging to a variety of Indigenous nations. Vetch also illustrated the
challenges inherent in such an endeavour, particularly the costs involved.37 It was
becoming obvious that the British would entrench their claims in America, espe-
cially in Nova Scotia, through maps and surveys of territory.
   Making territorial claims would not be easy because Nova Scotia had to be in-
vented as an imperial territory before it could be claimed. From across the Atlantic,
such a geographic fiction required a solid cartographic foundation. In 1715 Lieu-
tenant Governor Caulfeild wrote to the Board of Trade with a geographic report on
Nova Scotia in which he listed the main areas of settlement (the fort and settlement
at Annapolis Royal and an increasingly substantial Acadian village at Minas), their
location in relation to each other, and the quality of soil and number of harbours
in the region. After complaining that the Indigenous peoples came to Annapolis as
a last resort because the fortress was insufficienty provisioned, Caulfeild warned
the Board that the French were planning to fortify Cape Breton at St Ann’s and
St Peter’s and provided a map to illustrate his point.38 Caulfeild did not indicate
the map’s origins, but it was likely produced in Nova Scotia. Though the map
to which Caulfeild referred does not seem to have survived, he was accurately
anticipating the Board’s desire for graphic representations of Britain’s American
territories. Later that year the Board complained about the dearth of reliable maps
of the American colonies and requested the British minister at the Court of France
to collect the best maps he could find, sure that many good maps had been printed
publicly, or were held privately by men with interests in America.39 European gov-
ernments had long relied on maps to illustrate claims and facilitate administration,
but London was forced to play catch up.40 British officials remained cartographi-
cally disadvantaged and in 1719 the Board of Trade issued a circular letter to all
governors requesting more specific information about each colony’s boundaries
and limits, including maps, surveys, and naval charts if available. Governors were
also to include accounts and written records that would support their cartographic
materials.41 The request for supporting materials indicates that maps were most
valuable when they were authenticated by additional evidence.42
2.2 Extract from the Plan Annapolis Royal, 1710, illustrating a strong fort and its surrounding settlements. National Archives, London. MPG1/274.
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                           57


   Meanwhile, French officials were relocating to Île Royale and reimagining what
Acadia might look like with a stronger French presence on the Atlantic coast.
Though Louisbourg would become the new French Atlantic stronghold, an earlier
plan suggested a site that could have drastically shifted the balance of geographic
strength in Nova Scotia. In the summer of 1711, Pontchartrain received a letter
from M. Jourdan suggesting a new settlement that might preserve French authori-
ty in Acadia. Jourdan noted that Acadia could become one of the richest colonies in
North America, and listed “Chibouqetout” as a strong candidate for a French for-
tification. He argued that settling at this deep and protected harbour with its steep
inclines, rocky shores, and interior of thick but short shrubs would protect both the
French fishery in the region and the French inhabitants in Acadia. Moreover, “this
establishment would render the English conquest of Port Royal completely use-
less, so claim Sieurs Pessere and Delabat.”43 Sieur Delabat, an engineer stationed
at Port Royal until it fell in 1710, had gone so far as to map the harbour that the
English would later settle as Halifax (figure 2.3). Though the plan was never real-
ized, these early French maps and the ideas they represented foreshadowed the
geographic strength of Chebucto harbour.
   French attention turned quickly to Île Royale, an island with larger interior lakes
and good shores for fishing. Plans for establishing a strong French presence on
Île Royale began shortly after the French surrendered Port Royal and required the
construction of new pales within Mi’kmaw territory. A 1713 memorial on settling
the French on the island provided a detailed description of Île Royale’s size (ninety
leagues44 in circumference), its geographic position (between 45 and 47 degrees
northern latitude), and its shape (nearly triangular). The report explained that a
distance of about forty leagues separated Île Royal and Newfoundland, and there
was about a half league between the island and Acadia. The challenge was to select
a port that was both easy to defend and capable of holding many ships, a difficult
task because the maps available were created by those “with only an imperfect
knowledge of the island.”45 So sending a ship with capable geographers and engi-
neers would be an important undertaking.
   Settling the island was no small feat. Île Royale’s inhabitants had to be trans-
ported from the ceded administrative centres of Port Royal in Acadia and Plai-
sance in Newfoundland, the latter a valuable fishery in Newfoundland. There
was also confusion over which port in Île Royale would become the new capital.
Louisbourg, a suitable fishing harbour on the Atlantic coast, won early approval,
but in 1715 the French court at Versailles decided that Port Dauphin, located near
the centre of the island’s northern coast, was the better choice. Only after the ad-
ministration and the garrison had been transported to this new location was the
decision reversed again, and in 1718 everyone headed back to Louisbourg.46 While
officials in France debated the location of the new colony, they demanded a con-
stant supply of maps to inform their decisions. In 1717, the ministry of the Marine
sent an order to Pierre-Auguste de Soubras, the first councillor of the Superior
Council of Île Royale, informing him that Philippe Pastour de Costebelle, the gov-
ernor of Plaisance and Île Royale, had been requested to make “exact maps of
each inhabited area” listing “the name of the inhabitants and the amount of land
they hold.”47 Such cartographically rendered information would allow the Coun-
cil to “cast a glance” at the maps and learn more than detailed written plans could
58                              Homelands and Empires




     2.3 Delabat’s 1711 map of Chebucto. He suggested a settlement on present-day
     Cornwallis Island, with a fortress on the harbour’s coast. Nova Scotia Archives
                         and Records Management, F/240-1711.




provide.48 Both the Board of Trade and the French ministers at Versailles recog-
nized the importance of mapping territories and staking claims, and in the years
immediately following the Treaty of Utrecht both groups of administrators hinted
at the possibility of moulding what they knew about the region’s geography to ad-
dress specific concerns. What neither side could fully appreciate was the strength
of local Indigenous peoples and their ability to defend their ancestral homelands.
   Despite their ability to map territory and despite their ancestral claims, the
Wabanaki were not represented at the Utrecht negotiations and were considered
little more than French pawns. British and French representatives at the treaty ne-
gotiations raised Indigenous issues only when discussing how the division of land
would affect Indigenous allegiances. The imperialists believed an alliance could
also be imposed by treaty, and thus Britain and France divided between themselves
the Mi’kmaw, Wulstukwiuk, and Abenaki groups living in the northeast. After
1713, the Mi’kmaq continued to resist and attack British settlements in Nova Scotia,
which led British officials to protest to the French. Lieutenant Governor Caulfeild
wrote to Governor Vaudreuil in 1713 to complain that a group of Mi’kmaq, ap-
parently unaware that a treaty had been struck, had attacked a trading vessel at
Beaubassin. Caulfeild wanted “satisfaction” for the attack, reflecting the British
opinion that Quebec and the French missionaries controlled the eastern Indigenous
peoples. This claim was repeated into the 1750s.49
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                            59


   The Wabanaki residents of Mi’kma’ki, Wulstukwik, and the Dawnland oper-
ated with their own motivations and goals, many of which revolved around their
fear of European encroachment. While the Wabanaki were, for the most part,
closely allied with French missionaries, they were not inherently aligned with the
French government at Quebec.50 For their part, the French admitted at times to
being unable to control the Mi’kmaq and their allies. Particularly after the Treaty
of Utrecht, when both the British and the French needed to appear interested in
maintaining the peace, accusations of French complicity in Indigenous violence
against the English was a source of tension between the European powers. In 1714,
Costebelle wrote to the minister of the Marine to update him on the French settle-
ments. He had heard of the attacks on British ships, and assured his superior that
the Mi’kmaq of Acadia were irreconcilable enemies of the English, and even the
most peaceful supplications could not prevent similar attacks.51 Two months later,
Costebelle informed the minister that he had personally informed the English that
his administration had nothing to do with the Mi’kmaw attacks.52
   The British may have blamed the French, but they feared the Wabanaki. In 1715,
Francis Nicholson warned the Board of Trade that the Mi’kmaq were angry be-
cause they believed the British had cheated them. Nicholson feared they would
become violent.53 The Mi’kmaq were angry, and they did retaliate. Soon after the
British took Port Royal in 1710, a group of Mi’kmaq attacked soldiers sent to re-
trieve fleeing Acadians. Abbé Gaulin, a missionary to the Mi’kmaq in Nova Scotia,
described the attack to Costebelle, outlining how the Mi’kmaq killed a few officers
and held the rest in a house. The chief then sent a letter to the English garrison
threatening to burn the house and its inhabitants if the English failed to surrender
the fort.54 Although the English did not quit Annapolis Royal, they did find them-
selves hemmed in behind the fort’s walls and therefore unable to extend their ter-
ritorial control. Two months later Costebelle reported that the English were afraid
to leave the fort because the Mi’kmaq and the Acadians, who Costebelle provided
with guns and ammunition, continually threatened to recapture the garrison.55 In
this light, the maps of Annapolis Royal sent from the garrison to London take on
a new meaning: whereas officials in London might have seen a strong fort in an
increasingly “British” Nova Scotia, local administrators saw a fragile pale beyond
which Nova Scotia was largely imaginary.56
   Mi’kmaw resistance went beyond empty threats. Vetch was so concerned that in
1712 he proposed importing a Mohawk force from New York to defend the fort. He
argued that any number of Indigenous peoples in the British cause would be worth
twice as many British soldiers.57 Six months later Vetch reported that Mi’kmaw
threats persisted, but that “the Indian company is now of very great use to us, and
without them even in peace it will be hard for this Garrison to subsist, the Indians of
this country being never to be trusted.”58 Resistance extended beyond the Mi’kmaq
to their eastern Abenaki neighbours. In 1715, officials at Annapolis Royal sent two
commissioners to the Penobscots with instructions to issue a proclamation of King
George, demand an oath of allegiance, and encourage the Penobscot to come and
trade at Annapolis Royal. The Penobscot representative responded by refusing to
swear loyalty to any king, arguing on the contrary that the French king was never
his master. Nor would they go to Port Royal to trade, it being too far a distance to
travel; the English, however, were welcome to come to the open harbours of the
60                                 Homelands and Empires


Penobscot to trade. Finally, the Penobscot chief refused to acknowledge British ter-
ritorial control. “I do not like to be told that my land is under the authority of Port
Royal,” he responded, “I am the only master of this land given me by God, and I
depend on no one.”59 While the Penobscot wanted only peace, they would permit
no one to build forts in the Dawnland without approval.
   Unlike the British, who claimed authority over Nova Scotia but remained
trapped behind the crumbling walls of Annapolis Royal, the Wabanaki were able
to follow through on their threats. Six months after the commissioners met with
the Penobscot a group of Cape Sable Mi’kmaq attacked British ships and took the
men hostage. “The Indians say the lands are theirs,” one merchant reported, “and
they can make warr and peace when they please it’s feared they are animated
to do what they do by the French at Cape Britton.”60 Indigenous expressions of
geographic control over Mi’kma’ki were more than military threats; disrupting
trade and capturing merchant vessels hindered economic exchange in the region
and exacted a tangible price on what Indigenous peoples believed to be European
interlopers.61 This economic penalty was evidence of Mi’kmaw territorial juris-
diction. Claimed space could be controlled through a variety of methods, includ-
ing trade. By limiting the successful establishment of “corridors and enclaves
­of imperial control,” the Mi’kmaq maintained their “realm of sovereignty” in the
 face of European expansion.62
   While militarily superior, the Wabanaki recognized the importance of trade and
 were not opposed to sharing resources with the British on Indigenous terms. They
 were more likely to dictate terms in Mi’kma’ki – with its small British population
 and weak military presence – than in New England, where demographic changes
 had limited Indigenous military effectiveness. At a 1713 meeting in the Dawnland,
 the governor of Massachusetts explained to a group of Eastern Abenaki what had
 happened during the treaty negotiations in Europe: France had ceded to Britain
 much of the northeast and the English expected to hunt and fish in peace. The
 governor cautioned the Indigenous peoples from entering certain areas for fear of
 inciting a violent response from settlers still angry over Indigenous attacks during
 the war. A Wabanaki delegate responded to English claims by dismissing France’s
 territorial authority:

     You say … that the French gave you Plaisance, Port Royal and its surroundings. France
     can surrender what it likes; for me, I have my land that I have given to no one, that I
     will not give. I want always to be the master of this land. I know its limits, and when
     someone wants to live here they will pay.63

The Abenaki stated clearly that they were aware of their land’s “limits” and that
they would not suffer unwelcome intrusions, but, in contradistinction to British
views of private property, the delegate continued to assure the governor that as
long as there was enough water, game, and fish the English were welcome to take
what they needed.64 Just a century before, English leaders had made similar (though
less just) arguments. John Winthrop, the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay
Colony, argued for the distinction between the natural right of all men to hold
land in common, and the civil right of men who enclose land. In the early days
of Massachusetts Bay, Winthrop argued “if we leave [the Indigenous peoples]
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                           61


sufficient [land] for their use, we may lawfully take the rest, there being more than
enough for them and us.”65 As English acquisitiveness came to drive Indigenous
policy, Winthrop’s dictum was exposed as an obvious ploy to dispossess his
Indigenous neighbours. Yet the Wabanaki continued to hope for peaceful and prof-
itable coexistence on shared territory. If problems arose, however, the Wabanaki
would perhaps reconsider their offer.
   In 1716, the Wulstukwiuk responded to British land claims in a similar fash-
ion. Officials at Annapolis Royal indicated that the Saint John River valley in
Wulstukwik was always part of Acadia and therefore was now part of Nova Scotia.
The Wulstukwiuk replied that the land in question had always belonged to them,
and in fact they were never subjects of the French king but only allies.66 Their logic
here seems clear: no nation could surrender its allies’ land, and therefore Britain
had no claim to the western coast of the Bay of Fundy. The Wulstukwiuk joined
their Abenaki neighbours at a Boston conference a few months later to stand to-
gether against the English. The meeting’s goal, as far as the Boston governor was
concerned, was to form an English-Abenaki alliance; however, the Chief of the
Narantsouak, Ouaourené, was very firm in his desires. Père Rale, who reported
the meeting to Vaudreuil, noted that the Wabanaki would never allow the British
to settle within the limits they had set out.67
   The French missionaries and traders built networks that connected various
Acadian pales within Indigenous homelands, providing them with a distinct ad-
vantage over the land-hungry English. Missionaries were important figures in
Wulstukwik, the Dawnland, and Mi’kma’ki. The first arrived in the early seven-
teenth century and a network of itinerant priests developed over the following
decades, many of whom provided the French court with important information
about the local Indigenous peoples.68 A memorial concerning the missions among
the Mi’kmaq (dated 1715 but likely written in the 1730s) ensured that French of-
ficials were aware of the location and strength of the Indigenous peoples. There
were about 600 Mi’kmaq capable of carrying arms – presumably a rough estimate
of the male population over the age of twelve – and this group was divided into
several villages across Mi’kma’ki and Unama’ki.69 The memoir stressed that trust-
ed missionaries instructed the Mi’kmaq in the Catholic religion; Father Gaulin
had gone so far as to translate religious lessons into the Mi’kmaw language.70 The
missionaries themselves were stationed in a few key villages – Mariguaouguiche,
Malpec, and Shubenacadie – but the demands of their calling required they travel
great distances to serve the various groups.71
   Religion was important to the Mi’kmaq-French alliance, but the French had to
combine spiritual instruction, trade, and a tacit recognition of Mi’kmaw author-
ity to maintain access to Mi’kma’ki. Missionaries discovered that raising a church
and presbytery would not attract the Mi’kmaq if the location made hunting and
fishing difficult.72 The Mi’kmaq and their allies were also accustomed to receiv-
ing gifts, and would not hide their displeasure if one year’s presents were less
bountiful than those previous. The French feared that Indigenous dissatisfaction
could lead to disunion, and the Mi’kmaq were too valuable an ally to lose.73 Part of
the problem, argued Gaulin, was the geographic realities faced by the missionar-
ies. The Mi’kmaq were spread widely across Mi’kma’ki, from Chedabucto in the
north to Cape Sable in the south. At least one or two long trips were required each
62                                  Homelands and Empires


year to dispense presents and hold religious meetings, which required priests to
travel over the rocky interior and along the several principal river systems that cut
through the peninsula. By 1719 there was a concern that the English, who had been
making overtures to the Wabanaki, would win them over.74
   The French, aware that the Mi’kmaq and their allies could become as dangerous
enemies as they were valued allies, were forced to recognize Wabanaki sovereign-
ty over their homelands (perhaps superficially, likely begrudgingly) by support-
ing their right to much of the land and thus extending French territorial control by
proxy. Such a policy required careful diplomacy. In 1718, Intendant Bégon wrote
a memoir on the limits of New France and Acadia in which he argued that the
English had no right to the lands beyond the peninsula. Citing old maps, Bégon
argued that though the English cartographers attempted to colour the stretch of
land from Beaubassin to the St George River as part of New Scotland, the majority
of old maps marked the region as New France.75 After explaining the importance
to France of maintaining this stretch of land, he admitted,

     it is true that the Abenaki and Maliceet spread throughout this region claim that they
     are its first possessors, that the lands belong to them, and it is for this reason that on
     the enclosed map the region is marked as “Abenakis land,” but the 15th article of the
     peace [Treaty of Utrecht] notes that commissioners will regulate exactly and distinctly
     which Indigenous peoples will become subjects of France, and which will become sub-
     jects of Great Britain.76

For the French, geographic knowledge generally and maps specifically became
the conduit for successful double diplomacy. By simply adding Indigenous place
names to indicate their homelands, maps could limit European geographic fictions
by noting the presence of Indigenous territory. Like the British, local French offi-
cials told their superiors one thing and their allies another.
   French maps of northeastern North America produced in the early-eighteenth
century often emphasized the region’s Indigenous inhabitants and provided their
homelands with a cartographic existence. Henri Chatelain’s 1719 map illustrates
the complex and overlapping nature of imperial fictions and Indigenous home-
lands (figure 2.4).77 French-British lands are clearly divided at the Kennebec, but the
geographer has stretched the word “Acadie” across the Bay of Fundy and into the
region that France claimed was always considered Canada, not Acadia. However,
the map’s second most prominent typology is that of the region’s Indigenous peo-
ples, including “les micmaques” and “souriquois” (Mi’kmaw ancestors) on penin-
sular Nova Scotia; “Nations des Etechemins” (a general term used to describe the
region’s Indigenous inhabitants in the seventeenth century) on the Bay of Fundy’s
west coast; and, behind them, the “Nations des Ebnakis.” Chatelain straddled the
word “Canada” over the St Lawrence to claim the lands extending south from that
river for France. “Canada” nearly meets the word “Etechemins,” and is guarded
from “Nouvelle Angleterre” by the word “Abnakis.” The French and Indigenous
place names serve to hem the British along the eastern seaboard, which over time
became French officials’ primary goal. As a tool of geographic negotiation, this
map militated against British claims to an extended Acadia. Using maps such as
                              Mapping the Spoils of Peace                              63




2.4 Extract from Henri Chatelain’s Carte de la Nouvelle France, 1719. Indigenous toponyms
 feature heavily, serving as an important buffer zone between the French and the British.
          McGill University, W.H. Pugsley Collection, G3400 1719 C5 RBD Map.


Chatelain’s, the French could argue that Indigenous territory might not be French,
but neither was it British.
   A British map produced four years earlier demonstrates what little attention
Herman Moll, a British geographer of German origin, paid to the Indigenous pres-
ence in northeastern North America (figure 2.5). Compared with the Chatelain
map, Moll’s Acadia was deliberately uninhabited, a blank territory to be filled with
British settlers. Not surprising is the fact that Moll stretched the word “Acadia”
from just east of Casco Bay almost to the Isthmus of Chignecto. He also boldly
claims the land south of the St Lawrence River by beginning “New Scotland”
just south of Quebec, and “New England” just south of Trois-Rivières. Whereas
Chatelain’s map employed the anachronistic “Port Royal” to refer to the Acadian
capital, Moll’s Nova Scotia features “Annapolis Royal.” He also replaced “Baye
François” with “Fundi Bay.” These maps influenced how the public imagined
these regions, so the placement of names, the inclusion or exclusion of Indigenous
peoples, and the use of English or French toponyms imbued the map with a par-
ticular vision. As Denis Reinhartz has argued, mapmakers were concerned about
border disputes, and maps could shape both official policy and public opinion.
“Moll’s maps,” according to Reinhartz, “reached many who could not read and
made immediate strong impressions on those who could.”78 Maps hoped to depict
and thus reify the imperial fictions that British and French authorities were creat-
ing in the northeast.
64                             Homelands and Empires




2.5 Extract from Herman Moll’s A New and Exact Map … of North America, 1715. Regional
Natives are almost non-existent, and Acadia is marked along the disputed coastal region.
                  Dalhousie Special Collections, Map 48 (Morse) 1715.


   The Wabanaki did not have recourse to these maps, but they offered logical ar-
guments against British land appropriation. In a 1720 letter to Governor Philipps,
the Wabanaki made an obvious yet powerful point: they argued that if they want-
ed to move to England they would do so only after receiving permission from
the English. The British faced Indigenous resistance and aggression in Mi’kma’ki
because they had not asked for permission to settle and because they had dis-
rupted the peace.79 In the years following the Treaty of Utrecht, it was with such
clarity and logic that the Mi’kmaq expressed their disapproval of British encroach-
ment. French priests were clearly involved in writing letters on Indigenous peo-
ples’ behalf and must have influenced certain elements of their resistance, yet the
Wabanaki had their own motivations and goals, and, importantly, they were will-
ing to defend their homelands in the face of challenges from both the British and
the French. Though this resistance was common in North America, Nova Scotia’s
case was unique because there were so few British settlers. Settlements from New
England to the Carolinas grew quickly and were therefore more successful in quell-
ing Indigenous opposition.80 In the northeast, the events of the 1720s provided the
                            Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          65


Wabanaki with ample opportunity to assert their territorial control in the face of
French-British negotiations over the limits of an imaginary Acadia.

                                     •••
The 1720s witnessed an increased desire to settle boundaries and establish territo-
rial sovereignty in Europe and northeastern North America. The Treaty of Utrecht
had brought to a close the most recent imperial conflict, but undefined borders con-
tributed to violent clashes. Administrators wanted to settle the disputes and con-
centrate on reorganizing finances and military strength in Europe, and developing
trade in North America. The pattern of double diplomacy continued; European
officials argued over maps while administrators in Nova Scotia faced increased
Indigenous resistance and hostility. Examining geographic negotiations in Europe
and similar attempts at reconciliation in the northeast demonstrates how “double
diplomacy” operated in the specific case of boundary negotiations. Officials in the
northeast tempered European designs because they recognized that Indigenous
homelands could not easily be transformed into imperial territory. European maps
that emphasized boundary lines favourable to one side or the other could not pre-
vent the Mi’kmaq and their allies from exerting geographic control over the north-
east. At best, these maps and surveys provided administrators with an image of
their imperial fictions from which they could argue de jure possession. It was the
geographic negotiations that took place locally that established agreements and
limited conflict.
   As early as 1718, the Board of Trade was fielding requests to address the bound-
ary issues in Nova Scotia. Governor Richard Philipps suggested that metropoli-
tan officials establish a commission to examine the Treaty of Utrecht and set the
limits of Nova Scotia and New France.81 That same year at Louisbourg, which
at the time was a fishing village inhabited by officials and settlers transplanted
from Plaisance and Port Royal, the governor, Joseph de Monbeton de Brouillan, dit
Saint-Ovide, gathered an assembly of French and English inhabitants to discuss
territorial boundaries at the time of the Treaty of Utrecht.82 The following spring,
Governor Vaudreuil was informed that the king of France had charged his ambas-
sador in England with the same task. The French at Quebec were especially con-
cerned with English settlements in the Saint John River valley, which they wanted
removed. The king reminded Vaudreuil that Britain and France were at peace and
demanded that he be prudent in his actions towards the English.83 In 1719 the
Board of Trade was informed that one of its members, Martin Bladen, had been
named along with Daniel Pulteney to the boundary commission that would meet
in Paris.84 Bladen owed his position on the Board of Trade to his connections with
Thomas Pelham-Holles, the duke of Newcastle, a favour returned with twenty-
nine years of service.85 Pulteney was serving as a commissioner of trade in France
when he was appointed to the negotiation.86
   Attempts to settle matters in Paris came on the heels of an unsuccessful local
negotiation over the possession of Canso. Due to its increasing value as a fishery
and competing imperial claims to authority, Canso quickly gained Atlantic signifi-
cance. The British claimed the region, but the French, supported by the Mi’kmaq,
continued to fish in the area. Tensions between the British in Nova Scotia and
66                            Homelands and Empires


New England and the French at Île Royale increased, and in 1718 Massachusetts
governor Samuel Shute sent Captain Thomas Smart to destroy the French fishing
houses. He not only destroyed the huts, but he also captured two large French
ships. In 1720, Governor Saint-Ovide de Brouillan permitted a reprisal during
which French merchants and the Mi’kmaq took £18,000 from the British. These
sanctioned acts of privateering indicated that the region was valuable enough to
protect with military force. Richard Philipps staged a military occupation of Canso
to strengthen British possession.87 As the site of a valuable fishery, and situated
precariously (or so many thought) between Nova Scotia and Île Royale, Canso
came to represent the larger geographic conflicts surrounding Acadia’s unde-
fined boundaries. In 1719, Governor Shute of Massachusetts sent Captain Smart
and Captain Southack to Île Royale to meet with Governor Saint-Ovide and dis-
cuss the limits of Acadia. Shute informed Smart that Southack knew the regional
boundaries better than anyone and possessed a good chart of the area.88 This was
likely the map Southack had prepared in 1718 that would later become The New
England Coasting Pilot, published sometime in the 1720s or early 1730s.89 Dedicated
to Francis Nicholson, who was the governor of South Carolina at that time, The
New England Coasting Pilot consisted of various coastal charts and lists of distances
between locations. The title page boasted that it would be “of great Advantage in
this Part to the Navigation of North America,” and also noted that the author “has
been Cruizing in the service of the Crown of Great Britain Twenty-two Years.”90
Neither the map nor the surveyor’s pedigree impressed Saint-Ovide, who wrote
to Shute after the meeting arguing that the compass points on the British map
were unequal. Others who evaluated the map after its publication were less dip-
lomatic: “A very coarse and erroneous draught,” one 1755 review noted; a 1749
appraisal concluded “his large chart of the coast of Nova Scotia and New England
being one continued error, and a random performance, maybe be of pernicious
consequence in trade and navigation; therefore it ought to be publickly adver-
tised as such and destroy’d wherever it is found amongst sea charts.”91 So much
for twenty-two years of service. Regardless, it was impossible for Southack and
Saint-Ovide to reach an agreement working from the available maps. Taking just
one cartographic example, Saint-Ovide noted that following the rhumb lines, the
British could claim parts of Cape Breton and the French possessed areas around
St. Mary River.92 Saint-Ovide concluded by offering to remove all French settlers
and fishermen from the region until the issue was settled in Europe, provided the
English would do the same.
   Maps of Canso produced locally and imperially were causing problems that
had to be resolved with actions on the ground. In 1719, Governor Philipps arrived
at Annapolis Royal and shortly after travelled to Canso to oversee the construc-
tion of fortifications that would help protect New England fishing vessels from
French privateers. The Mi’kmaq continued to harass the British; one conflict re-
sulted in more than twenty Mi’kmaw deaths, and five Mi’kmaw heads were post-
ed on spikes around the fort.93 The British were convinced that the French were
behind the attacks, and Philipps doubted gifts would prevent future violence. He
informed Secretary Crags in 1720 that he had done his best with the Mi’kmaq and
given them £150 out of his own pocket, although he doubted that even £100,000
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                           67


could win the Mi’kmaq from the French.94 In fact, the group that had plundered
Canso in 1720 then returned to Minas and attacked and looted another English
ship. Exasperated, Philipps informed the Board of Trade that he had written to
the Acadians asking why they had not tried to stop the Minas attack, “which is all
I can do in my present circumstances.”95 Philipps’s attempts to fortify the region
concerned Saint-Ovide. “This affair [the boundaries] holds all the new colonies in
a state of unrest,” he wrote, “both nations equally desire to possess Canso and its
eastern coast which is without question the best and most abundant fishery.” 96
   These negotiations had not officially begun when they started to break down
over cartographic confusion. Bladen and Pulteney were sent to spar with much
higher ranking French officials: Victor-Marie d’Estrées, the maréchal de France
and former mentor of Comte Toulouse; and Abbé Guillaume Dubois, a cardinal-
minister with a knack for making peace who so annoyed the diarist and court
gossip Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon, that he allegedly hung a portrait of
Dubois in his bathroom.97 What required attention was how the geographic loca-
tion of Canso related to the wording of the Treaty of Utrecht. In 1719 Abbé Dubois
sent a coloured map of Cape Breton and its surroundings (figure 2.6) to James
Craggs, secretary of the Lord Justices. Dubois claimed that the map clearly indi-
cated that Canso was separated from Nova Scotia by water, and must therefore be
considered an island located in the mouth and Gulf of the St Lawrence. Like other
islands so situated, according to the Treaty of Utrecht, it belonged to France.98 The
map below, though unattributed, must be what Dubois sent Craggs. Now held in
the National Archives at Kew, the map’s author is unlisted and the date is estimat-
ed to be 1715–19. The accompanying text explains why Canso falls under French
authority: “The Island of Canceau cut into several channels, is a dependence of the
island called Cape Breton, according to the thirteenth article of the peace treaty.”
The description continues to note that the French were the first to inhabit Canso,
with the English arriving only within the previous two years. Dubois must have
believed that this map and the didactic text offered an unassailable French claim.
   Craggs was not convinced. The Board of Trade commissioned a report on Canso
to determine the validity of French claims. Not surprisingly, given the malleabil-
ity of geographic arguments, Canso was described as distant from both Cape
Breton and the Gulf of the St Lawrence. The French map that placed Canso within
French territory was not impartial, according to the report, but favoured France’s
claim to the fishery.99 Moreover, according to the passes issued by Subercase dur-
ing his gubernatorial term at Port Royal, Canso was clearly included in what the
French called l’Acadie. As the negotiations progressed, Britain continued to coun-
ter French maps with reports from Nova Scotia, illustrating both the weakness
of British mapping capabilities and the ease with which French maps could be
dismissed as overtly biased. The Board of Trade sought out additional sources
to support their claim to Canso, or at least to weaken French pretensions. In late
1719 the Board sent a letter to the Bishop of London, referring to the twelfth article
of the Treaty of Utrecht by which France was to cede to Britain all of Nova Scotia
and Acadia. On the day the treaty was ratified, the French king was to deliver of-
ficial letters concerning the land transfer to Queen Anne.100 The Board requested
that the Bishop inform them if he had, or had seen, any of these letters. If so, the
2.6 No author, no date [likely map Dubois sent to Craggs, 1719]. Coloured map of division between Acadia and Cape Breton,
                   with explanation of France’s claim to Canso. National Archives, London, MPG1/174.
                            Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          69


Board requested copies at the earliest convenience. The Bishop replied, assuring
the Board that he did indeed have copies of the succession papers signed by the
French king, and that he would forward copies immediately.101
  The treaty and related maps were separate yet complementary; both could be
misread or misinterpreted. In the final preparations for the boundary meetings,
Charles Delafaye, who had replaced Craggs as secretary to the Lords Justices, pro-
vided the Board of Trade with letters of instruction for Pulteney and Bladen. The
negotiations’ importance was made quite clear, as, once settled, British and French
subjects would be restricted to the territory granted to their nation.102 The Lords
Justices knew where the boundary should fall and they referred to maps outlining
their desired borders and instructed their commissaries to settle the limits accord-
ingly.103 The British were not wholly without cartographic evidence, though their
arsenal of maps was but a fraction of France’s. There was one last concern raised
by the Lords Justices: the language of the Treaty of Utrecht. Aware that France
was claiming Canso, the Lords Justices reminded Pulteney and Bladen not to al-
low France to use the French version of the treaty if it provided them with more
land than the Latin translation.104 Maps, and the language used to inform their
particular meaning as it related to the Treaty of Utrecht, dominated the short and
ultimately fruitless boundary negotiations that followed.
  Meetings weren’t scheduled to begin until late summer 1720, and in the mean-
time British officials attempted to cobble together maps and surveys that might
help their cause. A month before the discussions began the Board of Trade wrote
to Governor Philipps to inform him that the limits of Nova Scotia had not yet
been set, but that they believed them to begin at the St Croix River, extend north-
wards up that river towards the St Lawrence, along the St Lawrence to Cap-
des-Rosiers, down through the Gut of Canso, out to Cape Sable, and then across
the Bay of Fundy on a northwest course to St Croix.105 The Board must have real-
ized how inadequate their geographic image of Nova Scotia was, because one
week later the members sent a letter to the Lords Justices pressuring them to
send a surveyor to Nova Scotia to complete a full survey of the region.106 British
authorities had stalled and, as the boundary commissioners would soon learn,
they were woefully unprepared to challenge French maps with a cartographic
catalogue of their own.
  The production of maps was a difficult task and required skills that only few in
North America (or Europe) possessed. Even when a capable surveyor was avail-
able, any number of complications could prevent the successful mapping of un-
known territory. Canso had become something of an amorphous geographic entity
as far as the British and the French were concerned; its importance to claiming a
valuable area of Nova Scotia’s east coast serves as a perfect example of the very
basic challenges that could stand in the way of producing a map. Because Canso
was a popular fishing station, and because several English captains had spent time
in the region, Philipps received in 1720 a fairly detailed map of the region as sur-
veyed by Captain Southack (figure 2.7). The map includes water soundings, not-
ing the depth “in fathoms at low water on Spring tides.” Southack included the
geographic hazards in the regions, such as dry rocks and low-water marks, but
he was also careful to provide the region with a distinctly English character. On
Canso Island, Southack provided the exact location of fishing stages, houses, and
2.7 Captain Southack’s The Harbour and Islands of Canso, 1720. The region’s importance as a British fishery is demonstrated clearly
                               in this map. Library and Archives Canada, H2/240/Canso/1720.
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                           71


areas of “French intruders.” There can be no mistaking the importance of this re-
gion, as Southack included an inset of a fishing boat hauling in large cod.107
   Completing a new map of Nova Scotia’s Atlantic coast, including Canso, quick-
ly became an almost comedic exercise in futility. In May of 1720 Governor Philipps
sent a letter to the Board of Ordnance suggesting that the seat of government be
moved from Annapolis to Nova Scotia’s Atlantic coast to provide a more seclud-
ed and protected placement. He noted, though, that the Board’s desire for a sur-
vey of the coast would require a sloop to facilitate the process. Paul Mascarene, a
military officer and engineer who would later serve as lieutenant governor, was
capable of undertaking the task, so Philipps decided to appoint him to the local
boundary commission that would meet at Île Royale to settle the Canso matter; he
could simply make a survey of the area at the same time.108 Mascarene wrote to the
Board of Ordnance two days later, hinting at only one of the problems that could
prevent a timely survey. “The continual rains and bad weather we have had since
our arrival here,” he complained, “have hindered me hitherto from using my plain
table.”109 As it turns out, inclement weather, while not uncommon in Nova Scotia,
would be the least of the surveyor’s problems.
   The first challenge Philipps and Mascarene faced in completing their survey
was finding a suitable ship. The history of a survey ship, the William Augustus,
which was named after the third and youngest son of George II, recounts just how
difficult completing a survey (for local or imperial purposes) could be. There were
no sloops of appropriate size available in Nova Scotia, so Mascarene was sent to
Boston to “hasten” the construction of a ship.110 The ship arrived months later than
Philipps had wanted, and he was left with little time to do any surveying in Nova
Scotia. During the late summer and early fall of 1721, Philipps and Mascarene
undertook only a cursory survey of part of the coast from which they created a
rough map that was sent to the secretary of state. Plans to perfect the survey were
put on hold when the William Augustus was sent to Annapolis Royal to perform
other duties. When the sloop returned to Canso in December it was in bad shape,
having lost its anchor and split its sails. After minor repairs, the William Augustus
was used to transfer some of the garrison from Placentia to Nova Scotia. When this
task was completed, in August of 1722, the ship was in even worse condition and
unable to serve as a surveyor’s sloop.
   To compound the issue, Canso had recently been attacked by Mi’kmaw men
who had taken English vessels. The William Augustus was then called to duty to
counter this attack, and with two other armed vessels the British reclaimed all the
stolen ships and killed several of the Mi’kmaq. At the close of these hostilities, the
ship was sent to Boston for refitting and returned to Annapolis Royal in December.
For reasons unknown, the survey remained on hold, and the ship was laid up in
August of 1723.111 Two years later, Lawrence Armstrong, Nova Scotia’s lieuten-
ant governor and a difficult man who quarrelled with Philipps over a variety of
matters but shared the general idea that Canso was important, wrote the Board of
Trade and informed them that the ship William Augustus was in very poor condi-
tion, and asked if the vessel should be refitted to serve the province.112 Apparently
Armstrong received no advice on the matter, for two years later Philipps himself
wrote to the Board of Trade to update them on the state of Nova Scotia’s defenc-
es. Aside from the usual complaints of a weak fort and insufficient armaments,
                               Homelands and Empires


Philipps noted that the entire region needed an improved communication system.
He mentioned that there was a ship that had been laid up for four years, and asked
if the Board would be willing to refit the vessel as a communication ship.113
   By the mid 1720s, the Board of Trade’s focus had shifted away from Nova Scotia
and thus it is not surprising that Armstrong and Philipps received no final instruc-
tions for the ship. Aside from a 1722 letter in which the Board announced their
pleasure that a ship had been found for the survey, the William Augustus seemed
to matter very little to administrators in London.114 What the life of this ship il-
lustrates, however, is that there were practical realities that prevented the timely
surveying of Nova Scotia. There were soldiers to transport, provisions to secure,
and enemies to fight. The Board might announce that they needed new and better
maps, but their geographic desires often extended beyond the reach of surveying
capabilities. These limits to local navigation and communication capabilities, and
restrictions on surveying and mapping, need to be understood in the context of
wider Atlantic networks. Ian K. Steele has described the Atlantic Ocean as a high-
way that was crossed with increasing safety and regularity over the seventeenth
and eighteenth century, allowing settlers in British North America to remain in
contact with Britain.115 Once in North America, however, new networks were re-
quired to create spaces of empire to complement the Atlantic highway. To control
the coasts and inland waterways, European powers first had to negotiate with
Indigenous peoples to travel through and map them.116 These dependent spaces –
the Atlantic highway and the local coasts and rivers – represented two arteries of
imperial control. Yet mastery of the former did not guarantee control over the lat-
ter. Practical realities (such as securing a vessel) and outside forces (such as Indig-
enous maritime control) were major obstacles to securing claimed imperial space.
   Before the trials of the William Augustus lost the attention of the Board of Trade,
the ultimate goal of securing useful surveys of Nova Scotia to use against the
French occasioned a swift correspondence between the Lords Justices to the Board
of Trade. Expanding state activity, which included increased attention to overseas
possessions and delicate imperial diplomacy with France, led to an increased de-
sire for information about government actions and administrative regulation.117
There was bound to be some administrative overlap. Not two months after the
Board of Trade asked the Lords Justices for a surveyor to be sent to Nova Scotia, the
Lords Justices requested maps of Nova Scotia to aid Pulteney in Paris. Specifically,
Pulteney wanted to know the location of Sable Island and if Canso was attached
to Nova Scotia, as the British claimed it was, or if it was an island.118 The Board of
Trade had one map, but it was of little help. The 1715 map sent from Annapolis
Royal by Lieutenant Governor Caulfeild featured sites of French fortifications (ex-
tant or planned), a rough outline of Cape Breton, and Canso coloured as a French
possession (figure 2.8).
   If maps could not advance the arguments desired by British officials, perhaps
language could. Pulteney explained a point of crucial importance that tied territo-
rial knowledge and mapping to the perceived differences between the French and
Latin translations of the Treaty of Utrecht. The French argued that Canso was an
island, and therefore was not attached to Nova Scotia and should be considered
French territory. The British responded by citing a passage of the treaty that ceded
to Britain lands dependent on granted land.119 Unsatisfied with that response, the
2.8 Map of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, included in Lieutenant Caulfeild’s letter to the Board of Trade, 1 November 1715.
           Note that Canso (beside the compass) is coloured green as a French possession. H3/201/1715 LAC.
