                              Homelands and Empires


French attempted to favour the French translation of the treaty, which they ar-
gued granted all islands within the mouth of the Gulf of St Lawrence to France. In
contrast, the Latin version granted the French islands within the mouth of the St
Lawrence River and in the Gulf of St Lawrence.120 This was an important distinc-
tion because it could be argued that the mouth of the Gulf extended beyond the
limits that the British were willing to cede to France. The exact position of Canso,
and its definition as either an island on the coast of the Gulf of St Lawrence or the
Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, was now at the heart of the boundary dispute.
   Considering the value of the Canso fishery, it is not surprising that the French
attempted to claim the region as its possession. Pulteney reported that at the con-
ference the French agreed not to fish within thirty leagues east of Sable Island and
presented a map of those fishing boundaries. On the map they had drawn a line
starting thirty leagues east of Sable Island and travelling southeast. A second line
extended directly west from Sable Island to Nova Scotia hitting the province well
south of Canso, thereby leaving the region open to French fishing. The French
commissioners supported this boundary by arguing that France had established
governors at Cape Canso, which meant it was not part of Acadia and had therefore
never been surrendered to the British.121 Sir Robert Sutton, a British plenipoten-
tiary in Paris, summarized the meeting as a tumultuous encounter meant only to
provide the French with an opportunity to justify their possession of the fishery at
Canso. According to Sutton, France’s commissaries had even created false maps
to support their arguments.122 The British realized that the French were attempting
to deceive them, but proving the inaccuracy of French maps would be difficult.
   The French were in an equally difficult position about the importance of Canso
and the delicate peace that had to be maintained with Britain. They also faced the
added task of balancing relations with the Mi’kmaq and their allies, which entailed
continued gift-giving and military support while simultaneously distancing them-
selves from any Indigenous attacks on the British. The French were well aware
of Canso’s value as a fishery as well as its strategic geographic location. For this
reason, French administrators at Louisbourg closely monitored the British actions
on the islands. After the British attack at Canso in 1718, Saint-Ovide sent an emis-
sary to Boston to plead their case and demand restitution, but early diplomatic
efforts were unsuccessful.123 Appeals to Boston continued even while both nations
discussed Canso in Paris.
   For the French at Île Royale, Indigenous resistance to British pales in Mi’kma’ki
complicated matters. While the French were required to maintain their friendship
with the Indigenous peoples to ensure trade and prevent the Mi’kmaq and their
allies from forming an alliance with the English, Saint-Ovide was unable to im-
pose restrictions on what the Mi’kmaq could do with the presents they received.
In 1720, he met with about 100 Mi’kmaq to discuss the state of their relationship
and heard about the difficulties they faced as a result of declining gifts. Shortly
after, Saint-Ovide received an English visitor who informed him that the Mi’kmaq
had pillaged Canso and forced many of its English inhabitants to flee. Saint-Ovide
informed the officer that he was horrified at the news, and would do whatever he
could to bring those responsible to justice. He then reassured the British officer
that the French were in no way involved in these hostilities, admitting that the
Mi’kmaq followed only the orders of their chiefs.124
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          75


   The tensions in Mi’kma’ki meant that much was riding on the discussions in
Paris. While both sides relied on maps as evidence, each accused the other of forg-
ery. The French were as wary of British maps as the British were of French maps.
Père Joseph Aubery, a Jesuit missionary, warned French officials at Versailles, “the
English have falsified a map by placing Nova Scotia from the St. George River to
Beaubassin,” even though older maps never accorded this space to the English.125
Aubery, who lived and worked among the Wulstukwiuk along the Wulstukw
River, had been interested in resolving the Acadian boundary to ensure the English
didn’t extend into Indigenous territory. In 1715 he wrote to his superiors in France
and argued that Acadia was peninsular Nova Scotia, and that the division between
New England and New France should run along the high grounds from a fort at
Pemaquid on the Atlantic.126 While his proposal had no lasting influence, he con-
tinued to send maps to France in the hopes of protecting French and Indigenous
land from the English. After warning of altered or inaccurate British maps, French
administrators and religious figures dispatched a flurry of French maps to bolster
their claims. One was a map that claimed to place Canso on the French side of the
line drawn from Sable Island to the peninsula, as expressed in the Treaty of Utrecht;
another map demonstrated that Canso and the islands of that name were separated
from the mainland by an arm of water, positioned in the Gulf of the St Lawrence,
and therefore belonged to France.127
   The Board of Trade was eager to secure Canso for Britain and had to deal with
the problems that French maps were causing. Days after Pulteney and Sutton’s
letters reached Britain, the Board wrote to the Lords Justices outlining what they
knew and reminded the Lords of Britain’s cartographic paucity. The Board empha-
sized that Francis Nicholson and Samuel Vetch – the men who had captured Port
Royal in 1710 – had agreed that Canso was part of Nova Scotia. Unfortunately for
the Board, however, neither man could provide any more material for Pulteney.
They had no dependable maps of the region in their possession, and when they
requested some from the Admiralty they learned they had none either. The Board
pleaded once again with the Lords Justices to send a surveyor to North America
to make a map of the colonies. The French had completed this task and were reap-
ing its benefits, while the British remained in the dark.128 The British had not ad-
equately mapped the territory and therefore could not bring it into their sphere of
control, nor could they present a rigorous challenge to French maps. The French
king supported his commissioners’ claim to Canso because their maps argued it
was not part of Nova Scotia, because it was separated by an arm of water like that
dividing Île Royale from Nova Scotia.129 Pulteney himself informed the Board of
Trade that some Englishmen in the Canso region agreed that it was separated by
water as claimed by the French; therefore, the British would be wise to stake their
claim on the fact that Canso, even if an island, lay outside the Gulf of St Lawrence.
   As the debate over these competing fictions persisted, some French officials
wanted to restrict the limits of Acadia to weaken the British argument for its
imagined Nova Scotia. These efforts persisted even after the negotiations at Paris
ended. Abbé Jean Bobé, a Parisian cleric and member of the duc d’Orléans’s en-
tourage, wrote a memoir in 1723 on the limits of France’s possessions in North
America. When discussing Acadia, Bobé stressed that Port Royal was in fact part
of southern New France, not part of Acadia. He emphasized the need to influence
76                                 Homelands and Empires


how people envisioned or imagined Acadia, employing cartographic imagery to
support his argument. “In order to destroy these frivolous and unjust pretensions
of the English,” Bobé contended,

     I request that the trouble may be taken to read in the Memoir on the boundaries that I
     had the honor to present to Count de Toulouse what I state there to prove that Acadia,
     according to its ancient limits ceded by France, does not include all the imaginary
     Nova Scotia, but only all that is embraced between the South Coast of the Peninsula
     and a straight line drawn from Cape Forchu to Cape Campseau exclusively.130

It was clear to Bobé that because England had been ceded Port Royal and Acadia,
the former was not within the bounds of the latter. While these arguments had
little impact in the early 1720s, a map influenced by Bobé’s interpretation was to
cause quite a stir during the 1750–54 Acadia boundary negotiations.131 Despite the
conflicting interpretations of boundaries and land claims, the entire European ne-
gotiation was moot. Actions on the ground would determine who controlled the
region and what de facto boundaries would be established.
   Focus shifted from Canso specifically to determining the boundaries of Acadia
generally, which had been the original task of the commissioners sent to meet at
Paris. Despite fruitless negotiations in the French capital, local and imperial figures
persisted in searching for Acadia’s limits. Père Aubery sent “to the Court a map
more exact than any seen before, with a memoir to inform about the disposition
of these Acadian lands.”132 His efforts went unnoticed and in 1720 he wrote again
to stress his point: if France lost those lands they would also lose their Indigenous
allies who lived there.133 A second memoir reminded French officials that previous
governors in Acadia had interviewed Acadians who lived in the province in 1685
who could attest to the fact that Acadia was always considered only the penin-
sula. In fact, the 80-year-old Sieur Petitpas claimed that from 1604 to 1624, Acadia
was the stretch of land from LaHave to Minas and the rest was Indigenous home-
lands, “the country of the Etchemins, also of New France, just to the Kenebec, as
now there are no more Etchemins.”134 The report continued to note that LaHave to
Canso to the Gaspé was also considered New France.135
   Aware of Britain’s extended claims to Nova Scotia based on Sir William
Alexander’s grants, the French relied on the contention that settlement and im-
provement of lands in the Americas trumped paper grants or claims.136 Learning of
Philipps’s plans to fortify Canso would have been especially provocative in light
of this view. The French could challenge cartographic claims in official discussions,
but they were forced to respond in kind to news of British fortification efforts. By
the spring of 1722, officials in France issued an order to strengthen fortifications in
Île Royale. “We propose,” the order stated, “that without interrupting the fortifica-
tion of Louisbourg, measures should be taken to fortify … Port Dauphin.”137 The
same orders recommended improving the fortifications at Port Toulouse, which
was closer to Canso. To this end the French could amass strength along the coast
to counter the efforts of the English.138 As negotiations faltered in Paris, the French
and the British maintained a façade of peace while preparing for war.
   Though both sides kept a watchful eye on each other, the Mi’kmaq and some of
their allies were reasserting their territorial control while others were open to peace
                               Mapping the Spoils of Peace                                  77


agreements. In August 1720, a group of eleven Mi’kmaq, led by Peter Nun­quadden,
claiming the country as theirs, demanded and received £50 from an English mer-
chant for permission to trade at Minas. By paying the fee and taking no action
against the Mi’kmaq, the merchant (perhaps reluctantly) legitimized the Mi’kmaw
claim to territorial rights.139 Other Indigenous groups did not necessarily sup-
port Mi’kmaw actions. Philipps received letters from the Passamaquoddy and the
Wulstukwiuk reaffirming their desire for peace and distancing themselves from the
Mi’kmaw attacks at Canso. Philipps had in fact met with a group of Wulstuk­wiuk
and put their agreement into writing.140 The Wabanaki might have shared some of
the same goals, but the individual groups could also operate on their own motives
without the support of their neighbours. Yet in times of conflict the Mi’kmaq and
their neighbours were capable of coming together for a common cause.

                                        •••
While imperial negotiators quibbled over degrees of longitude and latitude, and
while local officials raised forts and arms to protect the Canso fishery and as-
serted the boundaries of a fictive Acadia or Nova Scotia, Pierre-François-Xavier
de Charlevoix collected his notes from his first visit to North America between
1705 and 1709. Charlevoix was a Jesuit priest who wrote voluminously on North
America. Voltaire, who was a young pupil at Louis-le-Grand when Charlevoix
was a prefect, remembered the priest as “a bit long winded.”141 Charlevoix spent
many years in North America and in 1719 wrote a report on the Acadian boundar-
ies. Though his account does not survive, extant summaries and references to the
tract indicate that Charlevoix believed Acadia to be the peninsula only, and that
France must ardently defend its right to the coast from the isthmus of Chignecto
to New England.142 During his extensive travels in North America, the Jesuit priest
spent much time documenting Indigenous life and culture. When he finally pub-
lished an account of his travels in 1744 (twenty years after he had completed his
voyage), Charlevoix offered descriptions of Indigenous reactions to English (and
French) encroachment on their territory that depicted the creation of European
pales in Indigenous homelands. Initially, the Abenaki tolerated encroachments;
after the Treaty of Utrecht, however, there began a slow English migration to the
Kennebec River that eventually failed to follow the proper protocol:

  An Englishman asked the Abenakis for permission to build on the banks of their River
  a magazine (storehouse) for trade, promising to sell his merchandise at a much bet-
  ter price than they could get at Boston. The Indians, finding a great advantage in this
  proposition, agreed. Another Englishman, a little later, asked for the same permission,
  offering conditions even more advantageous than offered by the first man, and it was
  again granted. The Indians’ facility emboldened the English; they established them-
  selves in great numbers along the River without troubling themselves to get permis-
  sion from the country’s original inhabitants.143

It was only when the English stopped asking permission that the Abenaki became
angered and demanded to know by what right the English invaded their land.144
It was just these types of incursions that bred conflict in the northeast.
78                                 Homelands and Empires


   By the time Charlevoix’s Histoire et description générale de la Nouvelle France was
published, the Indigenous territorial control that he described had led to no small
amount of conflict in the northeast. Charlevoix foreshadowed some of the looming
conflict in a 1720 tract on Acadia, in which he stated that missionaries informed him
that any plan to move the Abenaki from their land to Île Royale was ill-­advised, as
the Abenaki were attached to their territory.145 Charlevoix recounted a meeting be-
tween Vaudreuil and a group of Abenaki at which the Abenaki requested assistance
in their conflict with the English. The governor assured them that he would provide
weapons and ask other Indigenous peoples to join the cause. The Abenaki respond-
ed by mocking Vaudreuil, taunting him and threatening that if they so desired the
Indigenous peoples could combine their strengths and wipe all Europeans off the
continent. The threat was enough to make Vaudreuil quickly reconsider his offer,
and he assured the Abenaki that if they needed help he would assist them himself.146
   It is not surprising that Charlevoix came to understand North America not as an
imperial hinterland, but as a region of English and French settlements entangled
among much vaster Indigenous spaces and language groups.147 As a visitor and
voyager, Charlevoix saw North America’s European character quickly fade away
as he travelled through extensive homelands. In 1721 Charlevoix noted that the
Algonkian language begins in Acadia, and “makes a circuit of twelve hundred
leagues, turning from the south-east by the north to the south-west.” He continued,

     The Abenaquis, or Conibas bordering upon New England have, for their nearest neigh-
     bours the Etechemins, or Malécites in the country about the river Pentagoet, and fur-
     ther to the east are the Micmaks or Souriquois, whose country is properly Acadia, all
     along the coast of the gulph of St. Laurence as far as Gaspey, whence a certain author
     has called them Gaspesians, as well as the neighbouring islands.148

He noted that the Abenaki claimed most of the northeast coast and the rivers that
met there and suggested that France support them to prevent English encroachment.
   As the Jesuit recorded these impressions in the early 1720s, he couldn’t have
known how close the Wabanaki were to launching a war against the English. Nor
did he think the French were completely safe from Indigenous reprisals, despite
the religious and cultural links they had so carefully nurtured. Charlevoix was
concerned with how the Abenaki would react to French and English land claims,
and he knew that if France angered the Indigenous peoples they could easily side
with the English.149 The Abenaki had already questioned the French missionaries
about France’s right to cede Indigenous land, and the missionaries responded that
Abenaki land was not included in the Utrecht negotiations. Charlevoix recom-
mended settling the limits in the northeast and assuring the Abenaki that if to con-
serve “their country” they must fight the English, the French would join them.150
Charlevoix concluded by calling for quick action, as the Iroquois were already so-
liciting the Abenaki to join them against the French. An English-Abenaki-Iroquois
alliance could only mean the loss of New France.151
   By 1722, tensions between the English and the Abenaki had erupted into war.
Saint-Ovide and his administrators were aware of dangerous tensions between
the two sides in 1721. The governor of Île Royale had travelled from Louisbourg,
which was slowly transforming from a fishing village to a Vauban-style fortress, to
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                            79


meet with a group of Mi’kmaq in July with the intention of exchanging gifts and re-
ceiving information about the region’s Indigenous groups. After hearing Mi’kmaw
complaints about the difficulty they faced surviving on such meager gifts, Saint-
Ovide offered what he could to alleviate their suffering. In return he asked for in-
formation about the Wulstukwiuk and the Abenaki. He eventually learned that
a group of ten or twelve Abenaki had killed a number of cattle and the British
had captured two or three of their people and taken them to Boston as hostages.
Another Abenaki was taken hostage when he went to Boston to trade furs, though
he paid for his release and told his chief what had happened.152
   These attacks heightened tensions. An Indigenous force was raised and re-
sponded, killing twenty-eight settlers.153 The British at Boston declared war on the
Abenaki in 1722. The French at Louisbourg received letters from various mission-
aries outlining the troubles and the official declaration of war. By late December
1722, Saint-Ovide learned that the British at Annapolis had also declared war on
the Mi’kmaq and hoped to engage the French inhabitants in the fight.154 The French,
however, supported the Abenaki in this conflict, and Vaudreuil informed the gov-
ernor of Boston that he had brought these problems on himself by expanding into
the Dawnland without permission.155 The Wabanaki-French relationship was recip-
rocal; the French provided guns, ammunition, and reassurance of geographic con-
trol in return for continued Indigenous aggression against the British. Put simply,
Indigenous efforts to defend their homelands became, in the minds of French of-
ficials, a proxy war against the English.
   A 1723 memoir emphasized the importance of supporting the Abenaki to keep
the British at bay. Indigenous forts in strategic positions were France’s best defence,
and if the English could convince the Iroquois to fight against the French, only the
Abenaki could stand against them. More than serving as a buffer zone against the
English, the Abenaki often granted the French access to their resource-rich lands
and the French were eager to maintain those links.156 In 1724 the British destroyed
the Indigenous village of Norridgewock on the Kennebec River and killed the
missionary Sebastian Rale, prompting many Abenaki to retire to Montreal and
pursue peace negotiations. Their ability to dictate territorial use had been weak-
ened by the influx of British settlers and they were divided between those who
desired peace and those who wanted to continue warring against the English.157
Increasingly outnumbered and unable to rally to a common cause, unlike their
brethren in Mi’kma’ki, the Abenaki were forced to negotiate new terms of settle-
ment in their traditional lands.
   The Mi’kmaq took advantage of their military strength and ability to navigate
the wooded shores and serpentine riverways to launch attacks against the weak
forces at Annapolis Royal. Accompanied by a few Abenaki, the Mi’kmaq descend-
ed on the English pale from a settlement upriver, travelling in canoes that they had
confiscated from French inhabitants. As was customary in Indigenous warfare,
raids were usually brief but sufficiently violent to remind British soldiers that they
were not safe outside Annapolis Royal. In one attack, the Mi’kmaq lured soldiers
out of the fort to ambush them, killing eight and forcing the governor to close the
fort.158 Strategic geographic positioning was an important factor for the Mi’kmaq.
The ability to reach Annapolis Royal safely and undetected facilitated attacks on
the British, but at the same time the Indigenous peoples wanted to remain safe
80                             Homelands and Empires


from an attack themselves. In 1723, a group of Mi’kmaq moved to a settlement on
the Shubenacadie River which cut into the heart of Mi’kma’ki from the Atlantic,
where Gaulin, a missionary priest, had built a church and a presbytery. Saint-
Ovide reported the advantages of this river, including its position below the Minas
Basin and its path between two large hills, which included sections too rapid for
passage by boat. Though it was the French missionary who had built the church
in the region, Saint-Ovide implicitly recognized Mi’kmaw sovereignty when he
noted that five or six French inhabitants lived along the coast of the river on land
“that the Indigenous peoples gave to them.”159 A few leagues above these inhabit-
ants was a village of around forty Mi’kmaq who lived without fear of a surprise
attack because of the information networks that ran along the waterways.160 The
Mi’kmaq and the Acadians on the Shubenacadie shared land and information;
the French at Louisbourg received updates from both.
   After two years of raids and frontier violence, both the British and the Wabanaki
were ready to discuss an end to the conflict and by late 1724 negotiations to end
Dummer’s War were fast approaching. Both sides had to consult with their allies
on how best to proceed with the peace talks. The Nova Scotia Council at Annapolis
Royal received a letter from Lieutenant Governor Dummer asking what demands
should be made in Boston on Nova Scotia’s behalf. The Council proposed seven
articles: the first stipulated that King George and his heirs be recognized as the sole
owners and proprietors of Nova Scotia “to its utmost extent and boundaries”; the
second demanded that the king’s subjects be allowed to settle in Nova Scotia.161
In 1725, Dummer wrote to Lieutenant Governor Lawrence Armstrong to inform
him that peace with the Abenaki in Boston seemed certain, but that peace with
the Mi’kmaq at Annapolis Royal seemed “distant and uncertain.” Armstrong was
left with the task of ensuring that representatives arrived at Annapolis to sign the
peace, keeping in mind the interest of all British subjects.162
   Of equal concern for the British was French support for the Abenaki. What was
meant to be a meeting between the French and English at Montreal in March 1725
quickly became a larger discussion that included the Abenaki, who had representa-
tives in town. This was the beginning of a series of official (and unofficial) discus-
sions at which the Wabanaki illustrated both their territorial knowledge and their
insistence on acceptable boundaries.163 At the meeting in Montreal, the Abenaki
complained that British missionaries were invading their land and clearly noted
the Dawnland boundaries. Abenaki land began at the “Gounitogon” (Connecticut)
River, “otherwise called the long river, that is west beyond Boston.”164 This river
was, according to the Indigenous peoples, an incontestable boundary between the
Abenaki and Iroquois land, and therefore Boston and all settlements to the east of
this river were built on Abenaki land. The Abenaki were willing to tolerate those
settlements but demanded that the British withdraw from the region between Saco
River and Port Royal, which remained Dawnland, Wulstukwik, and Mi’kma’ki,
and had its own internal boundaries.165 The Abenaki announced that they were
aware of British claims to this land and demanded that they prove their title, but
the British argued that they claimed only land on the west side of the Kennebec
river. The Abenaki replied that the British must therefore admit that the Indigenous
peoples controlled lands east of that river.166 They also argued that lands to the west
                             Mapping the Spoils of Peace                          81


had been purchased under false pretences since the Indigenous peoples who sold
them could neither read nor write.167
   English settlements on the Kennebec had long been a source of tension in the
Dawnland. Three times since 1675 the Abenaki had pushed English settlers out of
the region, which they claimed nullified any land deeds the English had secured
earlier. In addition, those deeds were believed to have been finalized only after
the English had made the sachems drunk. When Massachusetts officials approved
new settlements in 1715 at Brunswick and Topsham, on the lower Kennebec,
they once again tested the Abenaki, who were not about to welcome new pales.
Three years later, a testy conference between Governor Shute and Abenaki dip-
lomats, including the speaker Wiwurna, did little to help the situation. Shute ig-
nored Abenaki protocol, made demands, and attempted to bully his way into the
Dawnland. After several exchanges, the Abenaki suggested a compromise: exist-
ing English settlements would be tolerated, but there would be no further expan-
sion. Shute scoffed at the proposal, and the Abenaki left the meeting “without
taking leave and left behind their English Colours.”168 The next day, exasperated
Abenaki delegates returned without Wiwurna and signed an agreement that, in
their minds, restricted English settlements to seventeenth-century limits.169 The
English believed the opposite, and thus the Dawnland remained a place where
homeland and imperial fiction collided.
   The meeting in Montreal concluded with an argument over the Boston region,
which the Abenaki claimed had belonged to them since time immemorial. They
agreed that the English had been settled there for eighty years, but countered that
the Indigenous peoples had continually resisted English attempts to seize land.
Besides Fort Saco, which had been built forty years earlier, all forts and settle-
ments that caused English-Abenaki conflict had been constructed after the Treaty
of Utrecht. The British had no reply to this argument. The Abenaki demanded rep-
arations for attacks and murders during the war: the right for French missionaries
to operate in the region, that no Protestant missionaries be sent to them, as well
as appropriate presents for the destruction of Indigenous property.170 To these de-
mands, the British responded only that they would consult with officials at Boston.
   After the Montreal discussions ended, British and Indigenous representatives
met several times to negotiate an end to the hostilities. These meetings provided
Indigenous groups with an opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge of bound-
aries and borders.171 The conference began in July of 1725, and immediately the
Abenaki representatives, Sauguaaram (Loron) and Atanquid, announced to Mas-
sachusetts lieutenant governor William Dummer that they would take whatever
was said and report it to the Wabanaki who “are all agreed as one” and who would
not let any “unknown tongue, that is the French,” dissuade them. The Indigenous
representatives also outlined their willingness to negotiate territorial control: “If
you can shew fair purchase of land,” they argued, “we do not insist on having
it, notwithstanding what we have said of claiming as far as Cape Elizabeth.”172
Although the Mi’kmaq and the Wulstukwiuk would sign a separate treaty with
Nova Scotia, they were represented at the Boston negotiations. Nova Scotia also
participated, sending Paul Mascarene to observe the negotiation and outline Nova
Scotia’s position.
82                                 Homelands and Empires


   Difficult discussions of land quickly came to dominate the negotiations. After
laying some of the groundwork for peace negotiations, the Indigenous represen-
tatives were granted forty days to consult with their neighbouring groups, and
return to sign the treaty. A second conference was held in November 1725. The
British officials outlined the articles of Peace, which included acknowledging the
sovereignty of the Crown, foreswearing acts of hostility, allowing the King’s sub-
jects to enjoy their property, and addressing any future problems through the court
system.173 Sauguaaram and Atanquid responded that they understood the articles,
but suggested that there was nothing new in this agreement. While the English
were hesitant to embark on this touchy subject without first reaching other agree-
ments, the Wabanaki claimed “we like it very well it is the main thing we want
to come to. But the custom of the Indians is to begin with the principal and main
things, and the rest will come easily afterwards.”174 Demonstrating their negotiat-
ing ability, the Indigenous representatives were careful to ensure all clauses were
understood. Two important parts of the treaty dealt with territorial sovereignty.
The English were to “peaceably and quietly enter upon, improve, and forever en-
joy all and singular their rights of land and former settlements, properties, and
possessions within the eastern parts of the Province” free from Indigenous harass-
ment. The treaty saves for

     the Penobscot, Norridgewock, and other tribes within His Majesties province afore-
     said and their Natural descendants respectively all their lands, liberties, and proper-
     ties not by them conveyed or sold to, or posess’d by any of the English subjects as
     afors’d. As also the privilege of fishing, hunting, and fowling as formerly.175

The clause that related to English settlements was of particular importance, and
the Indigenous delegates asked about the phrase “former settlements,” want-
ing to know if the British intended to build beyond where they were currently
located, likely keeping in mind the treaty they had struck with Shute in 1717.
The commissioners responded that “when we come to settle the bounds we shall
neither build or settle any where but within our own bounds so settled without
your consent.”176
  Apparent from the commissioners’ clarification was the fact that the exact land
boundaries were to be decided later. The following day the English officials sug-
gested that it should be inserted into the treaty that “a committee of able, faithful,
and disinterested persons” be appointed by the New England government to deal
with any land claims issues that arose in the future.177 In practice, New England
officials were suggesting that over the following year this committee would hear
complaints and go into the province with a group of Indigenous chiefs to settle
boundary issues. Such a proposition seemed to provide the British with the upper
hand as they would be in a position to make the final decision.178 The Indigenous
delegates wanted reassurances that the English really were interested in peace,
and they asked for a sign of good faith. To that end, the Indigenous representatives
requested that the English remove “as far as from Cape Elizabeth,” just south of
Casco Bay. Specifically, they wanted the English to abandon two forts between the
Kennebec and the Penobscot, noting:
                              Mapping the Spoils of Peace                                  83


  In case the English will quit St. Georges and Richmond it will show an inclination to
  peace and as everything which you have said is reasonable, so it seems reasonable that
  we should insist upon those two places only … it is the mind of all the tribes that if
  those two garrisons were removed, they would all think that the English were hearty,
  and in earnest for a lasting peace.179

The British were not pleased by this demand and countered that their government
had deeds to these lands but would be willing, if a peace was concluded, to use
the forts for commercial instead of military purposes. They presented their deeds
to the Indigenous delegates, who upon learning that some of the sachems who
signed the deeds were still alive, left the meeting to consult with the large group of
Wabanaki peoples who had travelled to attend the discussions.
   The Indigenous delegates returned in the afternoon to continue the question of
territorial boundaries. They had two primary concerns: first, although satisfied
with the deeds concerning St Georges and Richmond, they wanted to know if any
more houses would be built in those areas; second, since the deeds were separated
by vast tracts of land, the Wabanaki asked if they would be compensated for that
vacant intermediate land if it was settled by the English. The commissioners re-
sponded that there might be more houses built, but the settlers would be careful
not to encroach on Indigenous land. If the Indigenous peoples were willing to sell
the land they would receive consideration. In a concession that was sure to cause
future conflict, the English added that “the government will take due care that you
shall not be wronged, and you shall have free liberty of hunting and fishing etc.
anywhere, but in the Inclosures or lands that are fenced in.”180
   The push to enforce British legal frameworks to resolve conflicts and define future
settlements troubled Indigenous delegates, who refused to recognize British sov-
ereignty over their lands. Included in the treaty was the promise that the delegates
would meet at a future date with Lawrence Armstrong, Nova Scotia’s lieutenant
governor, to enter into a peaceful agreement with that government, represented
at Boston by Mascarene. While this was apparently accepted without reservation,
the first part of the treaty, demanding the recognition of the king as sovereign over
his lands and their inhabitants, was received with less enthusiasm. The delegates
responded “we shall pay our respect and duty to the King of Britain as we did to
the King of France, but we reckon ourselves a free people and are not bound.”181
Having concluded the initial negotiations, the Indigenous delegates left to dis-
cuss the agreement with other Eastern Abenaki and seek a ratification. Ultimately,
this effort was unsuccessful. When Sauguaaram and the other delegates arrived at
Casco Bay in July 1726 to ratify the agreement, they informed the English commis-
sioners that they represented only the Penobscot. Other Wabanaki peoples, such as
the Norridgewock, St François, and Wowenock, refused to appear, requesting in-
stead that the English officials meet them at Montreal. One sticking point was the
British refusal to remove settlements from St Georges and Richmond. Sauguaaram
argued that the houses did not have to be moved a great distance, but only from St
Georges to Pemaquid, and from Richmond to Arrowsick. Sauguaaram suggested
that had the government acquiesced to this demand, “we, with the other Indians
should all have come into a peace before now, and there would be no difficulty
84                            Homelands and Empires


with the others.”182 The lieutenant governor responded that it was beneath his
dignity to go meet with the Indigenous peoples in French territory. Furthermore,
the officials sent to Montreal that previous spring had no authority to negotiate
and were sent only to demand that the French cease supporting the Indigenous
peoples in their war against the English.183
   Sauguaaram’s reply pushed the land encroachment issue despite the deeds and
demonstrated the centrality of oral history and Indigenous memory. Looking to
the present generation of Indigenous peoples living in the area, he argued that
there were many young people who had no idea that the land had been sold. If it
had been sold, it was purchased for a very small amount, and therefore it would
not be a large matter for the government to “make allowances” for the land. When
asked to explain what he meant, Loron stated, “we desire that no houses or settle-
ments may be made to the Eastward of Pemaquid, or above Arrowsick, as for the
Penopscut [Penobscot] tribe in particular we don’t know that they ever sold any
lands.”184 The commissioners refused to surrender their settlements as Sauguaaram
requested, reminding the sachem that they had shown the deeds to these lands.
Sauguaaram did not back down. He informed the commissioners that there were
none among the Penobscot who remembered selling the land. The deeds pre-
sented the year before were signed by Madockawando (whose land deal with Sir
William Phips in 1693 had so angered the French) and Sheepscut John, neither of
whom were members of the Penobscot tribe. “We do not remember of any settle-
ments at St. Georges,” Sauguaaram argued, “we remember a pretty while, and as
long as we remember, the place where the Garrison stands was filled with great
long grown trees.”185 After further debate, Sauguaaram and his delegates agreed
to allow the fort at St George to remain as a truck house only, but forbade the con-
struction of additional houses unless permission was given.186 The Penobscot then
ratified the treaty. Sauguaaram informed Mascarene that he should send a vessel
for the Wabanaki, who would go to Annapolis Royal to ratify an agreement with
the Nova Scotia government.
   Saint-Ovide, governor of Île Royale, had been left out of these negotiations and
when word of the British-Wabanaki discussions reached Louisbourg in December
of 1725 he did what he could to disrupt them. Only a few months earlier, during
the height of the treaty negotiations, Saint-Ovide had reported to his superiors
that nothing of note had happened in the colony save for a Mi’kmaw-Abenaki at-
tack on Canso the previous January.187 When he learned of the treaty, Saint-Ovide
reported only that he had been informed that the British had struck an agreement
with the Wulstukwiuk and with several villages of Mi’kmaq on the coast of the
Bay of Fundy close to Minas. Obviously desirous to know more, he had written
to Gaulin, whom he expected would deliver a full account of the treaty the fol-
lowing spring.188 By the fall, Saint-Ovide had met with the Wabanaki on several
occasions and had also heard from Gaulin. At his conferences with the Mi’kmaq,
Saint-Ovide attempted to persuade them not to accept any offers made them by
the English; the French governor seemed to believe that they were amenable to
his suggestions.189
   As for the presumed treaty struck with a number of Mi’kmaw villages along
the Bay of Fundy, Saint-Ovide learned from Gaulin that accounts of this agree-
ment were perhaps exaggerated. The French missionary noted that in fact a small
                               Mapping the Spoils of Peace                                  85


number of younger Mi’kmaq from the Saint John River had negotiated with the
British, but the terms of those agreements were currently under consideration by
the village elders and a response was not expected until the following spring.190
Though seemingly confident that the Mi’kmaq would distance themselves
from the British, Saint-Ovide was ultimately unable to dictate the actions of his
Indigenous allies in Nova Scotia. The Mi’kmaq and the Wulstukwiuk were part
of a larger political organization that made decisions for their mutual benefit, and
in 1726, many members favoured peace over continued war.
   In 1726, seventy-seven Wabanaki, including Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Wuls­
tukwiuk, and Mi’kmaq, signed a treaty with the British at Annapolis Royal – a
copy of the 1725 treaty signed in Boston – to end their participation in the recent
conflict. As William Wicken has persuasively argued, although this war was about
land, the treaty that ended hostilities was not one of land surrender. These repre-
sentatives, by entering into a treaty of “peace and friendship,” agreed to recognize
British legal jurisdiction over Nova Scotia and to submit to King George as they
had to Louis XV.191 Yet the Wabanaki never submitted to the French Crown and
never signed any treaties with France.192 It is also important to recognize the dif-
ferent British and Indigenous interpretations of the treaty. One Abenaki delegate,
Panaouamskeyen, upon learning that the English considered the treaty a recogni-
tion of British territorial sovereignty in the northeast, issued a response in which
he clarified his understanding of the agreement:

  I answered – Yes, I recognize him King of all his lands; but, I rejoined, do not hence
  infer that I acknowledge thy King as my King, and King of my lands. Here lies my
  distinction – my Indian distinction. God hath willed that I have no King, and that I be
  master of my lands in common.193

The Eastern Abenaki recognized that the British had claims to some lands, just
as they could demonstrate the borders between Iroquois, Mi’kmaw, and Abenaki
lands.194 What they would not tolerate was the British assertion of complete geo-
graphic control in a territory where their political jurisdiction was limited to a
small settlement in Nova Scotia supported by larger ones in the northeast. This
idea surely would have spread among the men who signed the treaty in Nova
Scotia. While the English in the northeast in 1726 focused on the text of the treaty,
the Wabanaki explained the agreement as they understood it.195
  Among the Wabanaki confederacy, there was no unanimity regarding the peace.
Just as members of the Abenaki had refused to ratify the treaty at Casco, so too
were various Mi’kmaw groups wary of the agreement. In November of 1727, sev-
eral Mi’kmaq and some Abenaki groups met with Saint-Ovide, who had called
them to Île Royale in an attempt to derail negotiations with Governor Armstrong.
Tensions between the British and the Eastern Algonkians were high, as Indigenous
peoples had recently been killed at Boston. To take advantage of the cracks in the
newly minted British-Wabanaki agreement, Saint-Ovide informed the Indigenous
peoples that he had fallen sick and therefore could not meet them for conferences
in Nova Scotia. He requested that they come to Île St Jean to enjoy a feast and re-
ceive presents.196 He went further and invited the chiefs to visit him at Louisbourg,
which would have been bustling with construction as the fortifications took
86                            Homelands and Empires


shape, where he held conferences and warned them repeatedly that the English
cruelty they had suffered would continue until they had been “absolutely de-
stroyed.”197 The chiefs responded by requesting that Saint-Ovide maintain his
close ties with their people and help them when necessary, to which the French
governor happily agreed.198
   Before the chiefs left Louisbourg, Saint-Ovide asked them about the rumoured
British-Mi’kmaq treaty. They responded that it was the avarice of a few of their
younger members that had led to this agreement and that the treaty was of no con-
sequence to them. Saint-Ovide was reassured that the British were the Mi’kmaq’s
greatest enemy, and that the killing of their brothers in Boston would forever
weigh on their hearts, and the hearts of their children.199
   To assume that the French or the British were the only groups capable of “double
diplomacy” during this period is to discount the political savvy of the Wabanaki
confederacy. As Daniel K. Richter has argued, “modern Indian politics” had at its
root the capability (and necessity) of playing the British and French against each
other to establish political room in which Indigenous peoples could operate.200
Their politics also created geographic room by staking claims to territory and re-
fusing to sign treaties of land surrender. The Mi’kmaq and their Abenaki allies had
lived in the region, mapped it, and determined its boundaries. Europeans were
tolerated, but their presence during this era was continually negotiated with the
region’s Indigenous peoples, who proved worthy geographic adversaries. It is evi-
dent from the treaty negotiations that the Indigenous delegates were clear about
what land they considered Indigenous territory; while willing to negotiate, the
Wabanaki worked to retain their particular vision of the northeast.

                                     •••
The period from the fall of Port Royal in 1710 to the establishment of the first
British-Indigenous treaties in 1726 was one of almost constant negotiation. The
Acadians remained in their settlements and adapted to the British presence as nec-
essary; the French at Louisbourg hoped that Acadia could be retaken; the Mi’kmaq,
Wulstukwiuk, and Abenaki asserted their territorial control when European en-
croachment threatened their traditional lands; and the British, possessing only two
strongholds in Nova Scotia, were continually frustrated in their attempts to extend
authority beyond the walls of their forts. Nova Scotia/Acadia remained imperial
fictions in 1726, although residents of Mi’kma’ki were being forced to adjust to the
presence of new European opponents. Confusion regarding the region’s limits,
failed boundary negotiations based on suspect and suspicious cartography, and
treaty settlements that secured only Indigenous “peace and friendship” made it
clear that Britain and France were arguing over land that neither could control.
   European officials and local administrators could not use geographic evidence
to make the arguments necessary to claim territory. The stark disconnect between
the provinces that imperial powers wanted to build and control, and the limited
and largely ineffectual pales in which their citizens and soldiers actually lived,
could not be reconciled by the maps created on the ground or used in impe-
rial diplomacy. The Wabanaki confederacy was the most consistent in its territo-
rial claims, operating as it did with a much deeper understanding of the region’s
                              Mapping the Spoils of Peace                            87


geography. Double diplomacy was an instrumental element of these negotiations,
as each side struck alliances, emphasized their strengths over their weaknesses,
and tailored information (geographic and otherwise) to suit their specific needs.
What Daniel K. Richter defines as “modern Indian politics” could be attributed to
all sides: each “cultivated the mystique of exclusive loyalty” while keeping their
own interests at heart.201
   After the Treaty of Utrecht, Mi’kma’ki, Wulstukwik, and the Dawnland remained
central regions within an Indigenous network based on both land and maritime
connections. France succeeded in securing a place in this network because of the
cultural negotiations, alliances, and religious links they had established. The British
aimed not at fitting into the system, but replacing it. British officials in Nova Scotia
lacked the resources and personnel to collect surveys or reports detailing the re-
gion’s topography, waterways, and settlements necessary to exert territorial con-
trol. The Atlantic highway went only so far before local rivers and coastal paths
shaped how different groups interacted. The Wabanaki dominated this terrain and
controlled access to it, preventing their enemies from mapping, knowing, and ab-
sorbing their surroundings into imperial space. They set boundaries, defined their
limits, and were more successful in keeping them than either the French or British
were in breaking through. The treaties struck in 1726 established a framework for
future interaction and hinted at a reorganization of the alliance system. Of course,
Wabanaki, French, and British residents in the region would interpret these ar-
rangements in separate ways and work to mould them to suit specific strategies.
Having largely mapped the peace of 1713 and 1726, these groups now had to live
within its fluid and malleable borders.
                        3 A Time and a Place




The 1726 British-Wabanaki treaties were aimed at ending violence in the north-
east. After years of scattered fighting and surprise attacks, the prospect of peace
appealed to all sides. While open warfare was curbed, the treaties could do little
to prevent British and French authorities from attempting to increase their influ-
ence in Indigenous homelands. The treaties concluded at Annapolis Royal and
Casco Bay were vague enough to be misunderstood and misapplied by either
side. The lack of substantive change on the ground meant that while the English
were no longer engaged in official conflict, they remained a weak force in a land
inhabited by Acadians and Indigenous peoples, neither of whom were interested
in facilitating British expansion in the region. The Wabanaki hoped the agree-
ments would protect their territories from future encroachments. The French at Île
Royale weren’t pleased with the agreements and continued to press the Wabanaki
to fight the British.
   The result of these treaties was less a peace than a mutual recognition of coex-
istence. On the one hand, the British could not will Nova Scotia into existence,
but instead had to appeal to and negotiate with stronger Indigenous peoples and
the region’s Acadian settlers. The Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, and Passamaquoddy,
and to a greater extent the Abenaki, were forced to acknowledge the continued
presence of the British in or near their homelands and adapt to the changes that
their presence had forced upon them. The French, for their part, worked clandes-
tinely to disrupt British-Indigenous alliances while feigning fidelity to the terms of
the Treaty of Utrecht. This period was characterized not by conflict or unbridled
expansion, but by carefully constructed and monitored areas of interaction that
served to maintain a balance of geographic control.
   The imperial fiction of Nova Scotia in Mi’kma’ki after the 1726 treaties was both
a spatial and temporal entity. Finding Nova Scotia in the early eighteenth century
was a question of not simply where by also of when. Fishing sites buzzed with ac-
tivity during the summer and were nearly deserted in the winter; forts swelled with
soldiers during wars and were much reduced in times of peace. Indigenous groups
moved from summer sites along the water to inland territories to hunt in the win-
ter, traversing their homeland in ways the British could not. This was a region of
movement dependent on patterns of violence and sustenance. During the extended
period of peace between 1726 (when the British and Wabanaki signed Treaties of
Peace and Friendship) and 1744 (when the War of the Austrian Succession, known
in North America as King George’s War, ushered in an era of imperial conflict),
                                  A Time and a Place                                 89


Nova Scotia was governed by the construction and maintenance of shared spaces
that enabled largely peaceful interactions in a region where no single group at-
tained sovereignty. Focusing on three types of shared spaces – places of commercial
interaction (such as the Canso fishery), political negotiation (including forts and
sites of Indigenous migration), and spiritual accommodation (churches and dioces-
es) – demonstrates that spaces of power in the eighteenth-century northeast cannot
be assumed, were not always imperial, and were never static: these specific geogra-
phies must be understood as fluid, seasonal, and fleeting areas that served specific
purposes at specific times. Because the British were hemmed in at Port Royal and
thus vulnerable, French Acadians and officials at Louisbourg, not to mention the
Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, Passamaquoddy, and Abenaki, remained unconvinced
that the mere presence of Britons (within decaying forts, no less) would erase the
geographic identities of Acadia or the Indigenous homelands. An alternative inter-
pretation of British-French-Indigenous relationships is thus necessary to explain
how these groups interacted. Residents of the northeast developed the geographic
relations necessary to monitor relations, resolve conflicts, and live together in rela-
tive peace while sharing a hotly contested part of North America. Peace depended
on a balance of authority among the groups living in the province, none of which
could claim absolute sovereignty. Central to that balance of authority were the ne-
gotiations around geographic power, by which I mean the ability to enforce actions
taken on territory.1 Each group’s geographic power (drawing a boundary, raising a
fort, engaging in trade) was legitimated as authority only in select areas, while sov-
ereignty remained elusive. Limits on geographic power, imposed by resistance,
negotiations, and some violence, restricted the extension of authority and pre-
served a regional balance in the face of wider aspirations for territorial control.
   There were competing visions of territorial control in the region and no one
group was able to implement completely its own ideal to the exclusion of others.
Within each group were internal divisions that reduced its ability to present a
united front against challengers, and allowed for cooperation and collaboration
with competing groups. “Coexistence in the imperial world remained possible,”
Daniel K. Richter has argued, “because the interests of at least some groups in
the British, French, and Spanish colonies coincided with those of at least some
Indians some of the time.”2 What developed was a system of checks and balances
in which alliances and interconnections between groups appeared as necessary
and disappeared when they no longer served a purpose. These fleeting spaces of
negotiation, trade, or conflict help demonstrate that “spaces of power” were both
geographic and temporal. Therefore, we have to look for them and analyse their
significance in terms of both space and time. Tools of geographic control (includ-
ing religion, commerce, cross-cultural negotiations, threats of violence, and settle-
ment projects) were used to create and monitor fluid, seasonal, and temporally
limited areas of interaction and exchange in which problems could be addressed,
discussed, and, ideally, resolved.
   Nova Scotia and Acadia, as imperial fictions, are best explored as overlapping
and competing geographies of power (the ability to act), authority (having those
actions recognized as legitimate), and sovereignty (securing the ability to govern
singularly) in Mi’kma’ki. Competing groups relied on strategically shared spaces
to sustain relative peace in a region still shaped by conflicting geographic identities.
90                             Homelands and Empires


In lieu of a sovereign power, a system of territorial checks and balances in the form
of shared spaces that enabled these competing groups to interact peacefully, resolve
conflicts through negotiation, and maintain an acceptable division of geography
during a period of contested dominium (which, like authority, denotes territorial
possession and the ability to govern) and a complete lack of imperium (which, like
sovereignty, delimits the region in which only one ruler has jurisdiction).3 British
administrators held Annapolis Royal and projected their authority across the prov-
ince without the ability to enforce those claims; French officials established them-
selves at Louisbourg and argued that the British could lawfully claim only a portion
of what was called Nova Scotia; French Acadians remained as independent as pos-
sible, grew in number and wealth, and experienced a “golden age” under de jure
British rule; and the Mi’kmaq continued to adapt to changes while preserving their
traditional way of life in Mi’kma’ki as they had for thousands of years.4

                                      •••
In the years following the British-Wabanaki agreements, all groups in the north-
east focused on borders and boundaries. The goal was either to expand or to limit
the expansion of other groups into contested lands. The British-Indigenous treaties
of 1726 are significant less for the boundaries they established (general and misun-
derstood at best) than for the mutual recognition they signalled between members
of the Wabanaki confederacy and British settlers. The Abenaki in the Dawnland
had a longer history of interaction with the British than did the Mi’kmaq and
Wulstukwiuk, and by the early eighteenth century parts of the Dawnland were
being significantly threatened by British authorities.5 New England settlers were
eager to expand into the lands between the Kennebec River and the St Croix River,
and were unwilling to let the 1726 treaty derail their aspirations. What first stood
in the way of this expansion, however, were resistance and confusion within the
British administration itself. It was not uncommon in contested spaces to find
members of the same group pitted against each other.
   Before James Oglethorpe settled the colony of Georgia in southern British
America, London philanthropist Thomas Coram and surveyor David Dunbar at-
tempted to establish a Georgia of their own in the northeast. Sailing along the coasts
or venturing beyond the population centres illuminated the staggering amount of
land and resources available for exploitation, as long as the European imagina-
tion could transform Indigenous homeland into untapped wilderness. Europeans
were good at that. Thomas Coram seemed to be easily influenced by what he saw
on his travels. His mother died when he was young, he went to sea when he was
eleven, and eventually his father apprenticed him to a shipwright who worked on
the Thames. Later in life, Coram’s facility in auditing ship tonnage caught the at-
tention of London merchants, who commissioned the staunch Anglican to establish
a new shipyard in Puritan Boston. Ten years in New England led Coram to think
about the possibilities offered by establishing a colony in North America, and after
the Treaty of Utrecht he pushed, unsuccessfully, for a settlement in the putative
colony of Maine for disbanded soldiers. Coram seemed particularly attuned to his
surroundings and the opportunities they held. Shortly after his failed effort to colo-
nize Maine, Coram was living in Rotherhithe and doing business in London. His
                                                                                  91


regular route into the city took him past abandoned children, many sick and dying,
some already dead. To address this distressing problem, Coram worked to establish
a foundling hospital in London. Though his early efforts were unsuccessful, Coram
ultimately became best known as a philanthropist.6 Despite his affairs in Britain,
Coram kept pushing for settlement in North America and became involved in early
efforts to establish a colony in Maine and later in Georgia.7 Confusion within the
British administration in Nova Scotia, New England, and Britain over which colony
should control the lands between New England and Nova Scotia slowed attempts
at expansion into the Dawnland for a time. The Abenaki had been fighting with
settlers in lands lying between the Kennebec River and the St George River for a
generation; in fact, they drove out most English settlers during King William’s War
(1689–97).8 By the late 1720s, Thomas Coram was pressing the Board of Trade to
grant him permission to settle in the region and claim it for Britain.9 His petition
to the Board of Trade suggested that convicts could be sent to America working
for Britain’s benefit by clearing trees and cultivating the wasteland in prepara-
tion for settlement.10 Though his petition ultimately failed to win favour with the
Board of Trade, his interest in the project continued and a new acquaintance, David
Dunbar, provided renewed hope.
   David Dunbar, who would eventually go on to be lieutenant governor of New
Hampshire, had been appointed surveyor general of the woods in 1728 and had for-
mulated a plan to raise a settlement of his own in the lands between the Kennebec
and St Croix rivers. Maps dating from shortly after the Restoration of Charles II
made vigorous arguments in favour of the region’s English character. Christopher
Browne, a London geographer and mapmaker, emphasized the English pedigree of
all lands between the Kennebec and the St Croix by referencing the Duke of York’s
creation of the short-lived Dominion of New England on his 1690 map (figure 3.1).
After the Glorious Revolution, the appointment of Sir William Phips as governor
and the capture of Port Royal in 1690 set the stage for William and Mary to extend
the Massachusetts Bay Colony northeast to Nova Scotia by the 1691 charter. The
second capture of Port Royal in 1710, and the resulting debate of Acadia’s limits,
heightened the value of maps, surveys, or settlements that could support an impe-
rial fiction. Coram and Dunbar began consulting on just such a settlement project,
and soon offered the Board of Trade a new proposal to settle part of the Dawnland
with destitute Irish families from Massachusetts and a number of Palatines. The
Board of Trade favoured sending these settlers to Nova Scotia to bolster that prov-
ince’s Protestant character, but the Irish in Massachusetts argued that it was too
far for them to travel and Coram cautioned that the lack of civilian government in
Nova Scotia would weaken settlers’ resolve to stay. The Board of Trade eventually
agreed, and Dunbar was named governor of a royal province east of the Kennebec
called Georgia.11
   Leaving aside the fact that the Penobscot inhabited the territory so desired by
Dunbar and Coram, there remained significant jurisdictional problems with this
proposal. Governor Philipps of Nova Scotia and Governor Dummer of Massa-
chusetts both believed the territory in question fell within their colonies. Philipps
wrote to Thomas Pelham-Holles, the Duke of Newcastle and secretary of state for
the Southern Department, to clarify plans for the region. Philipps had learned of
Dunbar’s new position and of the creation of a new province on the lands bordering
92                                  Homelands and Empires




 3.1 Extract from Christopher Browne’s A New Map of New England and Annapolis (1690)
    indicating the “Duke of Yorke claimes Propriety from Kennebeck R. to Ste. Crux.”
           Map reproduction courtesy of the Norman B. Leventhal Map Center
                              at the Boston Public Library.


New England, “which I looked upon to have been a part of this Government, but if
it be determined otherwise I have no objection to make.”12 This was not quite true:
he did, in fact, have objections to make,

     As Colonel Dunbar is both Governor and surveyor he is at liberty to receive imme-
     diately all families that shall offer, whereas my hands have been tied up from the be-
     ginning, not to be loosed but by [Dunbar] having finished the survey of this whole
     Province, whereby its settlement has been postponed and baulked all the time of my
     government and may continue…some time longer for I look upon it not to be the work
     of months but years and unless (in the doing of it) regard be had to the harbours and
     places that are most proper for settlements, I am afraid to think that all encouragement
     will be quite taken away.13

Dunbar was in the enviable position of overseeing the survey of a province for
which he would be governor, and the very establishment of that province robbed
Nova Scotia of its surveyor and offered an alternative location for potential settlers.
                                   A Time and a Place                                       93


   While Philipps’s complaints seemed benign, Coram and Dunbar were increas-
ingly concerned about interference from Governor Dummer of Massachusetts.
Despite Dunbar’s explanation that the grant was carved from Nova Scotia (not
Massachusetts), Dummer argued that the new settlement fell within his jurisdic-
tion.14 Coram informed the Board of Trade that any involvement of the government
of Massachusetts “would infalabley be the destruction” of the settlement, as the
Penobscot and eastern Abenaki people had “in time past received so many injuri-
ous provakations by the base & fraudulent practices of the Massachusets in making
them drunk, then enticing them to execute deeds of conveyance for large quantities
of their land, when they knew not the meaning of those deeds.”15 In other words,
having so angered and abused their Indigenous neighbours, the Massachusetts
government would be unable to prevent violent reprisals on new settlers.
   At this early stage, Dunbar’s only allies in the project were the Penobscot; their
support, however, quickly waned. The 1726 British-Wabanaki treaties had limited
British expansion into Penobscot territory, and as long as Dunbar adhered to those
limits the Penobscot would welcome him as a friend. The chiefs of the Penobscot,
on hearing of Dunbar’s plan, sent him a friendly but cautionary response via trans-
lator and military captain John Gyles:

  Great Sir, we heard your Lettar, it was Red and Interpreted to Us by Captn Gyles &
  we Like it well & we hear your ar Planted at Pemaquid, it was Unknown to Us but
  since you ar Settling ye old Settlements that was formally we Consent to it, and not to
  Exccead ye old boundarys of Pemaqud we are well Plesd to hear of your Observing the
  articles of Peace made between Us & Ye Province of ye Masachussetts Bay. Good frind
  you say you ar Imploid by his Majty King George, if you Pass St Georges River we shal
  be Uneasy we mention this to you Beliving you are Imploid from his Majty & that you
  will be our frind. We say no more at Present & what we have sd is from our hearts, &
  what we concluded on at our Chief Village at Penobscot, and if any Pass St Georges
  River to Plant we shall not thinke them to be our frinds. We salute you Col. Dunbar.16

While British officials quibbled over jurisdiction, the Penobscot chiefs saw a new
settlement – one governed by a previous treaty – as an opportunity for new friend-
ship. Like other examples of Indigenous-European relations in North America,
mutually beneficial settlements were welcomed. Yet they were also controlled.17
   As in other parts of North America, Indigenous groups in the northeast wel-
comed English expansion if it was deemed beneficial.18 Yet the Penobscot worked
to control these new settlements, and they withdrew their support of the terms
of the treaty when the British extended their claims to the St Croix River.19 One
year after being welcomed by the Penobscot, Dunbar received an advisory letter
from Philipps on how to proceed now that the Penobscot opposed the settlement.
“I am sorry,” Philipps began, “that you inform me of the Penobscott … dislike
to the making of this settlement,” adding that the Indigenous peoples “have the
direction of Peace and War,” being the most considerable group in the province.20
Ultimately, Dunbar’s project was never realized. His gubernatorial appointment
was rejected by the Privy Council, which claimed that the land in question fell un-
der Nova Scotia’s jurisdiction. In 1732, Dunbar was ordered to leave the area and
the new settlement was officially scuttled.21
94                              Homelands and Empires




     3.2 A New Map of Part of His Majesty’s Empire in North America from Caroline to
     Newfoundland. Engraved S. Parker, London. c.1720. This anonymous map includes
              a shaded area that roughly corresponds to Dunbar’s Georgia.
             (National Archives, Kew, NA CO700/North America General 5).



   Dunbar and Coram were not the first to suggest establishing a new settlement
in the lands between New England and Nova Scotia. A map, believed to date from
around 1720, illustrated the region’s potential as an outlet for soldiers or other
Britons (figure 3.2). Engraved by S. Parker and based on Cyprian Southack’s map
from 1717, “A New Map of His Majesty’s Empire, in North America from Carolina
to Newfoundland” includes a coloured section in the lands around Maine in which
the map’s author echoed Christopher Browne’s map by noting “This Land from
Kennebeck River to St Croix was Granted to James Duke of York by King Charles
2d. in ye Year 1663.” This map exists in only a few places, one of which is the
Houghton Library at Harvard. where it is included in a larger petition (to settle
veterans in the area) that argues that the region is too far distant from Boston to be
administered effectively and must comprise a proper colony of its own.22 The region
that became Maine had experienced a fraught existence during the seventeenth
                                 A Time and a Place                                95


century, and these kinds of overtures to British officials indicated just how valu-
able the region had become.
   As Dunbar’s attempted settlement illustrates, contested areas were central
to maintaining a balance of geographic control even when those in competition
were members of the same larger group, in this case British settlers and admin-
istrators; yet conflict also existed between different groups. The British faced es-
pecially stiff resistance from the Indigenous peoples in Mi’kma’ki, and the men
(it was almost always men) who headed Indigenous groups became targets for
elite co-option. One such man was Joseph d’Abbadie de Saint-Castin, whose father
was the French officer who had married Pidianske (Marie-Mathilde), daughter of
Abenaki chief Madakowando. Saint-Castin was the fifth in his family to inherit
the title of baron, but he didn’t bother going to France to claim it. Given his up-
bringing among the Abenaki, he was more Indigenous than French; the Abenaki
themselves recognized his position and conferred on him the title of great chief.
French administrators also recognized Saint-Castin’s value and in 1726 made him
a French officer.23 The English were not far behind in attempting to win Saint-
Castin’s loyalty. In 1730, Saint-Castin issued a report on the state of the Abenaki
“of Acadia.” The English at Boston had established new forts at Pemaquid and
were intent on building more to establish a presence in the region. Officials had
pressed the Abenaki to rent or sell their lands, but with little success. The British
even went so far as to promise Saint-Castin a command of the British troops and
a monopoly on the trade, should he only declare himself a subject of the King of
England.24 Saint-Castin refused the offer, and the French authorities encouraged
him to continue resisting British expansion.
   Unable to win the loyalty of influential chiefs or people the region with subjects,
the British relied on forts to demonstrate military strength in the face of adminis-
trative weakness. With limited methods by which they could claim territory or ex-
press authority, British officials fell back on bluster and military intimidation. The
Kennebec River was not the only area of attempted British expansion. As Dunbar’s
efforts faltered, the government at Annapolis Royal looked to extend its authority
into regions inhabited by the Wulstukwiuk and the French. In 1731, Saint-Ovide
de Brouillan reported that the British had sent English families to the Saint John
River area, and were constructing forts in various places. However, the trappings
of power were poor stand-ins for territorial control. Saint-Ovide was sure that
British attempts to build new pales in Wulstukwik or Mi’kma’ki would trouble the
Wabanaki.25 He was correct. When British settlers attempted to build a storehouse
at Chignecto, the Mi’kmaq plundered the proprietor’s house “under a pretence of
a premium or rent due to them for the land and liberty of digging.”26 Showing that
he misunderstood or, at the very least, misapplied the 1726 treaties, Lieutenant
Governor Armstrong argued that such violence against the British was a breach of
the agreements made at Boston and Annapolis.27 Armstrong failed to realize that
his actions – attempting to build new settlements in contested areas – could also be
interpreted as a breach of the treaty. These attacks made it clear that the Mi’kmaq
denied British imperium and were unwilling to legitimize British dominium be-
yond Annapolis Royal.
   Armstrong knew that the Mi’kmaq and their allies were challenging his govern-
ment’s authority outside the walls of Annapolis Royal. At times, even government
96                            Homelands and Empires


within those walls was questionable. Armstrong complained that authority at
Annapolis Royal, like the fort itself, was weak “after having been so long as up-
wards of twenty one years (which may be said imaginarily only) under the English
government.”28 The British could barely exert control over their delapitated fort
let alone convince the Mi’kmaq that the king controlled the entire province. The
Mi’kmaq argued that Britain had conquered only Annapolis Royal, leaving Minas,
Chignecto, and other areas in the province unchanged.29 Armstrong’s inability to
win Acadian loyalty – despite repeated attempts at securing an oath – did little
to convince the Mi’kmaq that British government extended throughout the re-
gion. Though in the Treaty of 1726, the Mi’kmaq and their allies acknowledged
“His Said Majesty King George’s Jurisdiction & Dominion over the territories of
the said Province of Nova Scotia or Acadia,” they also agreed not to disturb the
English “in their settlements already made or lawfully to be made.”30 In contested
spaces, “lawful” was a relative term.
   Though British officials clung to the law, their legal frameworks alone were un-
able to extend sovereignty over Indigenous peoples or Acadians. Annapolis Royal
lacked the ability to delineate “lawful” behaviour and could not convert the re-
gion’s inhabitants into legal subjects. This failure had much to do with Whitehall’s
neglect in instituting measures that could bring Acadians into the British con-
stitution. Administrators were unable to secure an unconditional oath of alle-
giance from the Acadians, and British representatives came to depend on Acadian
deputies to settle legal matters that would otherwise fall under the Nova Scotia
Council’s authority. Acadians filed complaints based on their customary practices,
which likely derived from the Coutume de Paris. Because the British could not in-
stitute British law, they were forced to hear the complaints and adjudicate based
on established Acadian practices.31 This juridical weakness similarly demanded
that British administrators incorporate Indigenous customs into their negotiations
(demonstrated by the treaty process) as officials were unable to incorporate, assim-
ilate, or annihilate the Mi’kmaq. Considering the importance of legal spaces of em-
pire to the extension of imperial authority, British weakness in the face of French
and Indigenous resistance was a telling indicator of their tenuous position.32
   British attempts to extend their authority into contested areas met with Mi’kmaw
reprisals, but to assume a homogenous response belies the complexities that shaped
Indigenous society in Nova Scotia. In the summer of 1732, Henry Cope, a member
of the Nova Scotia Council, and an associate travelled upriver from Annapolis
Royal to the house of René LeBlanc, an Acadian notary at the bustling Acadian set-
tlement of Minas. LeBlanc supported the British administration and was trusted by
the governor and his council. In the late 1740s, the governor would refer to LeBlanc
as “old René” and assure traders that LeBlanc could be counted on to provide use-
ful information.33 Not surprisingly, LeBlanc’s leanings were evident to those who
knew him. When Cope and his associate were in Minas, three Mi’kmaw men ar-
rived – Jacques Winaguadesh, his brother Antoine, and their cousin Andress. After
threatening LeBlanc and disparaging his family as “dogs and villains,” Jacques
promised LeBlanc a violent end should the English build a fort in the area. Cope
assured the men that there were no such plans, but asked what the response would
be if there were. The Mi’kmaq responded that they would not suffer it, for this was
their land and the British had no business there.34 Cope was convinced that the
                                  A Time and a Place                                97


three Mi’kmaw men had been put up to the attack by a group of Acadians who
often treated LeBlanc poorly, but what is evident is that Jacques, Antoine, and
Andress did not speak for all the Mi’kmaq. Three days later a group of twelve
Mi’kmaw men approached Cope and asked for pardon on behalf of those who had
harassed Le Blanc. Cope informed them that they should make a proper apology
and indicate who had encouraged them to oppose the blockhouse. The Council
was forced to re-evaluate their plans for a storehouse at Minas, and while they ini-
tially settled on issuing a proclamation among the Acadians and Mi’kmaq stating
that such a building did not infringe on any of their rights (a tacit recognition that
Acadians and Mi’kmaq had rights to begin with), opposition was strong enough to
force them to abandon the plan.35 But the Mi’kmaq remained suspicious and vigi-
lant. Over the following months, various Wabanaki groups periodically gathered
around areas of British interest, which Lieutenant Armstrong suggested indicated
their intention to disrupt any British plans to expand.36 Though responses to British
movements varied, few Mi’kmaq welcomed British expansion into Mi’kma’ki.
   In 1740, seven years after Armstrong’s problems at Minas, the Abenaki continued
to stress the importance of restraining geographic expansion to the limits set in 1726,
but there were repercussions for English leaders who acquiesced to Indigenous
demands. At a meeting in Montreal, a group of Eastern Abenaki informed the
governor of New France, Charles de la Boische, marquis de Beauharnois, that they
had discussed settlement with the British. They had told the English to live in
peace and the English had invited them to leave their settlement on the Penobscot
and come down river to a house that they had built. The Abenaki responded that
they would not; in fact, they wanted the house destroyed or they would destroy it
