themselves. The British complied and removed the offending establishment from
the contested area, a clear indication that their power had not been legitimated.37
The Indigenous-English negotiation over the house (built above the English fort
at St Georges which the Penobscot had requested be removed in the 1726 treaty)
demonstrates the importance of contested space as an area in which territorial
control could be kept in check. The Abenaki, who had not complained during
the 1730s when the British established themselves at former English settlements
in the Dawnland, expected the English to honour the 1726 treaty as they had.
Jonathan Belcher, the governor of Massachusetts, agreed. Yet doing so angered
a group of smaller Boston merchants with interests in the region, many of whom
were already frustrated with Belcher’s entry into an argument about establishing
banks. The merchants then used their influence to have the governor replaced.38
The Wabanaki, however, had once again used their territorial control to challenge
British sovereignty.

                                      •••
The competition to control land included a variety of fronts and strategies. Acadi­
ans, whose settlements had expanded along the marshy shores of the Bay of Fundy,
primarily into the Minas Basin and around Chignecto Bay on the isthmus, claimed
their rights to live in these regions. In consequence, they served as proxy agents
keeping the Acadian imperial fiction alive. The British in Nova Scotia built forts
and storehouses to secure a foothold in the disputed region, which they would
98                              Homelands and Empires




      3.3 Extract from Henry Popple’s Map of the British Empire in North America, 1733,
  illustrating the area of contested British settlement from Pemaquid Fort to the St Croix
  River. French officials would later argue that Popple had no choice but to limit English
 claims and emphasize Indigenous names, as the English had no real claim to the region.
                       Library and Archives Canada, H11/1000/1733.


continue to do in response to French settlements along the Bay of Fundy’s western
shore. One particularly contentious location was the Wulstukw/Saint John River,
to which both the British and French claimed title (figure 3.3). In a letter to the
Board of Trade, Lawrence Armstrong noted that “a small colony of French have
settled themselves in St. Johns River, upon the North side of the Bay of Fundy,
who despise and condemn all authority here,” and asked for advice on how to
proceed.39 French officials were no less perturbed at British efforts in the region.
Quebec’s Governor Beauharnois complained to administrators in France that “the
English have continued to build forts in the Baie Française [Bay of Fundy] from
the St. George River to Beaubassin, which they claim is part of Acadia.”40 And so
the pattern continued: the French sent settlers and the British built forts. Acadia’s
role in French foreign policy was one of a bargaining chip often used to ameliorate
France’s position in Europe, evidenced by the Treaty of Utrecht. Yet Maurepas,
the French minister of the Marine, was increasingly concerned with British expan-
sion. Acadia’s limits served as the northeastern boundary of British settlement,
                                  A Time and a Place                                 99


which the French attempted to control by establishing a string of posts from the
St Lawrence River, along the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico.41 In their efforts to
prevent British expansion, the French and Wabanaki were often allies of conve-
nience. In the quest to strengthen one imperial fiction over another, administrators
envisioned Indigenous homelands as strategic buffer zones.
   Robert Walpole and Cardinal Fleury, however, were tired of fighting. Walpole’s
government had only recently come to power in Britain, and Fleury (Louis XV’s
closest advisor), remained sceptical of Gallic abilities to launch any new campaigns.
Both Britain and France were feeling the strain of prolonged fighting, and these
relatively new heads of government encouraged peaceful negotiations that would
allow for rebuilding state coffers and political power. In France, Louis XV found
himself surrounded by weakened allies suffering under the financial burdens of
war, many of whom required time to reorganize finances or were growing closer to
newer allies, as Poland was to Austria and Russia.42 France itself had only recently
suffered the collapse of John Law’s Mississippi Company, which had promised
riches for those who invested in French Louisiana but ultimately left many French
subjects financially ruined.43 Britain was concerned with the Jacobites who, with
the support of France, recognized James Edward Stuart, and then Charles Edward
Stuart, as the rightful king of Britain.44 In the larger context of balancing power
in Europe with aims towards peace, the local complaints emanating from Nova
Scotia rarely garnered a metropolitan response. France’s policy of British contain-
ment was defensive in nature, and Britain’s general disregard for Nova Scotia left
local officials with few instructions.
   Despite the lack of interest from London, the British at Annapolis Royal were
increasingly worried about specific land claims within the peninsula that limit-
ed how they could connect their English pales and thus extend their influence.
One particularly troublesome case was Agathe Saint-Étienne de la Tour, who took
the surname Campbell after marrying her second husband, British officer Hugh
Campbell. Her first marriage was also to an English officer, Lieutenant Edward
Bradstreet, but that union ended with Bradstreet’s death in 1718.45 In 1703, by a
decree from Louis XIV’s Council of state, Mrs Campbell’s family received the sei-
gneurial lands previously granted to her grandfather, Charles de la Tour. The grant
included part of Annapolis Royal, Minas, and Cape Sable. Though in fact she only
inherited her share of the grant – one fifth of the total – she laid claim to the entire
area, arguing that her uncles, aunts, and siblings had bequeathed their shares to
her.46 These interconnections posed a problem for the British.
   Nova Scotia could not be governed like other British provinces; it lacked English
and Protestant settlers and the entrenched powers – both Acadian and Indigenous
– were difficult to co-opt for the British cause.47 The British tactic of extinguishing
Acadian land grants and creating new ones for future Protestant settlers was not
easily implemented. Agathe Campbell’s case reveals the Atlantic nature of British
territorial expansion, as British officials had faced similar challenges to their au-
thority when they attempted to assert the king’s sovereignty over Ireland by re-
granting lands.48 Control over geography was of paramount concern, but the law
demanded that Britain recognize and legally terminate grants that existed before
1713. While in Canso during his second of two visits to Nova Scotia, Governor
Philipps wrote to the Duke of Newcastle about three or four Acadian families,
100                            Homelands and Empires


including Mrs Campbell’s, that were claiming large areas of Nova Scotia. For
proof, Philipps had received “a foul script of paper, which they say is a copy of
part of the original grant … but I have told them that all pretensions to seigneuries
fell to the ground at the conquest of the country.”49 Despite Philipps’s confidence,
the matter would not be settled quite so easily.
   Three years later, the question was still under consideration; without the ability
to determine how territory would be controlled and used, Britain’s rights granted
by the Treaty of Utrecht would be worthless. Philipps warned the Board of Trade,
to whom Mrs Campbell had presented a petition, that Campbell “imposes gross-
ly” by claiming that she is the sole heir to the lands, when several other descen-
dants laid claim to La Tour’s original grant.50 The Privy Council considered Mrs
Campbell’s petition and received the following advice from the Board of Trade:
“Whereupon we would take leave to propose that his Majesty should be gracious-
ly pleased to order a valuable consideration to be paid to the petitioner for her
said quit rents, and also for the extinguishment of her claim to any other part of
Nova Scotia.”51 Her right to the lands, though contentious, was recognized and
she was paid £2,000.52 The cost of extinguishing Campbell’s seigneurial holdings
was deemed necessary to ensure Britain’s ability to grant lands legally in the fu-
ture. Allured Popple, secretary of the Board of Trade, argued that Mrs Campbell’s
weakened health made the matter even more pressing, as there was no guarantee
that her heirs would be as anxious to settle.53 N.E.S. Griffiths has argued that the
extinguishing of previous grants and the purchase of Mrs Campbell’s title “was an
affirmation of the British crown as the sole source of property rights in the colony.”54
Britain might have gained de jure ability to grant lands, but their de facto territorial
control was far from established.
   Purchasing grants and subsuming Acadians into a British property system was a
contested process much more complicated than a simple exchange of grants might
suggest. Governor Philipps complained that the Acadians were “like Noah’s prog-
eny spreading themselves over the face of the province,” which meant securing
an oath of loyalty to King George was growing increasingly important.55 British
concern about Acadian loyalty began in 1710 and was exasperated by both the
close proximity of Quebec and Louisbourg and most Acadians’ refusal to swear
an unconditional oath.56 Surveys and grants were one way to make Nova Scotia
British, at least on paper: if Acadian land grants were replaced with those issued
from the British Crown, Acadians would be one step closer to becoming British
subjects. The British debated over several decades how to put an English stamp
on Acadia: suggestions ranged from expelling the Acadians and assimilating the
Mi’kmaq to Anglicizing the former while forcing the latter out of the region.57
Loyalty was important, as was ensuring that Britain had subjects to govern in
Nova Scotia; there were, after all, only a few hundred British citizens at Annapolis
Royal (most of whom were soldiers), so it was imperative to convert Acadians
into British subjects. Yet the Acadians resisted British attempts to control how they
would expand and by what right they would claim property. Lieutenant Governor
Mascarene wanted to use the dispensation of property to secure an oath of al-
legiance. Acadians would be granted legal title to their lands (and, presumably,
lands into which they might expand) only if they swore an unconditional oath
of allegiance. Mascarene believed that if he could convince the Acadians of the
                                  A Time and a Place                                101


advantages of holding their lands in the name of the king, and if he could per-
suade them to appeal to the Council to resolve disputes, he would be able to win
them over gradually to the British government.58 For most of the Acadians, how-
ever, there was little motivation to become British subjects because they paid such
low rents to the French government (which were only sporadically collected).59
   Administrators at Annapolis Royal had no choice but to compromise and rely
on local and organic negotiations to address what were at heart imperial prob-
lems. While surveys might suggest to administrators in London that Acadians
were slowly succumbing to British law and territorial practices, such was hardly
the case. Unable to secure territorial authority in Nova Scotia, but unwilling to
admit that the Acadians could move about the province as they wished, British
officials relied on the Acadians to monitor themselves. Regional deputies, elected
by Acadians and serving as conduits between the inhabitants and the government,
became increasingly involved in land management. The Council was flooded with
property disputes and had to wade through complicated French contrats and inher-
ited seigneurial grants, not all of which led to a clear explanation of title. As Thomas
Barnes has argued, “from the outset the British regime tacitly equated ‘right’ with
possession if supported by contrat or inheritance from contrat.”60 Issuing new grants
depended on completing new surveys, which was difficult because there was no
surveyor in Nova Scotia before 1732. Acadians resisted land surveys and were little
concerned with the threatened reprisals from Annapolis Royal, aware as they were
of the government’s weakness.61 When surveys were performed, local officials re-
lied on Acadian deputies to oversee the work and report on the results; it was not
uncommon for the surveys themselves to resolve little. A local solution was thus
required. In April of 1735, René Blanchard, of Minas, presented the Council with
a petition complaining that Anthoine Celestine, Claud Babin, and their associates
had trespassed on his land. A map was produced and both sides offered argu-
ments and responses. The Council turned the matter over to the Acadians: “The
Board agreed as by the plan their difference could not easily be understood, That
the Secretary should write an order to four of the Deputys to choose four of the
Antient Indifferent Inhabitants of the Grand Pré in order to go upon the Spot, to
visite the Situation of their ground & the road in dispute; & to make a Report &
plan thereof in order to be laid before His Honour.”62 Cartographic limitations
forced the British to rely on “antient indifferent inhabitants” who were as likely
to rely on local custom as they were on British law. Government officials also re-
lied on Acadian deputies to monitor settlers around an area known as “the Lake,”
when a map proved insufficient to determine property boundaries. Settlers were
warned not to expand beyond the present boundaries. They did anyway, aware
that officials’ threats were empty and that Acadian custom could regulate lands.63
   Creating surveys was a necessary step in the process of securing territorial con-
trol within a geographic fiction, but the opposite was also true: resisting surveys
was a direct challenge to administrative authority. Surveying was not an occupa-
tion that required extensive training, nor was it generally a career. It was a skill
that could be acquired through some instruction and perhaps an apprenticeship.64
In colonial Virginia, for example, “until the cadastral surveyor’s chain traversed
the land, it could not be converted to private property and personal advantage.”65
Determining Acadian land tenure was a difficult task. Before 1710 “metes and
102                           Homelands and Empires


bounds were probably the rule, but most farmers probably never held a notarized
deed from a seigneur for their land or paid any seigneurial dues.”66 The system of
metes and bounds provided a workable, though not always accurate, definition
of property. It relied on the local geography or other property lines to describe
the perimeter of a parcel of land, often citing distances and corner angles to clar-
ify possession. After 1710, surveying was informally completed by deputies and,
when available, a government surveyor. In 1731, the Council prepared to publish
a notice for the Acadian deputies ordering them to employ the king’s surveyor
(likely Dunbar or one of his associates) and reminding them that his work required
payment.67 The lack of progress in this matter suggests that Acadians were simply
unwilling to pay for a surveyor, whose work would result in increased quitrents.68
   While this refusal was frustrating to officials at Annapolis Royal, the Acadian
position provided a scapegoat for the failings of the province; as long as officials
could claim that Acadians were illegally occupying the best lands, there was a
reason for the paucity of British settlers.69 The Acadians, on the other hand, were
demonstrating their ability to extend geographic control over new territories. The
British recognized Acadian territorial strength (to an extent), and the Acadians
similarly supported titular British rule over the province. As N.E.S. Griffiths has
argued, the Acadians “considered themselves the rightful inhabitants of the lands
on which they lived, not just as negotiable assets to be moved about as pawns for
the purposes of a distant empire,” but also “accepted that the English officials at
Annapolis Royal had a final jurisdiction over a broad area of Acadian life.”70 The
struggle over geographic control clearly demonstrates how Acadians and British
authorities negotiated this difficult relationship.

                                     •••
Acadian resistance to surveys that would incorporate land into the British legal
structure and a general lack of useful maps that would make strong claims to
the British nature of Nova Scotia required the creation of local responses and ac-
tions that could allow Indigenous, British, and Acadian groups to coexist in the
northeast. British jurisdictional weakness (even when tacitly recognized by the
Acadians) and Britain’s inability to attract significant Indigenous support meant
that Mi’kma’ki remained a homeland, though one facing greater challenges from
competing groups. Consequently, the province abounded with opportunity and
ambition remained a driving force among the French, British, and Indigenous
groups. But as long as territorial sovereignty was regulated by each group’s desire
to limit the strength of the others, pockets of shared spaces – areas where the three
groups could interact for mutual benefit – provided outlets for the economic, po-
litical, and religious needs of Nova Scotia’s varied populace. These particular sites
of interaction were seasonal and temporal, influenced most heavily by migration
patterns, the push and pull of fishing seasons, and the annual conferences and
religious ceremonies celebrated by the French and the Wabanaki. With no single
authoritative body controlling the province, territory could be shared when the
conditions permitted.
   Shared spaces were often seasonal or fleeting, which indicates that time was as
important as place. Exploring when these areas operated (and not just where the
                                  A Time and a Place                               103


sites were located) helps explain how the system of interaction operated. Trade,
negotiation, and religion – all of which depended on the existence of certain shared
spaces – forced each group to attempt to understand the cultural norms of another.
Material goods served economic and spiritual ends; agreements were expressed in
terms that could reflect the world views of both European and Indigenous diplo-
macy, even when influenced by deceit; and shared religious beliefs brought differ-
ent groups together in ways that allowed each to learn about the other. Unlike in
the pays d’en haut, where, as Richard White has argued, refugee Indigenous groups
and a weak French presence demanded that each group express their desires in
terms that another could understand and support, there were in Mi’kma’ki de-
fined (though not homogeneous) groups with a strong sense of their own culture.71
However, during the relatively peaceful period of 1727–44, those groups had to in-
teract with each other in ways that would address individual needs and concerns
in a milieu of balanced territorial strength. Shared spaces in Mi’kma’ki – which
existed as temporary moments in time as well as at specific territorial sites – facili-
tated those interactions, but those spaces existed only when each group attempted
to understand the concerns of the others.
   Canso, the harbour and collection of islands on the northeast coast of peninsu-
lar Nova Scotia over which much ink (and no small amount of blood) had been
spilt at the close of the second decade of the eighteenth century, remained a con-
tested and economically important region in the 1720s and 1730s. Despite the vio-
lence and conflict that led to Canso’s eventual de facto control by British forces,
the region remained a shared site of economic exchange among the Mi’kmaq
and the British, and, to a lesser extent, the French. The Mi’kmaq had traded with
Europeans for hundreds of years, and their reasons for carrying out that trade
were myriad, such as material gain, spiritual development, and alliance building.72
In Nova Scotia, the Mi’kmaw ability to trade peacefully depended on how well
they balanced their economic interests with preserving their territory. The balance
was even more difficult because past violent acts were difficult to forget. In 1727,
the Wulstukwiuk and Passamaquoddy were worried that British ships (primar-
ily from New England) stationed at Canso might continue to harass Indigenous
peoples as they had before the peace of 1726. Lieutenant Governor Armstrong did
his best to convince them that such was not the case. Armstrong reassured the
Mi’kmaq, the Wulstukwiuk, and the Passamaquoddy that they would be safe and
invited them to continue fishing at Canso. He also invited them to visit him and re-
ceive “the marks of his friendship,” including gifts and reassuring words.73 Canso
was an important commercial site coveted by both the French and the British,
and the Mi’kmaq often raided settlers of both nations and suffered reprisals for
their actions. However, despite French complaints, the Mi’kmaq continued to visit
Canso and traded with the English as long as peaceful conditions persisted.74
   However, challenges arose even without an Indigenous presence until the late
1730s. It could be difficult for British settlers in Nova Scotia and their neighbours
in New England to share such a valuable area. The British encouraged trade with
the Indigenous peoples as a means of winning their allegiance, but the settlers
and officers at Canso were unable to secure from the Mi’kmaq the clothes, uten-
sils, and furnishings required for daily life. To secure these necessities, the British
at Canso were forced to rely on New England. Fishermen and merchants from
104                            Homelands and Empires


New England visited Canso, bringing with them necessary and valuable supplies
which the local inhabitants purchased at great expense.75 Tension over Canso be-
tween the British in Nova Scotia and the New England settlers began before 1720
and focused primarily on land use. Governor Philipps had done what he could
to regulate operations in the region by granting fishing lots and garden plots to
fishermen, hoping to mollify their complaints and increase the fishery’s utility.
Protecting the shared space was difficult because official British policy, that no
new fortifications be erected before a province-wide policy had been tabled, ran
counter to the immediate needs of New England fishermen. The government at
Annapolis Royal did what it could – relying on contributions from the fishermen
themselves to raise an inadequate fort – to regulate shared space in a way that
would bring more profits to those involved in the fishery while serving the needs
of the permanent settlers.76
   As a common space, Canso was not only shared but also seasonal. Buzzing with
fishermen and traders during the summer months, the region was largely deserted
in the winter. In 1729, only three families were reported to be year-round inhabit-
ants; by the mid 1730s there was a school with up to fifty students, but the settle-
ment remained largely transitory.77 Yet in 1735, Lieutenant Governor Armstrong
described Canso as the only place of value in the province, and encouraged the
construction of fortifications to defend the British against French attackers.78 French
fishermen continued to visit Canso and profit from its fishery, much to the dismay
of officials in London, who were aware of how Canso was shared but could do little
to stop it.79
   Canso demonstrates how seasonal and temporal forces influenced a region’s
importance. Different groups arrived at Canso at different times: the Mi’kmaq
during their hunting and fishing rounds, traders when the weather permitted ac-
cess, fishermen in the summer, and military personnel when administrators were
concerned about an attack. Even though the British had established a fort and a
small settlement, Canso remained an area of interaction that benefitted those who
could establish themselves there even temporarily. To the French, Canso remained
British-occupied French territory. The official negotiations over the collection of
islands held in the early 1720s had not resolved the issue, and though Governor
Philipps had managed to exclude most of the French from the region during the
1720s, it remained a disputed territory. In many ways, the debates over Canso that
went unresolved after the Treaty of Utrecht were reborn in the 1730s and early
1740s as Canso’s value transitioned from an economic site to a militarily strategic
one. The French argument rested, as it always had, on the wording of the Treaty of
Utrecht and a spattering of maps that supported their cause. The French translation
of the treaty suggested that all islands in the mouth of the Gulf of the St Lawrence
(Canso would perhaps fall into this category) belonged to France. At the time of
the dispute the English had presented a map of Nova Scotia to prove their point,
but the French believed that they had “demonstrated to the English by the same
map that the Gulf of St. Lawrence had three mouths.”80 The first fell between the
coast of Labrador and the northern part of Newfoundland, the second between
the eastern part of Île Royale and the southern tip of Newfoundland, and the
third between the western part of Île Royale and the land of Acadia. According to
the French, Canso rested in this third mouth, and therefore belonged to France.81
                                 A Time and a Place                              105


   The British had a response to these arguments, and a plan for the future of Canso,
in the figure of John Henry Bastide. Little is known of Bastide’s birth or parent-
age, but he joined a regiment of Foot at a young age. He eventually purchased the
rank of lieutenant and then focused on his work as an engineer, a decision that
prevented rapid advancement as engineers often found themselves in a largely
unrecognized military appointment. After several years’ service in Britain, Bastide
was appointed chief engineer at Annapolis Royal. He turned his attention to for-
tifying British forts and making maps and plans of extant and future fortifications
in the region. Bastide somehow managed to make a plan of the French Fortress
Louisbourg in 1734 that was so accurate historians and archaeologists used it more
than two hundred years later to reconstruct the fort’s history.82 Before the out-
break of war in 1744, Bastide was employed in assessing fortifications, making the
necessary changes, and preparing for conflict in New England and Nova Scotia.83
As an indication of Canso’s strategic importance, Bastide prepared several maps
for proposed fortifications on the islands and mainland surrounding the harbour
(figures 3.4 and 3.5).
   Canso was attacked and easily taken by the French in one of the first North
American campaigns of the War of the Austrian Succession on 24 May 1744. Had
the region been fortified to the standards set out in Bastide’s 1742 plans, however,
French troops might not have gotten off Île Royale. In his maps of Canso, Bastide
anticipated a strong fortress and grand battery bookending the peninsula known
as Canso Island. In between could be found an old blockhouse and the soldiers’ and
officers’ houses. An inset sketch, entitled “View of Canso Island, with the Fort
and Grand Battery as they would appear from W.So.W if Perform’d as Projected
and Propos’d,” depicted a strong and secure Canso. A second map contained a
more detailed depiction of the Battery and a garrison for three hundred men. Far
from the weak fortifications that would made Canso ripe for the taking, Bastide’s
maps helped local officials and the Board of Ordinance (who presumably request-
ed the surveys in the first place) envision northeast peninsular Nova Scotia as a
valuable military site worth defending and protecting, not simply a failing fishery
and sporadically populated collection of islands. That these drawings were pre-
pared suggests two things: Canso had previously been unprotected, and Canso
was not yet fully British. To transform a shared economic site into a well defended
British settlement was easily done on maps but never fully realized on the ground.
As long as the waters produced fish, the claims, counter-claims, and a desire to
trade ensured that Canso remained a shared space. When its prominence as a com-
mercial site diminished, confusion over boundaries and imperial aspirations kept
Canso central to negotiated territorial sovereignty.

                                     •••
Unlike economic spaces, which were often seasonal but recurred with regular-
ity, spaces of negotiation were temporary and existed briefly but could be recre-
ated as necessary. Their nature also depended on which parties were participating.
Indigenous peoples were most likely to frequent spaces of negotiation, where
groups met to discuss concerns, to resolve problems, or to engage in treaty mak-
ing.84 The Great Peace of 1701, at which the French formalized a long-desired treaty
106                              Homelands and Empires

 Scotia, 1742. The fort, projected fort, and settlements are indicated. National Archives,
                                 London. MR1/1783 (1–6).
3.5 Extract from J.H. Bastide’s Particular Plan and Survey of the Harbour of Canso in Nova Scotia, 1742. The fort, projected fort,

108                            Homelands and Empires


with the Iroquois, brought representatives from over forty nations to Montreal to
witness “a spectacular expression of this spirit of adaptation and of the intensity
of cultural exchange in the diplomatic sphere.”85 British-Indigenous spaces of ne-
gotiation were often located at British settlements and forts, or on important and
convenient transportation routes. This choice of location required the superim-
position of one space – that of negotiation – over another. French-Indigenous ne-
gotiations took place in forts, shared religious spaces, or Indigenous settlements.
Fundamental to French officials’ success with Indigenous peoples was their will-
ingness to travel regularly to sites of Indigenous significance, a practice British
administrators failed to implement. Spaces of negotiation were ultimately trans-
portable and powerful, as they could exist in areas otherwise avoided by one or
both sides. During this era of enforced peace, these shared spaces allowed all in-
volved to nurture relationships, resolve grievances, and monitor territorial limits
without resorting to violence.
   British spaces of negotiation, at Annapolis Royal and elsewhere, were particular-
ly ephemeral. From 1726 to 1728, the fort was periodically transformed into a more
welcoming space for Indigenous peoples where procedures such as exchanging
gifts encouraged cordial relations. It was there that Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk
leaders met with British officials to ratify the treaty struck at Boston. In his report
to the secretary of state of the Southern Department, Armstrong described the cor-
dial meeting: “In the month of May last an Indian tribe consisting of about 26 men
under the command of 3 or 4 of their sachems from the village of Meductoo, an
Indian settlement fifty odd leagues up the River of St. Johns, came here to ratify
the Peace concluded at Boston and to make their submission to the government,
whereupon I advised with the commission officers here in the Garrison about their
treatment and reception, who were unanimously of opinion that they should be
handsomely entertained while they staid and at their going away should receive
some testimonies and marks of his majestie’s bounty.”86 Confusion over the mean-
ing of the treaty notwithstanding, the negotiation itself illustrates the importance,
to both Wabanaki and British residents, of creating spaces of negotiation in which
the terms of a relationship could be discussed and debated. The exchange of gifts
was an essential element of Indigenous-European negotiation. The French relied
on annual ceremonies at which gifts were exchanged to renew alliances and re-
ceive information about events that had occurred throughout Nova Scotia. The
earliest records of these exchanges date to the 1690s and indicate that the French
government spent up to 4,000 livres a year on gifts for the Mi’kmaq, Penobscot,
Abenaki, and Wulstukwiuk.87 The British at Nova Scotia struggled to compete
with French gifts and often were unable to satisfy the Mi’kmaw demand for pres-
ents. When the Mi’kmaq appeared to warm to the British, the French increased the
amount of presents they gave.88
   The British regularly underestimated the importance of gifts and diplomacy, re-
sponding to perceived Indigenous wrongdoings by limiting or ending exchanges
and refusing to reanimate spaces of negotiation. This lack of cultural understand-
ing damaged British officials’ ability to exert their influence beyond Annapolis
Royal. In 1734, Governor Richard Philipps was asked to account for the money
allotted for Indigenous presents. He began by blaming one of his agents, Mr
Bamfield, for spending the money carelessly and keeping half for himself. “His
                                  A Time and a Place                               109


death,” Philipps explained, “prevented the more full detection of that Fraud.”89
Other reasons for not providing the Mi’kmaq with gifts included the poor weather
(which in 1721 prevented the goods from being shipped from Boston to Annapolis
Royal), and Indigenous hostility (which Philipps felt should hardly be rewarded
with presents). Even when the gifts were presented to Indigenous chiefs, Philipps
argued, there was little security that those good relations would last. After hold-
ing meetings with several chiefs at Canso and sending them off with presents,
Philipps learned that the Mi’kmaq had attacked British vessels, killed some of the
seamen, and kept others as navigators. In response, Philipps charged two ships
with a counter-attack. The sailors killed a number of the Mi’kmaq and returned
with a severed head to show Philipps, who recognized the victim as one of the
men to whom he had given presents just a few weeks before. Philipps concluded
that the gift-giving must end. “They will take whatever we give them,” he argued,
“and cut our throats the next day if our neighbours see it in their interest to disturb
our settlements.”90 Philipps, who spent more time in Britain than in Nova Scotia,
might not have understood the intricacies of Indigenous negotiation and alliance
building. On the other hand, his lieutenant, Armstrong, argued to the Board of
Trade just two months later that annual presents for the Indigenous peoples could
help secure their friendship.91
   Despite Armstrong’s suggestions, the weakest settlement in the British northeast
followed a policy that relied more on military strength than on creating places for
sustained diplomatic exchanges. In the end, threats of violence only masked a lack
of power. By failing to provide adequate presents or engage fully with Indigenous
diplomacy, the British in Nova Scotia were creating particularly ephemeral and in-
effective spaces of negotiation that did not allow for the airing of grievances or
provide an effective forum for dispute resolution. However, in other parts of the
northeast throughout much of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, there were
many negotiations in which the British recognized Indigenous strength, evidenced
by the fact that negotiations followed Indigenous protocol.92 These ceremonies were
rife with misunderstanding. Mohawk speechmakers “phrased their arguments
in a ceremonial language that differed almost as much from everyday Mohawk
speech as did the King James Bible from the ordinary discourse of New England
farmers raised in East Anglia.”93 The same was true for the Mi’kmaq. In diplomatic
exchanges with the French, Mi’kmaw orators expressed their ideas in metaphors,
allegories, and rich turns of phrase.94 But the ceremony itself was important as it
brought together different groups in an area of cultural exchange. Mi’kmaw ne-
gotiations with the French established a pattern that the British failed to follow.
Meetings usually took place in June or July, discussion rarely began until after both
sides had the opportunity to rest after their journey, and gifts were expected.95
   By the early eighteenth century, treaty protocol throughout eastern North
America followed a similar pattern that focused on creating a welcoming space.
First, an invitation to meet was dispatched, followed by determining who would
speak first. Next came a ceremonial procession to the site and an “At the Wood’s
Edge” rite during which delegates were welcomed and made comfortable. More
ceremonial stages followed until the site of the meeting was considered ready for
undertaking diplomatic business. Creating a space for negotiation was important,
and prospective meetings could be scuttled or cut short if the proposed site was
110                           Homelands and Empires


unacceptable or protocol ignored.96 Samuel Shute had learned this lesson in 1717.
At Annapolis Royal, however, British officials were prepared to meet to confirm
treaties but were less willing to engage in continued negotiations to develop lasting
alliances. The result was a fragile peace and territorial balance, but nothing more.
   The French were aware that one-time gifts did not ensure allegiance, and that
relationships with Indigenous peoples had to be constantly negotiated. For this
reason the governor of Île Royale made annual trips throughout the island, as well
as to Île St Jean, creating temporary but recurring spaces of negotiation to which
the region’s Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk were invited. The consistency with which
French officials engaged in these temporary meetings spaces facilitated a fluid but
enduring relationship with the Wabanaki. The discussions at these conferences –
which were as likely to be held at places of convenient access for the Wabanaki
as at the strongest French settlements – ranged from an exchange of news to de-
mands for assistance and requests for military alliance. The French officials were
careful to do what they could to help the Wabanaki without openly breaching their
peace with the British. In 1729, Saint-Ovide received a request from the chiefs of
Beaubassin and Pisiquid, two Acadian villages, who had suffered an English attack
and wanted revenge. They asked Saint-Ovide to assist them, but he informed them
that he could not and they seemed to understand.97 The French, unlike the British,
entered into an open dialogue with the Indigenous peoples to foster a stronger re-
lationship, one based on shared cultural knowledge and respect, that was capable
of withstanding minor setbacks.
   It was primarily through the consistent creation of areas of negotiation – though
seasonal or annual – that the French learned how Indigenous society functioned,
and what was required to maintain an alliance. Conferences exposed the alliances
and disagreements within the region’s Indigenous groups. Saint-Ovide learned
from a group of Wulstukwiuk that had arrived by canoe from the Wulskukw River
that a number of their nation had previously gone to Boston to make peace – the
treaty of 1726 – but others were not prepared to do so. They wanted to renew their
alliance with the French and, since they had not received presents in some time,
requested a gift. Saint-Ovide complied and the Wulstukwiuk were pleased.98 The
French governor also settled disputes between Indigenous groups that could oth-
erwise have persisted. When a few Wulstukwiuk complained that a Mi’kmaw had
murdered one of their nation, Saint-Ovide gave presents to atone for the death and
promised not to forget what had happened.99 These fleeting areas of interaction,
created and dissolved as the need arose, were as much about acquiring cultural
knowledge and giving groups a better understanding of each other as they were
about settling disputes.
   Another benefit of conferences and created sites of negotiation was the ability
of both sides to discuss their disappointment in the other and take the necessary
steps to remedy the situation without resorting to violence. More than simple sites
for exchanging gifts and discussing alliances, “the conferences with Native peo-
ples … functioned as a kind of court where cross-cultural transgressions could be
openly settled.”100 When Saint-Ovide learned that a group of Mi’maq had gone to
Canso and received alcohol, he informed their elders that if such behaviour con-
tinued they would anger the French, their “father.” The Mi’kmaw elders retired,
discussed the problem, and returned later to tell Saint-Ovide that they were aware
                                 A Time and a Place                               111


of the actions of a few of the young members, and that they would be willing to
summon them so that Saint-Ovide could chastise them as he saw fit.101 With this
matter resolved, the elders then expressed their concern that France had aban-
doned them spiritually, as they no longer enjoyed the presence of a missionary
priest. It was then Saint-Ovide’s turn to apologize, which he did by reassuring
the Mi’kmaq that he had requested more missionaries from France to serve in
their communities.102 The alliance thus refreshed, presents were distributed, the
shared space was dissolved, and all retired to their homes.
   Though the topics discussed at these meetings shaped how the two groups in-
teracted, the locations of the discussions – temporary sites established as need-
ed and then abandoned – demonstrated French and Indigenous views of shared
territory and illuminated barriers between local and imperial spaces of power.
French officials respected Indigenous migratory patterns but also emphasized the
separation of Indigenous and imperial sites of negotiation. Sometimes French of-
ficials would travel to Indigenous settlements or meet at a variety of convenient
spots along a popular Indigenous seasonal route, and at other times the Wabanaki
travelled to French forts. Though French administrators spoke on behalf of the
king and represented his authority and magnificence, there came times when
the Wabanaki wanted to see for themselves.103 Indigenous peoples had crossed the
Atlantic for hundreds of years. Alden T. Vaughan has documented the voyages of
approximately 175 Indigenous peoples who arrived in Britain before the American
Revolution, challenging the stereotype that most Indigenous peoples in Europe,
having been stolen from North America, were displayed as oddities and then
died. Vaughan suggests that most Indigenous peoples “crossed the Atlantic …
voluntarily, conducted serious business abroad, survived the exposure to deadly
viruses, and, safely home, influenced their own people.”104 But Indigenous peoples
who wanted to attend European negotiations were rarely granted permission to
do so. In 1737, New France governor the Marquis de Beauharnois, informed the
king that he had received requests from the Abenaki in Acadia to travel to France
so they could witness the king’s majesty and confirm his power for themselves.
He had interpreters tell them that there was no point in making such a journey.105
French officials wanted to control how authority was explained and displayed,
and therefore preferred to keep their negotiation sites local and temporary.
   The request to visit European monarchs was a reasonable reaction to the pro-
cess of land negotiations that often excluded an Indigenous voice. The Wabanaki
were aware that British and French monarchs granted land unilaterally, and they
were troubled by their exclusion from an important space of negotiation across
the ocean. The importance that Indigenous peoples placed on the spatial elements
of diplomacy (including sites of welcome and Wood’s Edge ceremonies) explains
Indigenous requests to cross the Atlantic and engage in discussions or protest their
exclusion from territorial decisions. Just as Indigenous groups invited European
officials to sit and discuss land issues at properly designated sites, so too did they
expect to be full and present participants in any European negotiations concern-
ing their territory. Beauharnois fielded complaints from the Eastern Abenaki, who
questioned the British practice of securing land concessions from their king. “An
English captain who went to England two years ago,” the Abenaki lamented, “car-
ried with him a map of our lands. Upon his return he told us that the King had
112                            Homelands and Empires


given him the concession and that he would seize our lands. We are confident
that no one can take the lands from us because they belong to us. But he wants to
act as if the lands belong to him and he has already started to build on them.”106
The Abenaki were willing to negotiate land dealings when proper protocol, in-
cluding a ceremony held in a shared space of negotiation, was followed. When
excluded from the process, they became concerned. The French reassured their
Abenaki allies that despite the peace between Britain and France, Indigenous ef-
forts to resist the British could proceed.107 Spaces of negotiation were important
temporary sites of cross-cultural interaction, but they better served willing par-
ticipants. The French, who had a longer and more collegial relationship with the
Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, Passamaquoddy, and Abenaki, and were willing to create
seasonal or annual sites of negotiation, therefore benefitted more than the weaker
British, whose limited territorial power was never legitimated as authority beyond
the walls of their forts.

                                      •••
Shared religious spaces also helped address power imbalances. The Mi’kmaq, Wul­
stukwiuk, and Eastern Abenaki had long been exposed to Catholic missionaries,
and most had been converted to Christianity. The Treaty of Utrecht preserved for
the Acadians the practice of their religion while reserving for British administra-
tors the right to appoint and dismiss Catholic priests in the region. Consequently,
religious spaces represented a strange amalgam: shared religious practice (among
the French and many of the Mi’kmaq) overseen and begrudgingly accepted by the
British (who remained distant and mostly excluded from these spaces). Examining
the administration of religious difference emphasizes the utility of shared spaces,
the complexity of their creation and maintenance, and the challenges faced by
British authorities who had to square local realities with imperial ideals.
   For all their influence, Catholic priests were largely unsuccessful in shaping
settlement patterns or religious-ethnic boundaries in Acadia. They were unable to
convince most French inhabitants or the Mi’kmaq to relocate to Île Royale and Île
St Jean after 1713, and their temporal authority was not regarded as beyond contra-
diction.108 Catholicism was not a monolithic force, and Acadian settlers, Indigenous
peoples, and British officials responded to religious demands in different ways.
Catholic missionaries and clergymen were instrumental in securing Indigenous
alliances and influencing the Acadian world view, but ignoring Catholicism’s in-
ternal debates (such as conflicts over Jansenism) elides the complexity of religion
in the eighteenth century. There was, however, a change in French religious policy
in the northeast after 1713 that led to the establishment of permanent missions
among the Indigenous peoples, and the construction of churches and presbyteries
to facilitate missionary work.109 This increased effort by the French was not imi-
tated by the British, who found it difficult to relate to the Mi’kmaq on a spiritual
level; efforts to sow Protestantism among Indigenous peoples yielded little fruit.110
   For French missionaries to be successful, they had to create sites of religious ac-
commodation or serve the Mi’kmaq in Acadian settlements. These spiritual houses
blended Catholic and Mi’kmaw elements and depended on the peripatetic na-
ture of missionary priests. Though not specifically seasonal, temporary places of
                                 A Time and a Place                             113


worship were portable and, since they depended on the presence of a missionary,
ultimately fleeting. The transition to permanent churches and chapels after 1722
took on a geographic element as missionaries encouraged relocation to areas bet-
ter suited to Indigenous winter hunting grounds (and, conveniently, more distant
from English settlements). Thus, in 1725, the missionary at Antigonish was moved
to Bras d’Or on Unama’ki/Île Royale.111 Though these new mission sites featured
well-built chapels, as late as 1745 Abbé Maillard found himself preaching to the
Mi’kmaq in a temporary structure constructed from birch bark and pine logs. As
William C. Wicken has suggested, such a building offered no clear demarcation be-
tween Catholic priests and Indigenous shamans. These spaces facilitated religious
accommodation and could be easily disassembled, and thus “did not constitute a
permanent symbolic intrusion into a village’s territory.”112
   When shared sites of religious interaction were wanting, the Mi’kmaq would
travel to Acadian parishes for important ceremonies such as marriages and bap-
tisms,113 which could turn the body into a shared spiritual site. Names given to
baptised Indigenous peoples defined the person as a shared site of religious hy-
bridity. Jean-Baptiste Cope, the leader of a Mi’kmaw tribe near Shubenacadie, was
baptised as a young boy in the early eighteenth century and given a name that
reflected his Indigenous heritage (Cope is a shortened version of the Mi’kmaw
word for beaver) and the Catholic faith (John the Baptist).114 Elizabeth Mancke has
argued that English monarchs claimed sovereignty over the bodies of their sub-
jects overseas, and those same subjects could claim rights due to them “even if the
only sovereign English space was their very bodies.”115 Similarly, in places where
sovereignty was contested at every turn, those bodies represented the shared and
somewhat ambiguous identities that moved through the region. Temporary sites
of religious exchange defined by portable and fleeting sites of worship, coupled
with naming practices that reflected spiritual hybridity, demonstrate how religious
spaces worked to encourage interaction and maintain a balance between French
Acadia and Indigenous homelands in the Northeast. British Nova Scotia remained
excluded from these interactions.
   British efforts to introduce the Protestant faith among Acadians and the Wabanaki
resulted in “unintended consequences and unexpected outcomes.”116 In 1730, Gov­
ernor Philipps expressed his frustration over the Board of Trade’s slow response to
overtures from Protestant proselytizers, sending the Duke of Newcastle a proposal
he received from a French Protestant missionary who wanted to settle one hun-
dred Protestant families in Nova Scotia. After receiving no reply, Philipps lamented
that such projects were not “embraced and encouraged” by London administra-
tors, especially considering the difficulties Nova Scotia was having attracting set-
tlers and granting lands.117 Officials in Britain faced financial and organizational
challenges, and Nova Scotia’s inability to introduce Protestantism to Indigenous
inhabitants (and Acadians) was indicative of the Church of England’s limited
success at converting non-Protestants in North America.118 One consequence of
failing to attract Protestant settlers who could convert Catholics was the limit-
ed pool of possible militia members, since “Papists” were ineligible.119 Its failure
to take full advantage of available French Protestants was a lost opportunity for
the British administration. French officials had long attempted to limit settlement
to Catholics, and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685) led to hundreds of
114                            Homelands and Empires


thousands of French Protestants looking for new areas to settle.120 As a potential
bridge between Acadians and British subjects (not to mention a formidable settle-
ment block that could have helped reorganize Nova Scotia’s internal borders and
boundaries), Huguenots might have been the assimilating force so desired by
King George’s representatives.
   Despite Protestantism’s weakness in the face of a largely Catholic populace,
British officials in Nova Scotia influenced shared religious spaces insofar as they
could approve the construction of chapels and had the exclusive right to appoint
or remove Catholic priests in the province. Lieutenant Governor Paul Mascarene
was particularly well-suited for his post in Nova Scotia and for the religious is-
sues he was forced to address. A French Huguenot who fled France with his father
after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, Mascarene was raised and educated in
Geneva before entering the military, serving in campaigns in Nova Scotia, eventu-
ally being named lieutenant governor. He did his best to remain on good terms
with the Acadians and expressed deep concern over their religious practices. In­
stead of deriding their faith, Mascarene entered into spirited, yet friendly corre-
spondence with leading members of the Catholic clergy.121 Like other government
officials at Annapolis Royal, Mascarene kept tabs on the comings and goings of
priests as best he could, and often chastised Acadian deputies for failing to report
the arrival of new priests.122 He was also forced to remind the religious authori-
ties in Quebec of Britain’s jurisdiction over clerical authority in Nova Scotia. He
reported to the Board of Trade that a bishop in Quebec “pretends to the power of
sending at pleasure his Missionaries into this Government, as presuming it a part
of his diocese, and would dignify one or more of those with the title of his grand
Vicars for the Province.”123 Mascarene viewed the attempted superimposition of
religious space (a diocese) onto an administrative unit (a province) as a threat to
his authority. He wrote to Bishop Pontbriand – addressing him as “monsieur” in-
stead of the more respectful “monseigneur” – and reminded him of the limits of
religious power. “I hope,” Mascarene wrote, “that the distinguished reputation
that you enjoy in your church will lead you to prevent the desolation and ruin
that certain of your missionaries have very nearly brought to this province’s in-
habitants.”124 Acadians could practice their Catholic faith under the guidance of a
French priest, but those priests were to be approved by the Nova Scotia Council.
Otherwise the British would have no influence over religion in the province, thus
weakening their ability to win the Acadians over to the British interest.125
   Mascarene was particularly concerned about competition from Catholic au-
thorities. Put simply, a diocese could not be allowed to challenge British civic rule.
Mascarene wrote to the missionary Jean-Baptiste Desenclaves to discuss how a
priest’s religious authority, when extended into a civic setting, would challenge
Britain’s position in Acadia. “Consider, Monsieur,” he stated, “how this tends to
render all civil judicature useless, & how easy it will be for the Missionarys to
render themselves the only distributors of justice amongst the people bred up in
ignorance; and of what consequence it is for the maintaining of his Maj’tys author-
ity to restrain that power which the priests are but too apt to assume.”126 Religious
tolerance, in other words, had its limits. When the curé at Annapolis Royal, Claude
de La Vernède de Saint-Poncy, went to Chignecto without the Council’s permis-
sion and refused to return when ordered, Mascarene cut off all correspondence.127
                                 A Time and a Place                             115


Mascarene refused to let the shared spaces of religion infringe on his duties as an
administrator for the province.
   Despite the difficulties inherent in policing the Catholic faith in Nova Scotia,
British administrators relied on spaces of religious gathering to facilitate commu-
nications with the Acadians. Suspicious of Catholic priests, officials attempted to
keep spaces of worship close to the English settlements – and, since the govern-
ment paid for chapels, they could decide where the buildings should be erect-
ed. In 1732, a chapel was built just outside Annapolis Royal, close enough to be
within cannon range. When the priest suggested he would prefer more distance,
the Council informed him that being so close to the armaments would serve as
a symbolic reminder of his predecessors’ misbehaviour.128 Chapels in more dis-
tant Acadian settlements provided the British with sites for communication with
French subjects. As a place of weekly congregation, chapels, or “Mass House[s]”
often found their doors adorned with proclamations (to be read aloud for the ben-
efit of all Acadians) from the Council at Annapolis Royal. This is how rogue priests
learned of their dismissal, how inhabitants were informed of appointments to dis-
cuss grievances with the government, and how British officials benefitted from
shared religious spaces.129
   Acadians were quick to complain if they felt that officials at Annapolis Royal
were preventing them from practicing their faith and thus using their regula-
tory power over shared religious spaces inappropriately, yet overseeing Catholic
practice required administrators to consider carefully which priests they allowed
to serve in the province. For the most part, Acadians were practicing Catholics
who attended Mass regularly and said their prayers before bed.130 Churches were
important enough spaces that Acadians would build them without government
permission, but such actions provoked reprisals to curb Acadian independence
and rebalance religious authority. In 1732, when residents of Cobequid began
building a church to attract a priest to their settlement, Lieutenant Governor
Armstrong admonished deputies from the settlement and the Bishop of Quebec’s
vicar general for British Acadia for failing to secure permission in advance.131 In
1736, the Acadians of the Saint-Jean-Baptiste parish wrote a memorial complain-
ing that they were without a priest, and that the British refused them their prayer
services.132 The British undoubtedly did what they could to maintain their posi-
tion within Nova Scotia’s shared religious spaces, and if they were not able to
prevent Catholic worship, they could develop relationships with Catholic priests
who emphasized the obligation to respect authority. At times these opportunities
presented themselves to the officials at Annapolis Royal because priests travelled
there to complain about jurisdictional authority. The British government had only
to determine which priest was most sympathetic to British rule and then find in
his favour.133
   Bishops in Quebec took an active interest in dispatching priests to, and declar-
ing clerical jurisdiction over, the Acadian settlers; French officials and religious
figures at Louisbourg, on the other hand, struggled to support their ecclesiastical
institutions. British officials complained of interference from Quebec, noting that
the French subjects “follow the dictates of their Priests and the Bishop of Quebec
(or those of Cape Breton) who orders not only the building of Churches here, but
sends whom and what number of Priests he may think proper.”134 These competing
116                             Homelands and Empires


religious and secular authorities created overlapping jurisdictions within Nova
Scotia. Officials at Louisbourg were concerned with maintaining their territorial
and military alliances with the Mi’kmaq and their allies, and religion played an
important role in that relationship. Many Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, and Eastern
Abenaki enjoyed close relationships with their priests, and government officials re-
lied on the bonds of religion and the influence of clerics to keep Indigenous peoples
in the French interest. Such efforts required financial assistance, and administrators
at Louisbourg received frequent requests from their missionaries. In 1740, Abbé
Le Loutre requested funds for building a church in Acadia because neither he nor
the Mi’kmaq were in any position to undertake such a project without help. His
superiors agreed and in turn suggested to the minister of the Marine that five or six
hundred livres should cover the cost.135 The minister also received assurances that
both the work of missionaries such as Abbé Maillard and the medallions provided
to the Mi’kmaq were successfully retaining the Indigenous peoples as allies.136
   Religious alliances were directly related to territorial oversight. Officials at
Quebec hoped that by responding to Indigenous requests for assistance they could
influence settlement patterns and geographic boundaries. Religious and secular
leaders in Quebec and Île Royale called for territory in Nova Scotia to be divided
along religious lines in a deliberate effort to separate the Mi’kmaq from the British.137
Many Eastern Abenaki, whose homelands stretched across the disputed regions of
southern Nova Scotia/Acadia, sent representatives to Quebec to complain about
their British neighbours or ask for assistance, and it was from Quebec that many
missionaries received their orders. In 1731, the king of France approved Governor
Beauharnois’s decision to send missionaries to the Abenaki at Narantsouak
(Norridgewock, on the Kennebec River) if necessary, but he “recommend[ed] them
to be continually attentive to the movements of the Abenaki to keep them close
and prevent them from going to live in their old village.”138 Clerics and missionar-
ies, French administrators hoped, could act as proxy government agents to direct
Indigenous actions and create borders that would protect French territory by limit-
ing British expansion.
   Eastern Abenaki allegiance to their Catholic missionaries did not necessarily ex-
tend to the French state more generally. Divisions within the Eastern Abenaki led
a significant portion of the population to search out an alliance with the British.139
The French were concerned because the British at Boston were attempting to make
inroads with the Abenaki by providing them with presents. Conferences and dis-
cussions between the British and the Indigenous peoples, however, were hindered
by the lack of regularly attended shared religious areas that could facilitate the ex-
change and interchange of cultural knowledge. Beauharnois assured the minister
of the Marine that “religion is a bond that will keep [the Indigenous peoples] in
our interests.”140
   British officials wanted an alliance with the Indigenous peoples and realized that
the French were successful largely because of the religious bond. As late as 1758,
an English publication argued that it would be possible to attract the Indigenous
peoples, as they “cannot be entirely rooted in the French interest,” even though
they are bound by religion. If they could be converted to the “more pure and
rational [faith],” perhaps their loyalty would follow.141 The difficulty facing the
British was that they spent less time with the Wabanaki in spaces of interaction
                                 A Time and a Place                              117


(such as those of negotiation) that produced the kinds of knowledge that facili-
tated cultural understanding. Attempts to win Abenaki allies by providing their
chiefs with commissions and gifts largely failed at shifting Indigenous alliances.142
Only with an improved sense of the Indigenous world view could the British have
developed shared religious tenets – and even that might not have been enough,
since the British, unlike the French, were not satisfied with adapting Christianity
to appeal to Indigenous spirituality but wanted instead to “obliterate and replace”
Indigenous religion.143 Creating and maintaining a cultural connection with the
Mi’kmaq required more effort and more shared spaces than the British were will-
ing to make – and perhaps more understanding.
   Religion was a source of identity, and true reconciliation with the British would
remain elusive while the Acadians and Wabanaki felt a stronger spiritual connec-
tion with the French. As Linda Colley has demonstrated in the British context,
religion served as a defining characteristic between British Protestants and French
Catholics on the continent; as long as there was a common and identifiable en-
emy, internal divisions could be overlooked.144 Similar conditions existed in Nova
Scotia’s areas of religious interaction, as the Mi’kmaq and Acadians could focus
on their similarities in opposition to the British. A single Catholic mission could
serve to unite a variety of groups. Religious ceremonies at Père Gaulin’s chapel at
Shubenacadie were attended by “Acadians, French travelers from Ile Royale, and
representatives of Algonkian nations from the region … and so the mission helped
to strengthen the links that tied the various Catholic peoples of the maritime region
together.”145 These groups could worship together, but could also share news and
pertinent information from throughout the region.146 The British, who were only
nominally part of this shared religious space – acting as administrative overseers
instead of active participants – were unable to benefit fully from these centres of
religion, save for improving communication with French subjects. Consequently,
British officials lacked a true understanding of how common religious culture af-
fected regional alliances and shared territory. Constructed and maintained areas
of religious interaction were effective tools for building and maintaining alliances
that favoured the French and Mi’kmaq at the expense of the British.

                                     •••
Instrumental to the system of checks and balances that monitored British and
French pales from 1727 to 1744 was the attempt to create and secure controlled
spaces that could provide each group with their own territory. In the complex
and changing world of eighteenth-century Mi’kma’ki, these locations signalled a
transition from the largely fluid and temporal areas of interaction to more perma-
nent settlements and strictly defined boundaries. The creation of settlements in-
volved inter- and intracultural competition, with members of Indigenous, British,
and French groups arguing both among themselves and with each other. These
groups projected outward signs of stability, though internal relationships were
shaped by negotiation and competition. Records of these internal contests illumi-
nate the mechanics of early settlement and conflict, which depended on territorial
control. Settlers participated in local governance by voicing their concerns over
property and boundary issues. An investigation into the creation of settlements
118                           Homelands and Empires


and boundaries sheds light on the inner workings of territorial sovereignty and
the role that controlled spaces played in balancing regional power.
   There were two primary settlements – Annapolis Royal and Canso – within
which the British were able to exercise authority without facing heavy or con-
stant opposition. The forts and their immediate surroundings marked the limits
of British geographic control in the region, and any forays beyond those limits
resulted in a reaction from the Mi’kmaq and the French, who monitored British
movements. Within the weak and uneven walls of Annapolis Royal sat a govern-
ment forced to recognize its impotence locally while projecting an image of British
expansion and authority to its superiors, who were often indifferent or discourag-
ing. It was not until the 1740s that Britain began strengthening its imperial author-
ity in North America.147 Before then, plans to implement British authority rose and
fell without any real impact on its imperial geographic fiction. In the summer of
1727, Lieutenant Governor Armstrong received a letter from Allured Popple, the
secretary of the Board of Trade, informing him that the Board was considering
plans for settling Nova Scotia with Protestants. The following October, Armstrong
learned that the death of King George I had slowed progress on the matter, but
that details would be forthcoming. That summer, the Board of Trade announced
the appointment of a royal surveyor of the woods, which would allow land grants
in Nova Scotia when he had completed his tasks.148 Colonel David Dunbar was
focused on his Georgia scheme and Nova Scotia’s survey would simply have to
wait. The British lacked the political will to assert control over Nova Scotia’s geo-
graphic development. France benefitted through British inaction, if only because
it left Nova Scotia vulnerable to future attacks. In the meantime, the Acadians
enjoyed demographic (and territorial) expansion and the Mi’kmaq lived largely as
they had before 1727.
   Canso, a shared but contested site, is a useful example of inter-imperial com-
petition and Indigenous strength, but the British attempts to control the region
also illuminated internal conflicts. Land grants among British administrators at
Canso often allowed for a certain amount of score settling. Governor Philipps and
Lawrence Armstrong, his lieutenant, did not get along. The governor was at times
blatantly vindictive towards his second in command, going as far as appointing
the lieutenant’s enemies (including Alexander Cosby and William Winniett) to
powerful positions.149 We can assume that Armstrong suffered from some kind
of depression, which would have exacerbated his interpersonal issues and surely
played a contributing role in his suicide by self-inflicted sword wounds in 1739.150
Alexander Cosby, who had lost out on the position of lieutenant governor of Nova
Scotia to Armstrong in 1725, feuded with his superior over various matters and of-
ten disobeyed orders to remain at his post at Canso. Armstrong was frustrated by
Governor Philipps’s decision to name Cosby lieutenant governor of the fort and
town of Annapolis Royal in 1727 and to appoint him to the governing Council.151
In 1731, Alexander Cosby petitioned for a “garden plot” – an area of land separate
from the settlement used to grow crops – at Annapolis Royal. When his request
demanded approval, Armstrong blocked it because (he claimed) a deed already
existed that favoured a different claimant. Cosby was forced to defer his claim
and hope to receive a plot at Canso.152 Small plots of land became symbolic of the
power struggles and administrative jockeying taking place in Nova Scotia.
                                 A Time and a Place                               119


   If Whitehall was guilty of “salutary neglect,” the same can hardly be said for
local officials, who were well aware of the importance of land management and
were expected to send regular updates to officials in London.153 Compromises
were necessary to address the tension between a general desire to people Nova
Scotia, and the requirement to survey and reserve large tracts of woods for naval
stores before any land could be granted for settlers. Sorting out the division of land
in British settlements helped keep the Board of Trade informed of how Annapolis
Royal was progressing. Though officials in London were often slow in responding
to letters and requests, administrators in Nova Scotia had to be prepared to answer
for their actions. In the fall of 1732, after organizing land grants and attempting
to sort through the quitrents owed and collected, Armstrong sent to the Board of
Trade “abridgements of the buttings and boundings of all the patents granted here
since my arrival, to whom, their quit rents, and terms of payment which, if judged
not sufficient, I shall order copies to be drawn out at length, and shall transmit
them accordingly.”154 Armstrong had moved quickly in this regard, having only
shortly before received permission from London to grant land even though the
200,000 acres of suitable woodland had not been surveyed and reserved for na-
val stores. The new regulation stated that for each section of land granted, one
of equal size was to be surveyed and reserved for the king.155 Such a compromise
was intended to increase the number of inhabitants and thus strengthen the British
character of the province.
   A plan to increase the number of settlers at Canso ended up revealing divisions
within Nova Scotia’s Council between civilian and military priorities. In 1739, by
which time the civilian population at Canso had dwindled to about ten families,
the government at Annapolis Royal ordered a patent for a township at Chedabucto
“by the Gutt of Canso,” which was to be surveyed, laid out, and granted to Edward
How. How, before he became the victim of Nova Scotia’s most infamous murder,
had long had an interest in the region. In 1725 he received a grant at Canso (How’s
Island) where he spent much time dealing with the Mi’kmaq, likely learning to
speak their language. By 1730, he was both a Justice of the Peace and a sheriff, and
he used his own funds (up to £800) to build necessary infrastructure for civilian
and military purposes. Given his personal and financial investments in Canso,
it’s not surprising that How hoped to revitalize the region with a sizable grant for
settlers. There had been some confusion over the process of surveying lands and
then issuing grants, stemming from the inability of a deputy surveyor to make and
keep detailed records of what land had been measured and granted because sev-
eral grants had been surveyed and distributed without his knowledge. Armstrong
was aware that the process had to proceed carefully to ensure that each grant
could be recorded “to Decide any Disputes between the King and Private persons
– or between Man & Man.”156 Later that day, however, Armstrong dispatched a
letter to William Shirreff, the commissioner of musters, saying that he had seen
a plan of How’s township, had been assured that no valuable timber lay within
its bounds, and that Sherriff was thus to execute the grant.157 Those with military
leanings, however, worried about what such a grant might mean for the Canso
garrison. Shirreff’s response to Armstrong noted that a survey was underway, but
he continued to complain that the decision to grant How’s township, made dur-
ing a Council meeting the previous August, was “then but a crude and indigested
120                             Homelands and Empires


answer to an indefinite demand till first bounded and surveyed.” He also noted
that officers and other men in the garrison expressed “what a prejudice such a grant
will be to his Majesty’s said garrison and his other subjects at the place.”158 Shirreff,
who had been charged with executing the grant, suggested the Council be recalled
to examine the matter as their decision might not have considered all factors.159
   Armstrong’s response illustrated the complexity of granting land, attracting set-
tlers, and creating a sense of British permanence in Nova Scotia. It was necessary
to balance military and civic affairs while adhering to stringent imperial regula-
tions. Annapolis Royal and, to a lesser extent, Canso, were increasingly permanent
British settlements, but the management of those spaces brought to light the inter-
nal problems that limited British geographic expansion. Maps and surveys were
the building blocks of settlement growth. After informing Shirreff of the lack of
precedent for recalling the Council, Armstrong cautioned his subordinate against
discouraging settlement. Grants must necessarily come before surveys, he argued,
because no settlers would finance an expensive survey without a guaranteed title
to the land. Surveys were more involved than taking a few measurements and
plotting them on paper. Vessels had to be located and hired and guides were nec-
essary to protect the surveyor as he plied the waters running through Indigenous
homelands.160 By the early eighteenth century, Indigenous peoples knew that set-
tlement did not lag far behind surveyor chains. Surveyors, assistants, and chain-
men were required to carry out the division of property at a cost (in the 1750s) of
ten pence/day, five pence/day, and 10 pence/month, respectively.161 Armstrong
added that he did not believe a settlement would disadvantage the garrison, nor
had he heard any complaints from the officers or commanding officers themselves.
It was the king’s wish to settle the region, especially considering the growing
Acadian population, and that was what he intended to do.162 William Shirreff pro-
vided a precedent for recalling Council to debate land grants. He argued that there
was no proof that profitable and unprofitable land was granted in equal measure
as demanded by the regulations, nor were all the settlers’ names known at the
time of the grant.163 The issue stalled in Council, and it was not until 1744 that the
grant went through, demonstrating the difficulties faced by local administrators in
securing a truly British space.164
   The French government in Paris was farther along than the British in collecting
and maintaining a geographic archive documenting their imperial fictions over-
seas, and officials expected to receive updated maps and surveys.165 To walk around
Louisbourg today provides an excellent example of what the fortress looked like in
the eighteenth century. Buildings were tightly packed, modest and unassuming
for the most part, save for the large citadel that housed the chapel, governor’s
apartments, and barracks.166 This was an impressive Vauban-styled fortress that
grew steadily after its founding in 1713, and officials in France expected to be
kept informed of its progress. Saint-Ovide complied with such expectations. In
1734 he sent to the minister of the Marine a detailed list of settlements presently
occupied by habitants and fishermen. The list also included an estimate of what
was required in the province both for the development of the settlement and for
the well-being of its inhabitants.167 An example from this survey shows how de-
tailed was the information collected and sent to France and reveals land manage-
ment practices in French settlements. George Lasson, an inhabitant and fisherman,
                                  A Time and a Place                               121


possessed a piece of land occupied by his nephews, Jean and Michel Lasson. It
consisted of a gravel bank that ran 107 toise long by 12 toise wide.168 The land
stretched from one marker to another and out to the sea in the harbour. It con-
tained, in total, 2,484 toise.169 The survey included numerous entries like this for
settlers around Louisbourg, and also traced the transfer of plots within a family or
from one resident to another. The French administration was therefore kept well-
informed of settlements and land use at Île Royale.
   Such detailed records were a boon for the government, but could also provide
litigious settlers with valuable information to support or challenge land claims.
Geographic documents were tools of both the state and the people and land man-
agement was one area in which a settlement’s propertied members could become
directly involved in local governance and even challenge official policy. In the win-
