ter of 1735, a year after he became the only judge of the bailiff court in Louisbourg,
Joseph Lartigue complained to the minister of the Marine about the plot of land
granted him in 1714. This seems to have been something of a habit for Lartigue,
who had a knack for purchasing land and building houses on plots that were soon
expropriated by the government, at which point Lartigue would send lengthy
complaints to the minister of the Marine. It’s possible that his position as judge
was granted in part to compensate for past inconveniences.170 In his 1735 com-
plaint, Lartigue argued that he had improved the land and made it suitable for
fishing – built a house, cultivated a garden, and constructed fishing flakes. He
argued that for the past twenty years the engineer (most likely Étienne Verrier
and his predecessor) had persecuted him over his land. He had built a house the
previous year, part of which extended onto land that was to become a new road;
he was ordered to take it down, and he did. He moved the house at great expense
and effort to a section of land previously marked out for him by the surveyor, but
his neighbour, Verrier, “constructed a large lime kiln quite close to the house which
was then often covered by flames and smoke.”171 He pleaded, “I find myself with
reason, sir, in a continual fear that [the house] will be consumed and I have good
reason to believe that it will not be able to stay if the lime kiln is not removed.”172
To illustrate his point, Lartigue forwarded a survey of his property and that of
his neighbour, indicating that Verrier had taken much of the land reserved for the
king to build his large house, garden, and shed. Had he not, there would have
been plenty of room for his own house, but instead he had been ordered to remove
his house and abandon his garden by spring. He asked the minister either to al-
low him to stay in his house so that he could support his family or for permission
to move his plot to the area he marked in yellow on the plan. Once a financially
secure settler from Plaisance, Lartigue was reduced to plotting his own map and
hoping that his government would see fit to let him live on the marked areas of his
choosing.173 Lartigue’s access to surveys and property management provided him
with an avenue into official affairs, and a voice in the governance of the settlement.
   In Acadian settlements on the peninsula, distant from French authorities at
Louisbourg and on lands the British claimed but could not control, the use of sur-
veys to record settlements and categorize them as English or French was often a
source of contention. The Acadians were the object of much cadastral interest, but
surveying Acadian plots became increasingly dangerous for the British as settle-
ments pushed farther into Mi’kma’ki or Wulstukwik. In 1732, a group of Acadians
122                            Homelands and Empires


from the Saint John River area arrived in Annapolis to swear an oath of allegiance
and receive grants issued by the British king. They were informed that a surveyor
would accompany them on their return trip to map the area, which would then
be granted. The Acadians replied “they could not answer for carrying with them
a person to survey the land, because of the Indians.”174 The matter was held for
consideration, and the survey was delayed indefinitely. Opposition to surveys did
not necessarily lead to violence, but there was often the expectation of opposition.
In a letter to the Acadian deputies at Minas, William Shirreff informed them that
he had dispatched George Mitchell, Colonel Dunbar’s deputy, to survey Acadian
lands. The deputies were to remind the inhabitants not to disrupt or affront his
work.175 Even in areas where surveys had been completed, Acadians were quick
to dispute their findings and challenge the quitrents collected as a result. Part of
the Acadian resistance to British territorial authority had always been economic
in nature: Acadians did not want to pay higher rents for their lands. Lieutenant
Governor Armstrong sent a letter to the deputies of Pisiquid and Cobequid, two
Acadian settlements on the shores of the Minas Basin, about the number of com-
plaints received about property boundaries, informing them that all inhabitants
must present their deeds of sale and contracts if any conflicts were to be settled.176
The act of resisting surveys and refusing to surrender old French grants for new
British ones helped the Acadians retain control over their settlements.
   While imperial officials relied on maps and surveys to bring imagined geogra-
phies closer to reality, Indigenous peoples continued to move through the home-
lands that had sustained them for thousands of years. The fluid boundaries within
which the Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk followed their seasonal migration patterns
stood in stark contrast to the surveyed lines on maps created by the British and the
French, but provided the Wabanaki with enough room to adapt to the presence of
Europeans. It is not surprising that in 1735 the Wulstukwiuk along the Wulstukw
River complained to Lieutenant Governor Armstrong about British attempts
to survey their land. Armstrong assured them that they had nothing to worry
about.177 There was, of course, much to be concerned about: the governor intended
to survey as much land as possible, distribute plots to settlers, and create as many
English pales on the river as he could. Indigenous responses to these attempts
demonstrate just how dearly the Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk held on to their ter-
ritorial rights. Mi’kmaw transhumance should not suggest that territorial sover-
eignty was unimportant; in fact, it was the land and what it could provide to the
Indigenous peoples that helped the Mi’kmaq resist European encroachment. They
had a relationship with the land and were united to it, not masters over it. “Viewed
from this perspective,” argues William C. Wicken, “Mi’kmaq occupation of defined
territories throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries indicates a degree
of social cohesion despite the spread of disease, the fur trade, European settlement
and colonial conflict.”178 There were eighteen principal settlements in Mi’kmaw
territory, most of which were along the coast or on major riverine routes.179 The
population of these settlements fluctuated with the seasons – there were summer
sites and winter sites – but there were established areas of habitation from which
the Mi’kmaq operated. Any attempt by the British or French to impose geographic
restrictions caused conflict, especially at a time when territorial sovereignty was
subjected to a system of checks and balances. The settlement areas, the migratory
                                 A Time and a Place                               123


patterns that linked them, the communications networks they created, and the
ease with which they could move between sites provided the Mi’kmaq with a
strong sense of territoriality. These elements combined to create their homeland,
from which they could judge the actions of European settlers who had established
themselves within Mi’kma’ki and were trying to make it their own.

                                      •••
During the relatively peaceful period from 1727 to 1744, geographic control was
increasingly divided in Mi’kma’ki. A system of checks and balances developed
by which each group could protect its possessions while limiting the aspirations
of the others. The migratory, seasonal, and temporary Mi’kmaw settlements in-
fused Indigenous geographies with an element of transhumance as the Mi’kmaq
travelled from one site to another according to subsistence patterns. The French
Acadians grew and expanded during this Acadian “golden age” that witnessed a
demographic increase and an extension of Acadian lands. Acadian deputies served
as quasi-official British agents to oversee territorial growth and land claims, pro-
viding the Acadians with the ability to monitor their own growth. Hemmed be-
hind the fort walls at Annapolis Royal and Canso, the British attempted to extend
their presence in the region by constructing forts and extending British law to
Acadian settlers.
   Although these were conflicting and conflicted territorial competitions (no
group was homogenous), their coexistence was facilitated by the creation of areas
of interaction. It was in these specific places (contested, shared, and controlled)
that relationships were formed, alliances built, and problems resolved. Contested
areas prevented any one group from extending its authority beyond acceptable
means; shared spaces allowed for the mutually beneficial interchange of com-
merce, religion, and negotiation; and controlled spaces provided each group with
its own (generally) undisputed territory. These areas of interchange also illumi-
nated the internal workings of the Mi’kmaq, French, and British. The intra-group
competition and disagreements made room for alliances with other regional pow-
ers that helped maintain a balance between established homelands and the impe-
rial fictions that were gaining purchase in the northeast.
   The nature of these areas of interchange speaks to the fluidity and temporality
of created spaces in Mi’kma’ki. Sites of interchange were created and maintained
only as long as they served a purpose for their participants. The period of 1727–44
was defined by imperial failure (on the part of Britain and France) and Indigenous
stagnation (as the Mi’kmaq and their allies were unable or unwilling to remove
foreign settlers). Maintaining peace became a shared exercise that required both
claiming and surrendering authority as manifested in controlling territory. Rather
than imperial officials projecting sovereignty onto their possessions, local officials
and Indigenous peoples in the northeast determined who could be where, and for
how long. Maintaining that peace provided the Mi’kmaq, French, and British with
a common cause. Yet conflict was unavoidable because each group expressed geo-
graphic control differently: the Mi’kmaq remained transitory and required large
swathes of land to carry out their traditional migrations; the Acadians expanded
rapidly and recognized British jurisdiction only nominally; and the British relied
124                            Homelands and Empires


on displays of power (often military in nature) because they could not exercise true
authority. Though power allowed for action, authority demanded that such actions
be accepted. British officials at Annapolis Royal readily admitted that they could
do nothing to stop the Acadians from expanding or the Mi’kmaq from travelling.
The Acadians and the Mi’kmaq were well aware that they could resist British ex-
pansion, but they could not remove the British altogether. The resulting balance in
territorial sovereignty shaped how each group dealt with the other.
  Spaces of interaction helped govern the relationships between and among the
region’s various residents. Those areas provided the opportunity for cultural ex-
change, which led to increased understanding and knowledge of other groups.
The French and the Wabanaki benefitted from these areas. The Mi’kmaq did not
increase their strength, but they maintained their traditional relationship with
the French and suffered little interference. Acadia persisted as an imperial fiction
within Mi’kma’ki, which allowed French administrators (in France and Île Royale)
to view the region as an illustration of British weakness. Yet British officials were
increasingly dedicated to their fictive Nova Scotia and willing to spend money to
establish bigger and more powerful pales. As will be demonstrated in the follow-
ing chapter, the founding of Halifax was a manifestation of this change. While the
project’s success was far from guaranteed, the settlement at Halifax pointed to the
British Empire’s desire to transform an imperial fiction into a territorial force that
could defeat French Acadia and pose a real threat to the Indigenous homelands
in the Northeast.
                        4 A Pale on the Coast




The founding of Halifax altered the geopolitical landscape in the northeast. The
various spaces that had operated within the province – shared, contested, and
defined – did not immediately disappear, but the arrival of Governor Edward
Cornwallis signalled a change in imperial policy that would force a realignment
in the contested territories of northeastern North America. The founding of Halifax
was an imperial watershed for the Wabanaki, British, and French groups not
because it accomplished settlement goals or resolved geographic issues, but be-
cause it made new British political and military intentions obvious. Instrumental
to those intentions was the collection and dissemination of maps, surveys, and
tracts, first by the British but then by the French and the Mi’kmaq. Territorial sov-
ereignty was no less contested, but after 1749 the French and the Mi’kmaq were
made aware that the British presence in the region was not only permanent, but
also growing. The period from 1744 to 1755 was one in which the British acted and
the French and the Wabanaki reacted. The geographic knowledge collected during
the settlement’s formative years shaped local and imperial ideas of British space
and influenced the sociopolitical organization of power. Spatial knowledge was
also instrumental to Wabanaki and French resistance against British expansion.
Borders and mapping practices became important instruments in the contest over
shaping the region’s geographic identity.
   The settlement (and the reactions it engendered) must be understood in the
context of territorial conflict, imperial competition, and developments in the field
of mapping and cartography. Halifax was not an immediate success and France
responded by strengthening its pales in the northeast. The Wabanaki also had to
reconsider how they would monitor and defend against the growing influence of
imperial pales pushing into their homeland. Indigenous residents of Mi’kma’ki,
Wulstukwik, and the Dawnland had to consider divorcing themselves from old
alliances to preserve their homeland by working with either side if common
ground was found. Bold British action in the northeast elicited an equally bold
response from the French and Indigenous peoples. Louisbourg was strengthened,
new French forts were founded on the isthmus, and the Wabanaki were forced to
re-evaluate their allegiances to ensure they maintained their independence.1 As
will be demonstrated, the French (both in Acadia and at Île Royale) were able to
resist, or at least oppose, British expansion into what they still claimed was Acadia.
Acadians refused to be subsumed by British law, which was one potential ave-
nue of extending control over the local geography.2 The Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk,
126                           Homelands and Empires


Passamaquoddy, and Abenaki were similarly capable of striking treaties that would
appease the British temporarily without surrendering control over important geo-
graphic resources. Viewed in this light, founding Halifax helped the British resus-
citate the faltering geographic imaginary of Nova Scotia. However, a new pale or
two could not erase the French idea of Acadia or convince the Wabanaki to sur-
render their traditional homelands.
   This chapter and chapter 5 work together to recount the local and imperial as-
pects, respectively, of the Halifax settlement and the boundary concerns it reawak-
ened. English and French officials argued over what made an imperial fiction real,
debates that rarely included Wabanaki participants. These actions demonstrate that
the founding of Halifax shifted British and French attention towards the northeast
from the southern colonies and sugar islands. A renewed British presence in Nova
Scotia under a different organizational model than previous settlements – Halifax
was funded solely by the British government for military purposes with little ex-
pectation of trade or resource extraction – clearly indicated the region’s strategic
worth. Questions of imperial boundaries re-emerged and dominated French and
British affairs until the outbreak of the Seven Years’ War. Geography was a vital
component of understanding settlement policy as British and French administra-
tors and diplomats marshalled cartographic evidence to support their image of
a colony, challenge that of their competitors, and use Indigenous homelands as
imperial placeholders.
   The founding of Halifax was a cause for concern at French forts, throughout
Acadian settlements, and deep into Indigenous homelands. Responses to the new
settlement were varied and at times disorganized: treaties were made and broken,
attacks in the region persisted, and the French built forts along the isthmus and
attempted to relocate both Acadians and the Mi’kmaq. The system of territorial
checks and balances that had facilitated coexistence was swept away and replaced
with violence, fear, and a hardening of regional divisions. At Halifax, land man-
agement remained an important tool of authority as settlers were encouraged to
clear their land and erect houses. The maps produced during this period served
local officials better than imperial administrators, as problems resulted from issues
over land tenure and property disputes. In Britain, “selling” the Halifax settlement
to literate Britons required the public distribution of appealing maps, several of
which appeared in popular magazines. Britons read about the settlement’s prog-
ress, but they were not always provided with a full picture of Halifax’s position or
the opposition it faced. Empires were envisioned, homelands were defended, and
it remained to be seen who would be left as the region’s dominant power.

                                     •••
The founding of Halifax was a direct result of the imperial contests that preceded
it. In 1744, European conflict once again reached North American shores, pitting
the British against the French in an Indigenous homeland peppered with Acadian
settlements. The War of the Austrian Succession, in which France and Britain
fought on opposite sides of a Europe-wide conflict, ended the peaceful years so
highly valued by Walpole in Britain and Fleury in France. In Mi’kma’ki, British of-
ficers and soldiers at Annapolis Royal and Canso found themselves under attack
                                 A Pale on the Coast                             127


from the French at Louisbourg and their Indigenous allies, who were fighting
as much for themselves as for France. With war declared, boundaries could be
pushed back or extended farther depending on which side claimed victory; con-
sidering the heated disputes over land and the delicate balance that had limited
territorial aspirations since 1726, all three groups involved in the war were eager
to secure their vision of the region.
   The French wasted little time in attacking the British. Canso was the obvious
first target. By 1744, it was of waning economic importance but increasing military
value. Plans for an attack on Nova Scotia dated back to 1739, when Isaac-Louis de
Forant, who succeeded Saint-Ovide as governor of Île Royale, proposed a detailed
amphibious attack from Louisbourg.3 Forant’s tenure as governor lasted only from
April of 1739 until his death in May of 1740, during which time he focused on
reorganizing Louisbourg’s garrison, particularly dealing with the rampant alco-
holism and ineptitude of many soldiers and officers.4 Forant’s death, and the ap-
pointment of Jean-Baptiste-Louis Le Prévost Duquesnel as his successor – holding
the title of commander, not governor – did not prevent Forant’s plans from being
realized. Though Duquesnel’s appointment came with instructions to strengthen
Louisbourg’s already formidable defences, he was also encouraged to act offen-
sively. After familiarizing himself with Forant’s plans, Duquesnel launched his at-
tack, first on Canso and then on Annapolis Royal on 6 September 1744.5
   The attacking force was under the command of François Du Pont Duvivier, a
member of an elite Louisbourg military family whose business and trade interests
had made him wealthy. To his natural business acumen was added preferential
treatment and favouritism from Louisbourg’s financial commissaries. His ascent of
the military ranks was similarly facilitated by those who favoured him, namely his
uncle (a major at Louisbourg) and Governor Saint-Ovide. His connections did not
always keep him out of trouble, however. Duvivier’s time at Île Royale met with an
untimely exit after several unsuccessful military ventures, and he later found him-
self accused of holding secret meetings with the English commissaries who were in
Paris to discuss the Acadian boundary.6 The force he commanded from Louisbourg
in 1744 faced little resistance at Canso and he captured the fort easily. The success
emboldened Duquesnel, who ordered his troops on to Annapolis Royal. His plan
was to coordinate a joint attack with troops from Louisbourg, naval ships from
France, and local Indigenous peoples. Support from France did not materialize, but
Abbé Le Loutre assured Duquesnel that the Mi’kmaq would help take the fort. The
Mi’kmaq positioned themselves outside the fort in early July, but when the French
reinforcements from Louisbourg failed to arrive, they were only able to launch a
weak and disorganized attack before retreating.7 Lieutenant Governor Mascarene
reported to the Board of Trade at the end of July that the French had taken Canso
but that Annapolis Royal was safe, having withstood the Mi’kmaq’s minor attempt
on its walls.8 Duquesnel was not disheartened and organized another attack on the
British fort, again selecting Duvivier to oversee the effort.
   Duvivier arrived in Nova Scotia to begin his second attack in early August but
was unable to attract much support from the Acadians as he made his way to
Annapolis Royal. He faced similar difficulties in convincing the Mi’kmaq and
Wulstukwiuk to join him so soon after the July debacle. Only about thirty Mi’kmaq
from Nova Scotia volunteered to fight a second time, and to them were added
128                            Homelands and Empires


about 100 Mi’kmaq from Île Royale. There were also about seventy Wulstukwiuk
from the Bay of Fundy.9 It is entirely likely that even with his limited force Duvivier
could have taken Annapolis Royal, but he hesitated, missed his opportunity, and
entered into a four-week siege with little offensive direction.10 Mascarene defend-
ed the fort well, aided by the arrival of reinforcements from Boston. Eventually
the governor at Île Royale dispatched Le Chevalier de Gannes from Louisbourg
to Annapolis Royal to inform Duvivier that the ships expected from France were
not going to arrive in time. With this news, Duvivier was forced to retreat first to
Minas, and then to Louisbourg.11
   The two attacks levelled at Annapolis Royal met with a limited but sufficient
defence and revealed a renewed desire for neutrality among some of the Mi’kmaq
and Wulstukwiuk. Mascarene learned of the attack on Canso and quickly notified
William Shirley, governor of Massachusetts, to ask for assistance. He specifically
requested a group of rangers (a force of English and Indigenous fighters) to act “as
Scouts and keep in awe the Indians of this peninsula who believe all the Indians
[who] come from New England are Mohawks of whom they stand in great fear.”12
Mascarene wanted to control the Mi’kmaq and the Wulstukwiuk, who, despite
their weak first attempt on Annapolis Royal, remained a dangerous fighting force.
Some Indigenous groups in Nova Scotia were less eager to fight. In May of 1744, a
group of Wulstukwiuk from the Wulstukw River visited Annapolis Royal to dis-
cuss how the actions in Europe might affect North America. “We have had news
from Canady and Boston,” Joseph, the chief’s son announced, “that peace still
continues between England and France, but that at the River St. Johns things are
variously reported wherefore we desire to know from your self how matters really
are.”13 The British reported that war was likely, and the Council stated its desire
to know the Wulstukwiuk intentions should the French encourage them to fight.
Joseph responded that if the French and English went to war, “our designs are
to lye quiet and meddle on neither side.”14 The conference concluded with both
sides stating their observance of the last treaty and addressing wrongs that had
occurred since that time; the Wulstukwiuk expressed gratitude for receiving such
friendly treatment and assured the British that they would “live with you and all
the English in friendship.”15
   It is not possible to determine if any of the Wulstukwiuk from this meeting at-
tacked Annapolis Royal with Duvivier, but the limited Indigenous assistance he
attracted makes it unlikely. Neutrality was also important for many Acadians,
but their long history of settlement in and movement through the region’s rivers,
marshlands, and connecting routes made them targets for forced participation in
British campaigns. What is clear is that many Acadians remained largely neutral,
refusing to fight with Duvivier and providing supplies to French troops only after
receiving threats.16 After the failed attacks, Acadian deputies arrived at Annapolis
Royal to assure Mascarene and the Council that they had nothing to do with the
recent violence, and had been forced to supply some of Duvivier’s troops. The
Council seemed to accept their statements, but Mascarene informed the deputies
that the Acadians would also be forced to serve the British. In lieu of supplies,
some Acadians would be exploited for their maritime experience, particularly
the ability to pilot vessels around coastal areas and into the serpentine riverine
networks. Mascarene informed the deputies that they could furnish a pilot when
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              129


requested, or one would be pressed into service when necessary. Arguing that vol-
unteering their services might anger the Mi’kmaq, the deputies chose the latter
option. Mascarene stressed that the British were not expecting them to fight, only
to help navigate ships.17 In this instance, navigational ability was more important
than military assistance.
   British officials quickly prepared a counterattack that relied on operational flex-
ibility and knowledge of the strengths and weaknesses of Louisbourg. Mascarene
received most of his military support from William Shirley, who organized a New
England force to attack Louisbourg. Shirley had been a relatively successful London
lawyer before financial hardships left him eager for a new start. He lost a good deal
of his personal wealth in the South Sea bubble and then set his sights on rehabili-
tating his professional life in North America. Relying on personal connections, he
secured administrative positions in Boston including, somewhat ironically, repair-
ing the colony’s troubled fiscal state.18 While in Boston, Shirley took an increased
interest in Nova Scotia and so it is not surprising that he worked to organize troops
to attack Louisbourg. In 1745, under the command of William Pepperell, the force
attacked. The plans and directives for the attack were founded upon an under-
standing of the region’s geography, allowing for improvisation where necessary.19
The attack was successful and the French surrendered Louisbourg to Pepperell
and Admiral Peter Warren, who had brought his squadron from Jamaica to assist
in the operation.
   In trying to explain the capture of the fort, French officials relied on explaining
the terrain through cartographic hindsight. “I have examined the map of the Port
of Louisbourg,” Gaspard-Joseph Chaussegros de Léry wrote to the minister of the
Marine in 1745, “I believe it would have been advisable to build a good battery
to the left of the port’s entry, below the lighthouse, and above the lighthouse a
fortified lookout.”20 Chaussegros de Léry was the chief engineer at Quebec. He
was likely trained by his father and would go on to train his son to succeed him.
Despite his spotty record of constructing and evaluating military strongholds, he
would have been one of the better qualified men to comment on Louisbourg’s
strengths and weaknesses.21 Just as Pepperell and his forces relied on good maps
to plan their attack, the French looked at maps to analyse what went wrong, and
to determine how the fort could be recaptured. Yet there was no immediate effort
to retake Louisbourg. The New England troops who captured the fort stayed there
to guard against the French; they also suffered from an illness that swept through
the fortress. The French in Quebec learned of the English suffering from their
Wabanaki allies. In 1746, two Indigenous peoples arrived in Quebec from Acadia
carrying letters from Le Loutre and another missionary, Père Germain. Le Loutre’s
letter described how the Wabanakihad intercepted letters from Louisbourg to
Annapolis Royal requesting that Mascarene send ships to Boston to collect 1,000 to
1,200 men “pour remplacer les morts.”22
   The French would suffer their own setbacks during the war, including the
famous fiasco of Jean-Baptiste-Louis-Frédéric de la Rochefoucauld de Roye, duc
d’Anville. D’Anville was the son of France’s lieutenant-general of the galleys, but
there is little indication that the father’s maritime prowess was passed along to
the son. Considering that he had no formal naval training, he was woefully un-
qualified to lead an expedition from France to Nova Scotia. And yet in June of
130                            Homelands and Empires


1746 French officials sent a fleet of fifty-four ships with d’Anville at its head to re-
capture Louisbourg and attack the British. The fleet encountered a rough crossing;
bad weather scattered the ships as they approached Nova Scotia, damaging many
and forcing several to return to France. D’Anville arrived at Chebucto Harbour,
the future site of Halifax, before the fleet and died shortly thereafter of an appar-
ent stroke. Command of the expedition fell to the rear admiral, Constantin-Louis
d’Estourmel, who attempted suicide three days later. Chebucto was an obvious
choice for the attack because of its strategic position; it was a protected harbour
with access via land and waterways into the peninsula’s interior. French officials
were well aware of the region’s geographic benefits from the maps and settle-
ment plans they created around the time Port Royal fell to the British. Before any
decisive action could be taken (and while ranking officials within the campaign
were dealing with d’Anville’s death and d’Estourmel’s failed suicide) an epidemic
swept through the fleet. Eventually the entire expedition was cancelled and the
remaining ships returned to France. Of the 7,000 men who set out, 587 died and
2,274 returned sick.23 Mascarene informed Newcastle of d’Anville’s unfortunate at-
tempt, believing that he had “died of grief believing all the rest lost.”24 Mascarene
also reported that the French fleet had buried upwards of 3,000 soldiers along
the shores of Chebucto and that the vice admiral had attempted to kill himself
after going mad. These were not quite the facts of the case (d’Anville was initially
buried on George’s Island before his body was moved to Louisbourg and then
France), but three years later, when Cornwallis arrived at the shores of Chebucto,
he found spots of cleared land and gravesites as a reminder of d’Anville’s crew
and their attempt on Nova Scotia.
   As the war carried on, little changed in the region. Though the British held
Louisbourg and fighting continued throughout Mi’kma’ki, neither side made
much progress in increasing territorial control because successes in one area were
balanced by stalemates in others. In short, imperial control over Indigenous ter-
ritory remained largely as it was before the war. Mascarene openly admitted that
Annapolis Royal was “the only place of strength in this province and the only
one where the English have now a footing.”25 One small advantage was that the
war had at least spurred on improvements to the fort, “which was in a very ruin-
ous condition” but had been “repaired in the best manner the situation and cir-
cumstances would allow.”26 A French memoir on the state of Acadia argued that
“the French and Indians currently possess the entire province save for a small
party at Annapolis Royal, and they strengthen their possession of it by the forti-
fications they have built at Chignecto, Gaspé, and other strategic places.”27 Even
with the fall of Louisbourg, Nova Scotia remained a collection of pales within an
Indigenous homeland. British territorial sovereignty remained largely coterminus
with the walls of their forts.

                                      •••
The conclusion of the war did little to reassure the British in Nova Scotia and New
England that their position was safe. The treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, signed in 1748,
returned a status quo ante bellum to the region, which meant that Louisbourg was
once again under French control. New Englanders were undoubtedly upset that
                                 A Pale on the Coast                             131


their singular accomplishment had been reversed, but just how angry the general
populace was is the subject of some historical debate. The return of Louisbourg
was hardly a surprise, there was no real public outcry, and many Boston mer-
chants were pleased that illicit trade with Île Royale could recommence.28 Gov­
ernor Shirley helped soften the reaction in Massachusetts by asking Britain to
reimburse the colony’s wartime expenses.29 It is also important to view the peace
of 1748 not solely in a global context – marking the end of the War of the Austrian
Succession – but in the very local context. Locally, war was a more constant state
as the Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk were not signatories at the Treaty of Aix-la-
Chapelle and therefore continued to fight, albeit sporadically, until the treaties of
1760–61.30 Peace with the French and continued conflict with the Wabanaki meant
that the focus shifted from outright and sustained warfare to short skirmishes and
a renewed interest in boundary lines.
   The peace was more like a ceasefire during which geographic contests replaced
military engagements. Imperial subjects and Indigenous peoples operated under
the assumption that increasing territorial influence (in the case of the geographic
fictions of Nova Scotia and Acadia) or defending ancestral homelands (in the case
of the Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, Passamaquoddy, and Abenaki) was a vital tactic to
prepare for future engagements. The French had not given up their aspirations to
revive Acadia, and they had in their possession no shortage of tracts on the subject.
A 1748 memoir demonstrated the detailed information French officials possessed
about Acadia’s landscape. They knew who lived where, and how the land was
used. “From Canso to Musquodoboit the country is inhabited only by Indians,”
the memoir explained, “who hunt in the woods of Shubenacadie and fish in the
abundant rivers.”31 Foreshadowing British plans for the region, the memoir de-
scribed Chebucto as one of the region’s best harbours, large enough to fit an in-
finite number of ships. Importantly, the report added, the Mi’kmaq were always
loyal to France and received gifts regularly and bounties for English prisoners and
scalps during times of war.32
   What the French knew, the British were eager to learn. To that end, Mascarene
commissioned Charles Morris, a Boston surveyor, to chart sections of the province
and provide maps and descriptions. Morris, the son of a successful Boston sail-
maker, taught at a grammar school before he somehow made the acquaintance of
William Shirley and was commissioned to travel through Nova Scotia.33 Morris
was put in command of a ship going to Minas Basin, as “this gentleman is well
skill’d in taking drafts of coasts harbours etc and as there never was a compleat
draft of this Bay yet made I thought it would be an importance service.”34 Morris’s
surveys were an invaluable addition to the British geographic archive. For over a
century, Morris or one of his direct descendants (son, grandson, and great-grand-
son) held the position of surveyor general in Nova Scotia.
   While Morris was mapping regions that the French knew well, putative impe-
rial boundaries in Wulstukwik were again brought into question as British and
French officials competed for control of the Saint John River and its inhabitants.
This winding river was perhaps the most valuable waterway in the northeast; un-
like the St Lawrence – which was difficult to navigate under the best conditions
and impassable for several months in the winter – the Saint John was a viable and
reliable route to the interior. Before the War of the Austrian Succession, France and
132                           Homelands and Empires


Britain had claimed the Saint John River area as their own, or at least described it
as a disputed area inhabited by the Wulstukwiuk and Passamaquoddy. The war
itself did not resolve the issue, so both sides continued to express their concerns
over the presence of the other. In 1749, William Shirley wrote to the governor of
New France, Roland-Michel Barrin, le Marquis de la Galissonière, responding to
a letter the French governor had sent Mascarene in which he asked if the Abenaki
– who had joined the war as French allies – were to be included in the peace.
Shirley argued that the Saint John River had been long considered the “heart”
of Nova Scotia. The inhabitants residing there, both Acadian and Indigenous,
were therefore subjects of the British king and received the same protection from
the governor of Nova Scotia as all other subjects living in the province did.35 La
Galissonière angered Shirley because of two inflammatory statements that he in-
cluded in his letter to Mascarene. First, he informed Mascarene that the Abenaki
were French allies and if they were not included in the peace he would have to
support their efforts to continue the war in Nova Scotia or Massachusetts. Second,
he referred to the Abenaki and the region they inhabited as “dependances du gou-
vernment de Canada.” Shirley responded angrily, noting that the Abenaki had
acted treasonously by attacking Annapolis Royal after promising Mascarene to re-
main peaceful. Yet Shirley was perhaps mistaken in identifying which Indigenous
group had done what. He referred to the group of Wulstukwiuk who visited
Mascarene to discuss the possibility of war and who promised the British to live
in peace. Shirley then described how “three weeks later they returned with oth-
ers from their village and their priest, Le Loutre” to kill British officers found
outside the fort, slaughter cattle, and burn houses.36 Le Loutre, however, worked
with the Mi’kmaq at Shubenacadie. It was Père Germain who counselled the
Wulstukwiuk and Passamaquoddy of the Wulstukw River.37 Despite the confu-
sion over Indigenous groups, Shirley argued forcefully that the Saint John River
area was part of Nova Scotia.
   In early July of 1749, Captain John Rous arrived at the Saint John River to claim
the region for Britain. Upon his arrival he found Charles Deschamps de Boishébert,
a French naval officer, who had been charged with preventing the British from
building forts in the region. Rous announced that he had orders from the king
to investigate the harbours and ports and collect geographic information, and
he wanted to know by what authority Boishébert was in the region.38 Though
Boishébert struck his colours and admitted that the territory was contested, he
later explained to Cornwallis, the new governor of Nova Scotia, that he had been
sent to the region by La Galissonière and ordered to prevent the British from build-
ing any fortifications until the two Crowns had officially settled the boundary dis-
pute.39 The French had another source in the region from whom information could
be collected: Charles Germain, a Jesuit missionary who had served among the
Wulstukwiuk since 1740. A few days after Rous confronted Boishébert, Germain
told the authorities at Quebec what he had witnessed. Germain wrote to Jacques-
Pierre de Taffanel, Marquis de la Jonquière, who had replaced La Galissonière as
governor of New France two days after Rous and Boishébert met on the river. The
priest explained to the recently arrived administrator that the British interpreted
the Acadian boundary quite widely (which, since the British claimed to have con-
quered Acadia in 1710, would allow them to unfurl their fictive Nova Scotia over
                                  A Pale on the Coast                              133


the formerly French region). In fact, the British argued that their territory stretched
to a place thirteen leagues closer to Boston than the Saint John River, and went
quite a distance inland.40 This was not a new claim, but its persistence, coupled
with renewed British interest in Nova Scotia, troubled the French.
  It would be up to appointed commissaries in Paris to attempt a boundary settle-
ment, but possession was apparently one of the strongest proofs the British could
muster. The British were quite anxious to determine Nova Scotia’s limits, and
Mascarene himself had pleaded with the Board of Trade that Spring to have the
matter looked after. Mascarene had always considered the inhabitants of the Saint
John River to be British, and he was concerned over the news that the French were
building a fort and a new settlement at the river’s mouth.41 He had “maintained
the rights of the British Crown on the foot they have appeared to us here to be es-
tablished in these parts of the world.”42 His efforts were well and good, but what
Britain needed was a much bigger foot.

                                      •••
The settlement at Chebucto – later renamed Halifax, an impressive harbour sur-
rounded by forests and dense brush than ran up a steep incline – was long in the
planning. Calls for establishing a new imperial fortress began in the 1720s, origi-
nating from officials at the weakly-fortified Annapolis Royal; in the late 1740s,
however, William Shirley began repeatedly memorializing the Board of Trade and
Plantations. Over time these pleas became more urgent and expressed a need for
both a physical and cartographic presence in Nova Scotia. Shirley argued in a let-
ter to the Board of Trade in 1745 that the French presence at Louisbourg had to be
counterbalanced, possibly with a large fortified and garrisoned place “erected at
Chibougto.”43 Shirley’s concerns were heightened during the War of the Austrian
Succession when the French admiral, the duc d’Anville, attempted to attack Nova
Scotia via Chebucto.44 Shirley wrote directly to the Duke of Newcastle, the secretary
of state of the Southern Department who oversaw colonial administration, to ex-
press his desire to establish a stronger British presence on the Atlantic coast of Nova
Scotia. Shirley argued that the province’s French inhabitants were prepared to join
d’Anville, or any French force for that matter, in an attack against Annapolis.45
   With time, calls for strengthening British pales in the imagined Nova Scotia
were expressed increasingly in cartographic and geographic terms. Using maps
to secure land title had become important in Britain and in the colonies.46 That co-
lonial authorities employed map imagery, therefore, whether intentional or not,
is not surprising. In early 1748, Shirley wrote to the Duke of Bedford, who by then
had replaced Newcastle, complaining about French encroachments at Crown
Point, a disputed site along the British-French boundary at Lake Champlain, that
Shirley argued must be secured for the British. Shirley pleaded with Bedford,
arguing that it was “absolutely necessary for commissioners to run lines between
his Majesty’s colonies and Canada, that the boundary may be settled in such a
manner if possible as to take away all pretence of dispute which will otherwise
perpetually arise between the subjects of the two crowns and to put an end to the
continual encroachments of the French.”47 These boundary lines between the col-
onies would appear on maps, and would thereby provide British administrators
134                            Homelands and Empires


with an official cartographic foundation upon which to base their land claims.
Shirley understood that maps could be used as tools of imperial authority, and he
therefore supported the creation of a cartographic record that would favour British
territorial expansion over that of the French.
   In that same letter, Shirley voiced his concern about the possibility of French in-
habitants becoming loyal British subjects in the putative Nova Scotia. Britain had
neglected the administration of Nova Scotia since it captured Port Royal in 1710,
allowing the Acadians to live as they had been in their several marshland villages
in Mi’kma’ki. As the War of the Austrian Succession came to a close in both Europe
and North America, careful land management was required to assert authority
over long ignored regions. Shirley doubted that the French in the province would
transfer their allegiance to the British Crown without the influence of British set-
tlers. To that end, Shirley commissioned Charles Morris to create a survey of the
Bay of Fundy. Shirley “directed Capt. Morris in his survey to see what room there
was for interspersing British settlements to be seated in a commodious and defen-
sible manner among those of the French within the aforementioned tract, which
he has done, and marked out in the enclosed plan.”48 Morris’s manuscript map
and accompanying survey provided both local and imperial officials with the geo-
graphic and cartographic information necessary to make decisions about imperial
expansion (figure 4.1).
   Morris was instrumental in the creation of official geographic and cartographic
knowledge relating to Nova Scotia generally, and eventually to Halifax specifi-
cally. In his detailed reports sent back to Shirley, Morris recorded that he was to
locate “places in the Province of Nova Scotia a number of Protestants may speed-
ily settle,” and to ensure that they could support and protect themselves.49 His
report divided the region into the three areas most heavily populated by Acadians:
Annapolis Royal, Minas, and Chignecto. Morris determined the limits and loca-
tion of the Bay of Fundy, provided detailed settlement proposals, and suggested
how the region could be defended. When he described the proposed settlements
around Annapolis Royal, Morris suggested that families there could support the
garrison “in the labour of repairs, in finding timber, boards, shingles and fire-
wood.”50 He suggested that each lot include waterfront acreage to allow commu-
nication with other settlers and access to the central garrison, at which the settlers
could sell their goods to help sustain themselves while clearing their land. When
describing the area around Chignecto, Morris explained how the area’s natural
geography would defend against French attacks. Providing a blueprint for the fort
building that would begin a few years later, Morris noted that a virtually inde-
structible fort could be erected at Chignecto because “the marshes surrounding it
for a mile distant, except toward the Basin, would render it impregnable and large
ships cannot approach within half a mile and that only upon the top of high water
and in great danger by the rapidity of the tide and their grounding in two hours.”51
Moreover, settlers would benefit from the ample pasture for cattle and sheep and
large tracts of arable land.52 With the 1748 survey of the Bay of Fundy, Morris
served as the thin edge of an expansionist wedge. His work in the region estab-
lished his imperial importance, and his cartographic contribution was rewarded
with additional commissions.

  4.1 Extract from Charles Morris’s A Draught of the Upper Part of the Bay of Fundy, 1748.
    The indication of “Fort Edward 1750,” and “French Fort build 1750” suggests that
     this map was used for strategic purposes after its creation. Morris noted Acadian

   After Morris completed his survey of the Bay of Fundy and supplied his draft
of the region to William Shirley, the Massachusetts governor commissioned him to
complete a survey of the entire province of Nova Scotia. Again, he was instructed
to define the limits of the province, record areas of current French habitation, pro-
pose areas for English settlement, and describe the province’s climate and geogra-
phy. Defining the limits of this imperial fiction was of great importance because the
Treaty of Utrecht had left the issue unresolved. In “A Brief Survey of Nova Scotia,”
Morris divided the province’s geography into three regions: lands bordering on
136                           Homelands and Empires


the Canada River (St Lawrence River), lands bordering the northern part of the Bay
of Fundy, and Nova Scotia’s peninsula. Morris was well aware of Nova Scotia’s
imperial importance, and his surveys and reports suggested ways that Britain
could strengthen its territories in North America. If settled with Protestants, he
argued, Nova Scotia “will then be not only a barrier to all other Brittish Colonies,
but with their assistance may sooner or later, either ruin the French Provinces, or
at least greatly distress them.”53 He provided a history of the province, beginning
with Cabot’s voyage of 1496 and ending with the Treaty of Utrecht, and com-
pared the provincial boundaries as defined by the French and the English. The
French boundaries were more fluid than those of the English. France had stretched
its claim from the mouth of the St Lawrence River in the north to the Penobscot
River in the south when favourable relations with the Wabanaki permitted. But
the French could also claim that Acadia was limited to peninsular Nova Scotia –
minimizing the amount of land ceded to Britain in 1713 – since no record clearly
indicated otherwise. Morris’s “Draught of the Northern English Colonies” notes
that Nova Scotia must include the peninsula, present day New Brunswick, and the
Gaspé region of Quebec. The map also suggested, “this country from Kennebeck
river to Cape Rozier was always called by the French ACCADA” (figure 4.2). As
tools of British expansion, Morris’s maps and reports were important local and de-
tailed geographic descriptions presented in a language that superimposed Nova
Scotia over Acadia while ignoring Mi’kma’ki, Wulstukwik, and the Dawnland.
These surveys made a significant contribution to the development of imperial pol-
icy because the extent of land under British control was of central importance to
the metropolitan administrators.54
   The pleas and plans for settlement that originated primarily from New England,
Morris’s reports and maps, and a plan for civil government drafted by William
Shirley assisted George Montagu Dunk, the 2nd Earl of Halifax and president of
the Board of Trade, in creating “A Plan for Settling Nova Scotia.” Halifax, the son
of the 1st Earl of Halifax, had been a brilliant student at Cambridge and married
well. His wife, Ann Dunk, carried a dowry of over £100,000, but there was a catch:
a condition of her family’s inheritance was that all heirs must take the surname
Dunk. Halifax, who took to signing his name “Halifax Dunk,” apparently thought
the new name was a small price to pay. He became a Lord of the Bedchamber in
the household of the Prince of Wales and then a Master of the Buckhounds for the
Pelhams before being appointed president of the Board of Trade and Plantations.
The Board of Trade’s influence had deteriorated over the course of the eighteenth
century, and Halifax was determined to reinstate its authority.55 His direct involve-
ment in the settlement’s planning is characteristic of Halifax himself, who fought
for “his right, and the right of the board, to be regarded as the directing force in
colonial affairs.”56 Halifax’s plan addressed most requirements for a successful set-
tlement, but he emphasized surveys and cartography. Careful land management
was important because the availability of land served as a primary attraction for
potential settlers. Halifax had specific instructions for future governors and sur-
veyors about how best to lay out towns and settle new citizens in Nova Scotia. Five
settlements were proposed, with two to be marked out “containing one hundred
thousand acres or 12 miles each … at Chibucto, which is intended to be the me-
tropolis,” and each town was to be allotted an equal number of inhabitants.57 These
                                  A Pale on the Coast                                137




      4.2 Extract of Charles Morris’s Draught of the Northern English Colonies, 1749.
   Morris notes clearly that Nova Scotia’s boundaries extend to Gaspé and he indicates
     the location of Mi’kmaq missions and settlements. Map reproduction courtesy
          of the Norman B. Leventhal Map Center at the Boston Public Library.


settlements were to be surveyed in such a way as to provide for expansion when
required, so sufficient land was to be left surrounding the original settlement. The
plan was overly optimistic, and upon their arrival at Chebucto the settlers were
able to establish only one of the proposed five towns. The Indigenous residents of
Mi’kma’ki continued to protect their homeland against British expansion.
  Halifax also included instructions for the specific placement of the settlements
and the general manner in which the towns should be laid out. Towns were to be
surveyed to ensure that each lot shared a common boundary with its neighbour,
“taking care, however, that the said lands do not extend in length along the sea
coast, but only a necessary part therefore do abut upon the sea.”58 Unlike the
French Canadian seigneurial system, in which each lot fronted onto the water to
facilitate travel and communication, Halifax was explicit in his desire to establish
an English grid-style township.59 He repeated this sentiment when he instructed
the governor, with whom the final design for the town layout would ultimately
rest, that “a regular plan ought to be observed in the laying out the streets and
buildings of each town,” and that although some alterations to such regular plans
138                           Homelands and Empires


may be required, that he “should be directed to observe as much regularity as
possible in this.”60 A town laid out in a “regular” fashion would stamp the new
geography with a British design.
   Halifax was also aware that carefully placed surveys could bring the French in-
habitants under the power of the British authorities, a concept that echoed Morris’s
surveys and maps. Surveyors were to ensure that towns laid out for the proposed
settlement, and any future settlements, included land currently inhabited by the
French. As the number of towns grew, each carefully surveyed to encompass a
section of Acadian settlement, French settlers’ property rights would then be de-
fined and controlled by the imperial authorities as part of a renewed effort to in-
corporate Acadians into the British legal regime. Land surveys would also help
British authorities keep track of French inhabitants whose lands could not be ex-
propriated by careful town planning. Halifax instructed the governor to make a
prompt account of French settlements, including their placement and the number
of inhabitants at each. Furthermore, Halifax required “that a survey be now like-
wise made of their lands now under actual improvement, specifying the numbers
of acres cultivated by each particular person.”61 Careful town planning, as far as
Halifax was concerned, could control the French as long as detailed geographic
surveys were employed as tools of imperial power to support the British military
presence in the colony. Though the British had previously been largely unable to
use land grants for imperial purposes, a stronger settlement provided new oppor-
tunities for success. Spatial knowledge, from Morris to Shirley to Halifax, served
two important purposes during this early reconnaissance phase: first, the land was
measured, mapped, and therefore known; second, these geographic descriptions
and depictions were presented as evidence that the imperial fiction of Nova Scotia
could be administered and controlled, thus making it real.

                                     •••
Promoting the proposed settlement in Nova Scotia was an instrumental element
of its success. The British government needed to attract both settlers and pub-
lic support for what would become an expensive endeavour. In 1749, just before
British settlers left to establish a new pale in the northeast, an anonymous author
published The Historical Geography of Nova Scotia, a 110-page tract meant to do for
the public in London, especially potential settlers, what Morris’s A Brief Survey of
Nova Scotia had done for the officials. A map is conspicuously absent from this re-
port, but the author explained “my first design was to accompany the descriptions
with a general map of the country, and particular draughts of the most remarkable
bays and harbours in it. But as the intended settlers are now on their departure,
I chose to publish it without the charts; this account being drawn up in such a
manner as to be useful to those people in furnishing them with some necessary
knowledge of the country to which they are going.”62 Even without the map, the au-
thor provided a thorough account of Nova Scotia’s geography and also included
a general history of the province, as Morris had done. The author employed a de-
tailed written map to define the province’s limits and location in terms of latitude
and longitude, as well as to describe major geographical landmarks. The author
was concerned when describing the benefits of settling at “Chibouctou” about
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              139


military vulnerability, arguing that the “harbour lies more open and exposed to
the weather, and the entrance is not so easy to defend”; the author agreed, how-
ever, that the best place to settle was the Atlantic coast.63
   Definitions of the boundary lines between Nova Scotia and New England as
well as Nova Scotia and Canada are scattered throughout this tract, most often
when the author discusses treaties between the French and the English. However,
the author dealt with one of the most contentious issues in the cartographic history
of Nova Scotia – the “ancient” boundary of Acadia – in a cursory, almost dismis-
sive manner. The author informed his audience, “soon after [the attack on Port
Royal], in the year 1712, was signed the peace of Utrecht, by which a perpetual
cession is made to England of Acadie, or Nova Scotia, in its full extent, according
to its ancient limits … and what those ancient limits are, I presume sufficiently ap-
pears from the course of this history.”64 The Acadian and Nova Scotian boundary
issue had confounded British and French officials for decades, and, despite the
author’s claim, this tract shed little light on the limits of these imperial fictions.
This cartographic stalemate would have been of particular interest to the author’s
audience, potential settlers and curious Britons alike, who were interested in what
was happening in North America and looked to the popular press for information.
Imperial developments in general were the subject of debate among informed
British citizens, many of whom expressed their opinions in a variety of ways, in-
cluding contributing content to periodicals.65
   “Geography is so necessary to illustrate history,” wrote French geographer
Jacques-Nicholas Bellin, quoted in The Gentleman’s Magazine in 1746, “that they
ought to be inseparably connected.”66 The monthly magazines published in Britain
during the eighteenth century often emphasized the connection between geog-
raphy and history by printing maps to illustrate the accounts that appeared in
their pages. With a circulation of up to 15,000 copies for a single issue, these pub-
lications were effective vehicles for influencing public opinion.67 Edward Cave,
a shoemaker’s son with intellect and ability – and an independent spirit that got
him expelled from school – became London’s leading printer and magazine pub-
lisher when he launched The Gentleman’s Magazine in 1731. Borrowing liberally
from other published works and exploiting his connections at the Post Office to
procure news, Cave’s operation was enough of a threat that a group of booksellers
in London began the rival London Magazine in 1732. Given the lack of clear copy-
right law at the time, it was easier to compete with Cave in the printing business
than attempt to beat him in court. For much of the eighteenth century, these two
magazines battled for readership among literate Britons by publishing parliamen-
tary news, poems, gossip, and accounts from British settlements overseas.68
   In March 1749, The London Magazine printed the Earl of Halifax’s call for settlers
to travel to Nova Scotia. A general description of the province and Kitchin’s map
accompanied this call (see figure 4.9), providing potential settlers with a geograph-
ic depiction of the region. Other articles in these magazines supplied an historical
context for the province’s imperial significance, including details of the 1621 land
grant issued to Sir William Alexander by King James I, which Britons believed
established the original land claim to Nova Scotia from which Britain could assert
territorial sovereignty.69 Several issues in the 1740s carried descriptions of Nova
Scotia’s landscape. The reader was informed that the province was “surrounded
140                           Homelands and Empires


by the river of St. Lawrence, the gulf of that same name, the gut of Canso, Cape
Sable Shore on the Atlantic ocean, and the Bay of Fundy.” The boundary between
Nova Scotia and New England was traditionally set at the Saint John River, which
flows southeast from the St Lawrence into the Bay of Fundy, although “a late order
of council” set the boundary at the river of Holy Cross, which drains into the Bay
of Fundy farther south.70 This general description of the boundaries was followed
with more exact limits of the province and of Annapolis Royal, set in latitude and
longitude. Readers engaged with the geographic, cartographic, and historical de-
pictions of Nova Scotia, and many editorial contributors, were able to identify
geographic imaginations with imperial aspirations.
   Cartographic imperialism, the process by which maps delineated imperial pos-
sessions and laid claim to geographic areas, was central to accounts of Nova Scotia
in The London Magazine. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 may have ceded the French
possession of Acadia to Britain, but Britons were concerned that the French were
using maps to manipulate the size of the area that they were surrendering.71 “The
French,” one contributor to the London Magazine argued, “since the property of this
country has been vested in the English, affect to confine the name of Accadia to
the peninsula only: but their own maps, made before the cession of this province,
give it the limits we have now assigned. I will add, that the words of the treaty do
not contact it within narrower limits than were before allowed to Accadia.”72 The
author continued to note that although many old French maps supported English
geographic claims by providing a much larger depiction of Acadia than the French
would prefer to cede, new French maps attempted not only to reduce the extent
of Acadia but also to position recent French land claims – especially that of the
Gaspé fishing region – in the province. He continued, “this name [Gaspé] they
do indeed sometimes extend so far, as to take of the greatest part of Nova Scotia,
and leave us little if anything, more under the title of Accadie, than the peninsula
before mentioned. Such a paper encroachment, if not well attended to, may, in
time, be construed into a sort of claim by prescription.”73 Informed Britons were
aware of and concerned about cartography’s ability to influence imperial develop-
ment, especially when the result was detrimental to the British cause. That these
discussions of cartographic imperialism took place in a public forum indicates an
increasing interest in maps and geography among educated Britons during the
years prior to the founding of Halifax.74
   When the time came to announce plans to establish a new settlement, the British
government placed advertisements in popular British newspapers and magazines.
In March 1749, an advertisement appeared in The London Gazette aimed primarily
at “officers and private men lately dismissed His Majesty’s land and sea service,”
the rationale being that these men now had few other military responsibilities,
were free to move, and could therefore settle in Nova Scotia.75 The notices and
accompanying maps were so successful that the mayor of Liverpool wrote to the
Board of Trade asking for money to support those “who came from distant parts
of the country” to travel to Nova Scotia. The mayor wrote a week later asking if
any more ships would be leaving for Nova Scotia that season, to which the Board
replied that it was too late in the year to arrange extra ships and suggested “not to
receive or enter more persons, than will be sufficient to fill the ship now receiving
persons at that port.”76 With the promise of free land, no taxes, and a year’s worth
                                 A Pale on the Coast                             141


of provisions, the Board of Trade was able to enlist 2,500 people to sail with
Edward Cornwallis to Chebucto. When their ships arrived, the passengers would
have marvelled at the size of the harbour, explored the coastline, and walked
through the fir, pine, and birch trees that would have to be felled and turned into
shelter, and perhaps wondered what might grow in the rocky soil beneath. In the
years following settlement, interested British citizens continued looking to print-
ed maps, the popular press, and published travel accounts to learn more about
Halifax. Although the available information was not always detailed, the public
discussion on geography and cartography that took place during this period, as
in the pre-settlement era, suggests that many literate citizens were curious about
developments at Halifax and relied on maps and geographic reports to inform
their image of the settlement. Unfortunately for those who wanted to receive the
most accurate maps and the most truthful reports on the colony, sources passed
through several filters before being presented to the public. In the map-publishing
trade, economic barriers and limited access to official information defined what
maps could be published and how often each would appear. Periodicals such as
The Gentleman’s Magazine or The London Magazine were able to provide maps and
colonial correspondence to a wide audience at an affordable price, but because
these publications relied on contributions from settlers or excerpts from other
printed sources, many months could pass between updates.
   Geographic detail was often sacrificed for both aesthetic appeal and imperial
objectives; instead of a simple reflection of regional geography, these maps pro-
vided an idealized image aimed at striking an imperial chord in the metropole.
The best example of a Halifax settler contributing to popular magazines is that of
Moses Harris, whose unpublished map captured some of the dangers at Halifax,
while his published efforts reflected the British settlement that imperialists wanted
to see. In 1749, the nineteen-year-old Harris and his wife arrived at Chebucto on
the Winchelsea with the first group of settlers sent from England. Harris’s interests
included nature and geography. He had studied entomology since his youth, and
at fourteen he began an apprenticeship with the London geographer Charles Price.
Harris left for Halifax before he could complete his apprenticeship, and within a
short time of his arrival he had produced three maps of the infant settlement.77
Two of his surveys appeared in various forms in either The Gentleman’s Magazine,
published maps, or both, but Harris’s first survey, which demonstrated the dan-
gers at Halifax, was never printed or released to the public. Comparing his un-
published map to those made available to Britons illustrates the ways in which
colonial promotion and the nature of the map trade influenced what kinds of maps
were made public.
   According to the records surrounding his voyage to Halifax, Moses Harris was
a sawyer. This entry in the passenger list was possibly a mistaken entry for “sur-
veyor,” which would explain why Harris made a few maps and then quit the
colony.78 His work may have benefitted from, but did not infringe upon, that of
Charles Morris and John Brewse, official surveyors and mapmakers in Halifax,
who were far more interested in facilitating expansion than submitting their maps
for publication. The first map Harris created at Halifax was never published for
reasons that seem obvious when the promotion of a settlement is weighed against
a detailed geographic depiction. A Plan of Chebucto Harbour with the Town of Hallefax

(figure 4.3) isolated the settlement on the edge of a densely wooded peninsula
with only a single path cleared towards the Northwest Arm. Ships in the harbour

of the map features an angry dragon, both of which symbolize the potential threat
posed by the region’s wildlife (figure 4.4).80 Including dangerous animals – mythi-
cal or otherwise – was not common in maps aimed at colonial promotion, and in
later versions of Harris’s maps these predatory animals were replaced with much
friendlier ones.81
   Dangerous animals were not the only aspect of this map omitted from later ver-
sions. Trees were thinned, the topography was tamed, and all evidence that Halifax
was built on a harbour frequented by the Mi’kmaq was erased. Harris’s first
map is rare because it offered evidence that Halifax was in Mi’kma’ki, not Nova
Scotia. Across the harbour from the town, nestled among the trees at present-day
Dartmouth, Harris drew an Indigenous wigwam. Other maps may have includ-
ed an Indigenous presence, but it was often an abstracted rendering situated at
a distance from the Halifax settlement. Harris, on the other hand, depicted the
