Mi’kmaq using an Indigenous dwelling and placed them within striking dis-
tance. Although Halifax settlers were well aware of the Mi’kmaw presence, this
image of Halifax was not to be the one that informed curious Britons.82 Harris’s
next two maps provided a gentler image of the colony, one that emphasized the
town’s strength and imperial importance while at the same time pushing the
dangers at Halifax off the page.
   The Porcupine map, (figure 4.5) which appeared in The Gentleman’s Magazine in
1750, is the most famous of Harris’s collection and is often admired more for the
inclusion of insects and animals than for its cartographic depiction of Halifax. The
sketch itself provides few details about the region, instead offering its viewers
a glimpse of wildlife and imperial symbols. The local animals and insects, espe-
cially the porcupine, replaced the daunting topography and Indigenous presence
in Harris’s earlier map.83 The map’s scale is no longer guarded by a dragon but by
a “Musk Beetle.” Also included on the map is “The Ensign of Nova Scotia,” as well
as the coat of arms of the colony’s seven baronets, an allusion to the imperial pres-
ence in the new colony.84 The names given to various locations on the Porcupine map
reflected contemporary imperial figures: what was Rowses Island on Harris’s first
map became Cornwallis Island; Torrington Bay became Bedford Bay; and Hawk’s
River was renamed Sandwich River for the First Lord of the Admiralty. This map
144                            Homelands and Empires




 4.5 Moses Harris’s Porcupine map, 1749. Wildlife and imperial symbols, not geography,
  dominate this chart. Special Collections, Dalhousie University. Map 38 (Morse) 1749.



was meant to render Halifax familiar to a British audience by employing common
names and symbols, presenting a tame landscape, and offering a view of interest-
ing wildlife. Geographic details were of secondary importance.
  To make maps for public consumption, British geographers compiled as much
information as they could. In 1749, the engraver and copperplate printer Edward
Ryland published Moses Harris’s A plan of the town of Halifax in Nova Scotia, which
was a simple map indicating the layout of the town.85 The map resembled John
Brewse’s survey of Halifax, only Harris included some trees and wooden pick-
ets surrounding the more formally constructed palisades. Thomas Jefferys, who
would become one of Britain’s most influential map publishers, was anxious to
compile a new and impressive map of Halifax and Nova Scotia.86 To that end,
he combined Harris’s Porcupine map and town map (originally published by
Ryland) with a chart of Nova Scotia based on the surveys of the French geographer
Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d’Anville. The result was A New Map of Nova Scotia,
                                  A Pale on the Coast                                  145




    4.6 Thomas Jefferys’s A New Map of Nova Scotia, 1750. Insets of dubious accuracy
      and a dedication to the Board of Trade take up most of the space on this map.
            Special Collections, Dalhousie University. Map 40 (Morse) 1750.


(figure 4.6) an attractive map that though it did little to increase actual knowledge
of Nova Scotia’s inlets, marshlands, fertile valleys or natural resources, epitomized
the process of British mapmaking.87 The map drew from a variety of sources, none
of which were created from officially commissioned professional British surveys.
The main section of the map is a version of the Porcupine map, but instead of fill-
ing unknown areas with animals and insects, Jefferys included three insets. At the
top left corner is a map of Nova Scotia oriented with Boston as a reference; in the
top right is a replica of Harris’s A Plan of Halifax with a legend to identify town
buildings; and at the bottom right is a landscape portrait of the settlement, en-
titled “A View of Halifax drawn from the topmasthead.” Examining the details of
this map illustrates the difficulties and restrictions cartographers in Britain faced
when compiling the latest geographical findings.88 The inset of Nova Scotia con-
tains many of the same misrepresentations as other regional maps published in
the mid-eighteenth century. Chebucto Harbour dwarfs St Margaret’s Bay, which
in reality is the larger of the two, making Halifax appear to be situated on the most
146                            Homelands and Empires


welcoming bay on Nova Scotia’s Atlantic shore. Jefferys, unable to acquire original
surveys for the Atlantic coast, used d’Anville’s map. The inset of Harris’s plan of
Halifax is an overly simplistic topographic representation. There is no attempt to
indicate the slope upon which the city stood, the trees are sparse, and there are
no indications of a Mi’kmaw presence.
   The final inset, a landscape portrait of the town, illustrates the way in which
landscape art was used to provide a British vision of overseas settlements. British
colonial landscape art during the mid- to late-eighteenth century attempted to por-
tray geography in a realistic fashion. But these paintings can also be interpreted as
illustrating how the British wanted these regions to appear. Like maps, landscape
art allowed Britons to define themselves as a “civilized and civilizing” people by
presenting alien environments in an aesthetically familiar way, minimizing the
cognitive leap required to associate a strange wilderness with an imperial posses-
sion.89 The bird’s-eye view of Halifax on Jefferys’s map, although not picturesque
like the typical landscape art of the era, provided a British vision of Nova Scotia to
which British readers could relate, emphasized by the British flag flying at the gates
of the settlement.90 The clearing upon which the settlers have built their homes is
level, although both outside streets seem to be marked with striations, which may
be an attempt to indicate slope. Particularly important is the inclusion of tents on
the outskirts of the settlement, nestled among felled trees and their stumps. Some
settlers had yet to construct their homes at Halifax, so the inclusion of these tents
hints at the harsh settler reality in an otherwise largely optimistic image of Halifax.
   This Jefferys map, like many others, was dedicated to the Board of Trade and
Plantations. The Board had a complicated relationship with maps published for
the general public. While Halifax and other members relied on commercially
available maps to get a sense of colonial geography, they were receiving the lat-
est manuscript surveys and reports and could commission maps to provide more
detailed information. The flow of official geographic knowledge from settlement
to metropole, although not always fast, was direct, multifaceted, and largely unfil-
tered.91 As a result, the Board attempted to distance itself from British geographers,
allowing them to dedicate maps in its honour only to help with sales, even though
the Board never “superintended or approved” the manner in which these maps
were executed.92 A dedication to the Board of Trade gave maps an air of authority
that would attract subscribers, even though the Board itself was not completely
comfortable with the relationship. Its members did not want to appear as spon-
soring geographic arguments over which they had no control. Geographers also
inserted additional headings onto maps, hoping to increase sales by claiming them
to be based on the “most recent surveys,” or calling them “newly improved.”
There was a cognitive disconnect between the language geographers used to
explain their maps and the content of those maps, just as there was a tension be-
tween the map’s image and the reality it represented. British geographers catered
to the public’s curiosity, aesthetic tastes, and imperial outlook to increase sales.
Imperialist Britons were more likely to purchase imperialist maps, especially those
featured in popular magazines with an imperial bias. Though most mapmakers
considered themselves arbiters of geographic “truth,” almost all faced accusations
from their competitors of serving state interests.93 It was just as likely, however,
that they were responding to market demands.
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              147


                                      •••
Upon his arrival at Chebucto, Edward Cornwallis, the new governor of Nova
Scotia, dutifully began corresponding with the Board of Trade. Cornwallis was
from a family with enough connections and power to secure a successful future
for Edward and his twin brother Frederick. The two young boys became royal
pages at the age of 12, and in the following years Edward secured military posts
and administrative positions: he sat in Parliament, he fought at Culloden, he was
appointed a Groom of the Royal Bedchamber, and, in 1749, he was named gover-
nor of Nova Scotia.94 Cornwallis arrived at Chebucto aboard the Sphinx on 21 June
1749, leading a convoy carrying almost 2,500 army officials, soldiers, and settlers.
In his first letter, he gave the commissioners an idea of the region’s geography,
informing them, “the country is one of continued wood, no clear spot to be seen or
heard of.”95 Aside from the small area of land cleared by d’Anville’s fleet during
its aborted attack on Nova Scotia in 1746, the settlers recognized few changes in
the region’s natural geography.96 A month later, Cornwallis again emphasized the
labour required to clear the forests, but added that twelve acres had been opened
in July and that he was confident he could have all the settlers in homes by winter.
Along with this letter, Cornwallis intended to send a plan of the settlement draft-
ed by military engineer John Brewse.97 The plan merely anticipated construction,
but as the first of only a few maps sent to London during this period, Brewse’s
contribution was quite influential. Little is known of Brewse’s career before he
arrived in Halifax with Cornwallis. However, military engineers made a consider-
able contribution to European mapping and surveying during the early modern
period. Since the sixteenth century, military engineers had surveyed potential bat-
tlegrounds and in the 1740s they took a leading role in cartographic development,
often drafting town plans and fortifications. As artillery improved, cities could no
longer be protected by high walls and instead relied on thicker, lower ramparts
able to deflect artillery fire and support defensive cannon. These new fortifications
required careful planning prior to construction and military sketches often served
as the basis for town development, providing engineers with a central role in es-
tablishing British plantations.98
   Brewse wasted no time in creating a Project for Fortifying the Town of Hallifax; in
Nova Scotia, 1749 (figure 4.7), which was sent to the Board of Trade in Cornwallis’s
letter of August 1749. This letter also included Captain Durell’s map of the har-
bour, created in the 1730s; the combination of both charts gave the Board of Trade a
visual representation of the region. “From seeing the plan only,” wrote Cornwallis,
“one would be apt to choose Sandwich Point as the best situation for a town,” but
the governor continued to list the faults of Sandwich Point (Point Pleasant) and the
benefits of the situation he chose, which is where the city stands today.99 Brewse’s
map is less informative than other military plans, which usually included forests
and other aspects of the natural environment to give authorities enough infor-
mation to make strategic decisions. The use of striations on Brewse’s map was
an attempt to provide an idea of relief, but the markings do little to portray ac-
curately the incline upon which the city was to be built.100 Yet the town’s layout
was meant to project power. The placement of the governor’s house, the church,
the parade ground, and the military citadel anticipated a settlement dominated
148                                 Homelands and Empires




         4.7 John Brewse’s Project for Fortifying the Town of Hallifax; in Nova Scotia, 1749.
       There are no trees to be cut and the well-organized town is surrounded by strong
      fortifications. The position of the church (marked B) and the government building
        (marked C) are reversed. This error was reproduced on Halifax maps long after
         both buildings were constructed on their respective ends of the Grand Parade.
                      Library and Archives Canada, H3/240/Halifax/1749.


by local authority, religious figures, and military strength.101 The planned palisade
was substantial and included a proposed earthen ditch, a cross-section of which is
provided at the map’s lower right corner.
  The exclusion of Indigenous peoples on Brewse’s plan illustrates how the
British image of Nova Scotia changed as administrators developed new policies.
“It is in the nature of all maps,” the late J.B. Harley noted, “to construct a world in
the image of society rather than to hold a mirror to an ‘objective reality.’”102 When
the settlers arrived at Halifax they renamed the region, replacing Indigenous
terms with British ones in an attempt to claim the land and superimpose British
references that suited the purpose of the colony. Ignoring the Mi’kmaw presence
and providing new names helped create a British sense of order out of a home-
land seen as pure wilderness.103 Unable to understand Mi’kma’ki as a homeland
with a history, culture, and spirituality closely tied to the land itself, Britons saw
the image of Halifax and started to believe in the imperial fiction of Nova Scotia.
However, Nova Scotia was an idea, an imperial aspiration. Halifax became an
                                  A Pale on the Coast                                 149


impressive pale in a faltering homeland, but territorial competition persisted and
there was no certainty that Europeans would be the victors.104 Despite their re-
duced numbers, the local Mi’kmaq were formidable foes who controlled much
of the regional geography until the arrival of the Loyalists in the mid-1780s and
exerted considerable influence into the early nineteenth century.105 An investiga-
tion into British maps of the Halifax region must recognize this tension and not
simply argue that the Mi’kmaq were ignored. Individual mapmakers could choose
to exclude Indigenous peoples from British maps, thereby denying them a place
in the British image of Nova Scotia. Mapmakers who did recognize Indigenous
peoples could choose where and how they were represented. Yet, on the other
hand, the fact that the Mi’kmaq in Mi’kma’ki (and the Wabanaki more generally in
their respective homelands) found their way onto European maps indicates that
Indigenous peoples participated in mapping their territory into the imperial fic-
tions meant to subsume them.106
   In the settlement’s early days, there were signs that the Indigenous-British re-
lationship might be less strained than it had been. In August and September of
1749, Governor Cornwallis and the Council met with Wulstukwiuk chiefs from
the Wulstukw River as well as a Mi’kmaw representative from Chignecto. At this
meeting, the Wabanaki agreed to a renewed treaty based on that signed in 1726.
Their understanding of the previous treaty was stated clearly, and present at the
negotiations were several men who had attended the 1726 meetings. Similarly,
British Lieutenant Governor Paul Mascarene witnessed both the 1749 and 1726
treaties.107 The impact of the 1749 treaty is debatable. Exactly how many del-
egates participated, what fraction of the Mi’kmaw and Wulstukwiuk population
they represented, and whether this agreement created a wedge between the two
Wabanaki groups is not entirely clear.108 Determining the effects of this treaty is dif-
ficult because although chiefs signed the agreement, there is no record that it was
widely ratified by other members. Most Mi’kmaq distanced themselves from the
agreement and continued carrying out hostilities against the British.109 According
to Père Germain, the missionary priest serving at the Wulstukw River, even the
Wulstukwiuk failed to ratify the agreement to which their chiefs had agreed.110
The French had spent decades establishing their relationship with the Mi’kmaq
and the Wulstukwiuk while remaining careful not to encroach on their lands. It is
unlikely that the British would succeed in cementing a lasting agreement shortly
after arriving to construct a military fort.
   While there is confusion over the reach and strength of the 1749 treaty, general
Mi’kmaw opposition to the British settlement was made clear by letters sent to
Halifax. One letter, likely written on behalf of the Mi’kmaq by Père Maillard, a
missionary at Île Royale, outlined Mi’kmaw anger over British encroachment in
terms that illustrate the Indigenous spiritual connection with territory and their
separate racial identity. “The place where you are,” the letter begins,

  the place where you live, the place where you are building a fortification, the place
  where you want now to establish yourself, the place of which you want to make your-
  self the absolute master, this place belongs to me. Me, the Savage, I am sprung from
  the land as doth the grass. I that am savage, am born there, and my fathers before
  me. This place is my land, I swear it. It is God who has given me this land to be my
150                              Homelands and Empires


  homeland forever … My king and your king together distribute these lands and it is
  because of that they are presently at peace, but for me I can make neither alliance or
  peace with you. Show me where I could, an Indian, withdraw to. As for you, you hunt
  me down. Show me then where you want me to take refuge. You have taken over
  almost all of this land, so that the only resource left to me is Kchibouctouk [Halifax].
  Yet you begrudge me even this piece [of land] and you even want to chase me from it.
  That is what makes me know that you have sworn to not cease to make war on us and
  to never enter into alliance with us. You are proud of your great numbers. I, who am
  in very small number, can only count on the God which knows what this is about. An
  earthworm knows to rise up when it is attacked; I, an Indian, know at least as much
  as an earthworm and will similarly respond forcefully in defence when I am attacked.
  Your residence at Port Royal did not give me much cause for concern, therefore you
  see that for a long time I left you in peace, but now you force me to speak out because
  of the considerable theft you have made.111

This response left no room for doubt; some Mi’kmaq considered the founding of
Halifax a “theft,” and they demanded that the fort be removed. Whereas before the
Mi’kmaq had fought only sporadically against the British settlement at Annapolis
Royal, they were now more concerned for their territorial rights. The British, how-
ever, were ready to dig in their heels as never before and maps would play a cru-
cial role.
   Halifax maps of the mid-eighteenth century illustrate how cartographic rep-
resentations had changed, especially in relation to the inclusion or exclusion of
Indigenous peoples. There is reason to suggest that Indigenous peoples were able
to express their concepts of geographic space to British settlers. In New England,
seventeenth-century land deeds demonstrated Indigenous peoples’ use of cartog-
raphy to sketch what lands they were willing to sell, even if the terms of sale were
not always understood by both sides.112 In Nova Scotia, the Mi’kmaw chief Aikon
Aushabuc in 1761 used his hand as a map to explain the region’s geopolitical situ-
ation to an English captive. Making an open circle with his thumb and index
finger, Aushabuc explained the relative positions of Quebec (tip of index finger),
Montreal (joint of index finger), New York, Boston (joint of thumb), and Halifax
(tip of thumb). He then pressed his thumb to his index finger to illustrate how
the British presence was threatening his people.113 As this example demonstrates,
there were multiple interpretations of Nova Scotia’s boundaries and many ways of
explaining the region’s importance at the time of the Halifax settlement. Although
the evidentiary record favours a western interpretation, Indigenous mapping re-
mained centrally important to the Mi’kmaw quest for territorial sovereignty.
   Despite Wabanaki military prowess and geographic power, British geographers
(and their maps depicting the founding of Halifax) controlled and sometimes
removed the Mi’kmaw presence in Nova Scotia. Comparing British geographer
Henry Popple’s 1733 map with those that appeared at the time of the Halifax
settlement illustrates cartography’s ability figuratively to clear the land in prepa-
ration for settlement. Although Popple’s rendering of Nova Scotia’s coastline
leaves something to be desired, he indicated in large font the areas of three promi-
nent Indigenous groups: “Micmaques,” “Souriquois,” and “Etechemins,” which
were current and historical names used for the Mi’kmaq, Wulstukwiuk, or their
                                  A Pale on the Coast                                 151




      4.8 Extract from Henry Popple’s A Map of the British Empire in America, 1733.
        Like French geographers, Popple included prominent Aboriginal names.
                     Library and Archives Canada, H11/1000/1733.


ancestors (figure 4.8). Fewer than twenty years later, when the geographer and
mapmaker Thomas Jefferys was circulating his influential maps in Britain, this
Indigenous element was conspicuous by its absence. The Mi’kmaq had not disap-
peared, but certain maps made it appear as if they had.114 Jefferys’s cartographic
competition in London, Thomas Kitchin, did not ignore Indigenous peoples but
he did exert power over their representation. “Ind. Vil.” appears only in three loca-
tions on peninsular Nova Scotia, although none on its Atlantic coast, where Britain
was to establish Halifax (figure 4.9). Maps produced locally for official use, like
Morris’s Draught of the Northern English Colonies, were only marginally better than
the popular cartography produced for public consumption in Britain.
   Morris’s peninsular Nova Scotia is nearly empty, save for a small marker ex-
plained by the text, “Here is a church for the Cape Sable Indians” (figure 4.2).
Morris may have been more interested in justifying British claims to the region
than in illustrating who was living within it, but he and the other geographers
demonstrated a British cartographic ambivalence towards Indigenous peoples.
When included on maps, the Wabanaki were often controlled and suppressed on
paper in ways that were impossible in reality.

        4.9 Thomas Kitchin’s Nova Scotia Drawn from Surveys, 1749. “Ind. Vil.” marks

  In practical terms, Mi’kmaw resistance to Halifax forced Britain to change its
settlement plans. The Earl of Halifax wanted five settlements, but Cornwallis es-
tablished only one, arguing, “while there is any danger from the Indians the more
compact we are the better.”115 The Mi’kmaq had good reason to be angry. The treaty
process between the British and the Wabanaki that began in 1725 – by which time
the British presence in Nova Scotia was sufficient to demand an official acknowl-
edgment by the Mi’kmaq – had been compromised in the years between 1725 and
1749. The French had encouraged the Wabanaki to harass the British and fight on
the side of France during the War of the Austrian Succession, forcing the English
to realize that new treaties were necessary to secure Mi’kmaq cooperation.116 The
fact that the British arrived unannounced and erected a new pale in Mi’kma’ki
did not endear the settlers to their Indigenous neighbours, who made their disap-
proval evident.
  In 1752, the British tried yet again to secure a lasting peace with the Mi’kmaq.
As with earlier treaties, the government in Nova Scotia took its cues from Massa­
chusetts. The government at Boston had struck a treaty with members of the East­
ern Abenaki in 1749, but that treaty was never ratified and the subsequent violence
                                  A Pale on the Coast                               153


forced the British to invite the Wabanaki to discuss their issues and ratify the ear-
lier agreement. Massachussets officials were most concerned with the Abenaki at
Norrwidgwock (Kennebec), who continued their attacks on rural English settle-
ments that pushed into the Dawnland beyond the limits set in 1726. One Abenaki
went so far as to return the 1749 treaty.117 Present at the meeting in 1752 was Louis, a
Penobscot authorized to treat on behalf of his tribe, and Quinoius, a Norridgewock,
also charged with representing his tribe. The Wulstukwiuk and Passamaquoddy
sent Joseph and Sabadis on their behalf, though they were authorized only to listen
and to report back what had been discussed. All were gathered to reaffirm their
commitment to the Treaty of 1726.118
   Instrumental to this treaty was the division of land that set boundaries on who
could settle where. The Indigenous delegates at this meeting informed the repre-
sentatives from Boston that there had indeed been violence, but that it should end.
They then reminded the British that the treaty had concluded “that the English
should inhabit the lands as far as the salt water flowed, and no further; and that
the Indians should possess the rest.”119 The Eastern Abenaki made it clear that the
land was theirs: “Brethren, as I said before, so I now say, that the lands we own, let
us enjoy; and let no body take them from us. We said the same to those of our own
religion, the French. Altho’ we are a black people, yet God hath planted us here
God gave us this land, and we will keep it. God decreed all things; he decreed this
land to us; therefore neither shall the French or English possess it, but we will.”120
To this the representatives from the Wulstukw River concurred, “the tribe of the
St. John’s say the same.”121 The new treaty was read aloud and the Indigenous
representatives authorized to do so ratified the agreement.
   The government at Halifax was in a similar position to that of Boston, having
also struck a treaty in 1749 that brought little security or peace and illuminated the
internal divisions among the Wabanaki. The Mi’kmaq captured a ship at Canso
and attacked vessels at Chignecto. In late September, they attacked a group of
British men cutting wood at present-day Dartmouth. Four men were killed and
one was taken away. Rangers were sent in retaliation, and when they caught up to
the Mi’kmaq two were beheaded and one was scalped.122 In response, Governor
Cornwallis declared war on the Mi’kmaq and offered a bounty for their scalps.123
The British waged this war against the Mi’kmaq only, as the Wulstukwiuk had
agreed earlier that summer to be peaceful allies.124 Yet Wulstukwiuk anger to-
wards the British was evident by their role in an attack (with the Mi’kmaq and
Abenaki) against British soldiers at Minas where they captured nineteen soldiers
and held them for a week.125 The bounty brought in many scalps, but in time the
violence died down and the British at Halifax tried yet again to strike a treaty with
the Mi’kmaq.
   What differentiated the Nova Scotia treaties from those made in New England
was the implementation of boundaries. The Eastern Abenaki knew that their land
began where the salt water ended, and while this was a vague and perhaps unen-
forceable limit (one never accepted by the British), it served as a basis from which
the Abenaki could make complaints. Earlier treaties had also set limits on where
the English could settle. In Nova Scotia, there was no demonstrable boundary
limit between British and Mi’kmaw land because the British claimed land well
beyond their settlements but had never exercised control much outside the fort
154                            Homelands and Empires


walls. Soon after the founding of Halifax and the weak 1749 treaty, the British at-
tempted to extend their geographic control by establishing military posts on the
isthmus. Cornwallis sent Lieutenant Colonel Charles Lawrence to the region in
the summer of 1750, and though his first attempt was thwarted he returned in
the fall to construct the fort that took his name. The French built their own fort at
Beauséjour, and so both posts stood at opposite ends of the thin strip of marshland
connecting the peninsula to the mainland.126 Given the presence of new military
fortifications so soon after establishing Halifax, it should have come as no surprise
to the British that Mi’kmaw resistance would spike.
   When that resistance quieted, the British did what they could to secure a lasting
peace. In 1752, Cornwallis sent a messenger to the Mi’kmaq, who were gathered at
Port Toulouse on Unama’ki, and invited them to come treat with the British. Jean-
Baptiste Cope, who claimed to be a chief of the Shubenacadie Mi’kmaq, arrived at
Halifax to treat with Governor Peregrine Hopson, who had replaced Cornwallis.127
Cope and Hopson discussed their issues, and a new treaty was struck. Based on
the 1726 agreement, the 1752 treaty did not specifically address land but repeated
the promise that the Mi’kmaq would not be bothered in their hunting and fish-
ing.128 As the British learned soon after, the treaty and the Indigenous delegates
who signed it had little influence over the Mi’kmaw population.
   The winter of 1752 passed in relative peace, but in the Spring of 1753 British set-
tlers and Mi’kmaw residents once again clashed in violent encounters when two
English men, James Grace and John Conner, sailed into Halifax Harbour claim-
ing to have escaped Indigenous captivity after the Mi’kmaq murdered their ship-
mates. This was far from the truth; in fact, they had been part of a crew that robbed
an Indigenous sloop at Jeddore, a harbour roughly fifty kilometres up the coast
from Halifax, and then shipwrecked when they encountered rough weather. A
group of Mi’kmaq rescued and cared for the two survivors, who then turned on
their caregivers and killed them to collect the bounty on Mi’kmaw scalps.129 The
Mi’kmaq were enraged and wanted vengeance. Cope, upset that his 1752 treaty
had been broken, set a trap for the British. He dispatched his son to Halifax to re-
quest a provision ship and an escort back to Jeddore. The British sent a captain and
a group of men, including Anthony Casteel, to assist Cope. Shortly after the sloop
arrived, the Mi’kmaq attacked. The men were taken ashore and forced to lie on the
ground. Casteel, who must have understood enough of the Mi’kmaw language to
pick out key words, had enough time to tell his compatriots that they were about
to be killed. Their deaths satisfied the retribution necessary for the murders perpe-
trated by James Grace and John Conner. In addition, British scalps were valuable;
in 1753, French officials at Louisbourg were paying Mi’kmaw warriors for British
scalps (just as British officials at Halifax were paying their soldiers for Mi’kmaw
scalps).130 The Mi’kmaq killed all on board save for Casteel, who relied on his flu-
ency in French to convince the Mi’kmaq that he was not British.131
   Casteel’s survival depended on his ability to redefine himself as French or British
as necessary and to provide those into whose hands he fell with specific details of
territory he traversed.132 Casteel made his way through Mi’kma’ki with his cap-
tors and was eventually taken to Louisbourg where he met with Abbé Le Loutre
and Comte de Raymond, the governor of Île Royale. Raymond was particularly
interested in the route Casteel had taken. After being summoned to the governor’s
                                 A Pale on the Coast                             155


quarters, Raymond “unfolded a map of this coast, where I showed him all the
rivers, creeks, and places I was in.”133 Thus informed, Raymond eventually freed
Casteel, who returned to Halifax to inform the authorities of his experience. Upon
his return, Casteel was subjected to an investigation by British authorities, who
were likely concerned that he had consorted with the Mi’kmaq and the French
during his captivity. What the British learned, more than anything, was that the
1752 treaty had failed and that more would have to be done to extend Nova Scotia
into Mi’kma’ki.

                                     •••
When not attempting to strike alliances with the Mi’kmaq and Wulstukwiuk or
expand into the peninsula, the local British administration relied on surveying,
plotting settlements, and land management to govern what territory they did con-
trol at the Halifax settlement. The distribution of land facilitated administration
in several ways, most of which required direct involvement on behalf of the sur-
veyors themselves. At one of the earliest Council meetings held aboard the ship
Beauport in August of 1749, Cornwallis informed the Council that Charles Morris
and John Brewse had laid out the town lots and were ready to allocate land to
the settlers. But Cornwallis wondered whether the lots should be granted before
the colonists had been put to work building a line of defence around the town. The
Council minutes record that a unanimous vote decided that the next day settlers
would be told that they were to spend “a few days to cast up a line of defence” be-
fore they received their lands, and that afterwards they would be allocated lands
upon which they could construct their houses in security.134 Using land allocation
as a reward for performing the necessary task of strengthening defences secured a
modicum of safety for all Halifax inhabitants. The common depiction of the origi-
nal settlers as lazy often misrepresents the situation; settlers were eager to build,
although less eager to spend time on public works when still in want of personal
shelter. An initial line of defence, however, was a project in which settlers could
find comfort.135 The promise of land allocations following this brief employment
would have eased the tension between settlers and administration that seems to
have slowed much of the town’s construction.
   Granting land to hundreds of families was bound to cause confusion or encour-
age deceit, and the first few months at Halifax witnessed both, keeping Brewse
and Morris busy settling disputes. At a Council meeting in November, Beamsley
Glasier, an army captain who seems to have received a land grant but never settled
in Halifax, brought a case against Lance Shipton, arguing that while he was away
Shipton had built a house on his lot, number 25, on the north side of the town.136
In his defence, Shipton argued that the lot had been lawfully granted to him, and
the land register was called for. Finding Mr Glasier’s name assigned to lot 25, the
Council asked Shipton why he had built on a lot to which he clearly had no title.
“Mr. Shipton,” according to the minutes, “said he could prove that Mr. Brewse
the Engineer who had the laying of the lots had given him the choice of that lot
No.25 or No.3.” Shipton had first built on lot 3, but had since yielded that land
to a Mr Crosby. Both Brewse and Crosby were sent for. The land registry showed
that Shipton’s name had appeared in lot 3 but had been erased and Crosby’s name
156                             Homelands and Empires


put in its place. To avoid future confusion, the Council passed a motion that the
exchange of lots must be completed in the form of deeds, and must be recorded
in a separate register.137 Mr Shipton agreed to give up his title to the land, and
Mr Glasier agreed to allow Mr Shipton to remain in the house he had built until
that spring.
   Now that he had been evicted from lot 25, Shipton could not convince Crosby,
to whom he had ceded his original grant of lot 3, to move off the plot. Both parties
appeared before the Council to argue their case. Shipton claimed that he had yield-
ed his property only on the condition that his claim to lot 25 should stand, which
it had not. Crosby denied the condition, and Shipton called for his wife to cor-
roborate his story. The Council did not believe Shipton or his wife, and confirmed
Crosby’s title. By adapting to changing demands in town development, the sur-
veyors were able to resolve the conflict, and another lot was laid out for Shipton.138
The entire affair was not resolved until the following May, when Shipton visited
the Council once again, this time requesting that he be granted lot 25, the lot over
which he and Glasier had originally quarrelled. Glasier had allowed Shipton to
remain in the house he built on the lot until April, but the record indicates that
Glasier was out of town when Shipton’s time expired. As a result, Shipton request-
ed that he receive permission to remain on lot 25, and the lot that had been set
aside for Shipton be ceded to Glasier upon his return. The Council, undoubtedly
wanting to put the entire ordeal behind them, agreed.139 The daily administration
of the colony required the Council to deal with situations as they arose, and land
management required a system of record keeping that could be adjusted when
necessary to facilitate governance.
   During the first years of settlement, cadastral surveys were tools used by both
the state and the settlers. Cadastral maps were essential to settlers because they
defined and secured individual grants and land title.140 Ordinarily, a cadastral map
would be used by the government to assert control over settlers primarily through
the collection of rents and taxes. In Halifax, however, lands were held tax- and
rent-free for the first ten years, as promised by the Earl of Halifax in his official call
for settlers.141 Certain conditions had to be met to retain title to any piece of land,
and enforcing these conditions required surveys and surveyors. Unlike in several
other colonies, the governing Council at Halifax did not grant large plots of land to
proprietors, who would then subdivide the land and form a council themselves to
govern the area. Instead, lots were granted to individual settlers, allowing admin-
istrators to keep a watchful eye on land use and ensure that lots were being “im-
proved” as required by the conditions of the grant.142 Controlling land tenure was
important during the first years of settlement at Halifax, but the Council would
experiment with privately organized settlements after the town was established.
Cornwallis’s primary concern was guaranteeing that the basic conditions of settle-
ment were reached and that town plans were employed to that end.
   There were times when land management was both practical and fiscally con-
servative, but when these two concerns clashed, practicality took priority. Some
public works that would have required hiring labourers were performed by set-
tlers as a condition of their land grants. In July 1750, Cornwallis declared that
each settler in possession of a lot in Halifax was “obliged to clear opposite to his
lot to the middle of the street, the whole length of the grant.” Should land holders
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              157


refuse or not clear the land within six weeks, labourers would be hired to perform
the work at the expense of the lot.143 Clearing trees and fencing lots was a peren-
nial concern, and eventually the Council offered bounties for settlers who reached
specific goals. In April 1752, Governor Hopson demanded that all grants be fenced
and cleared within twelve months. The fence had to be at least four feet high, and
no more than ten trees per acre were permitted to remain. Each settler was prom-
ised twenty shillings per acre cleared within the twelve months, demonstrating
that the local government was willing to spend money to get results.144 This kind
of administrative control required careful surveys. Only by looking at the surveys
and sketches and matching a plot of land to a settler’s name as recorded in the al-
lotment book could the Council be sure that the right settler was on the right plot of
land, and that all the specific demands of settlement were reached. Charles Morris
and John Brewse were essential to this process; they were called upon to resurvey
land when a dispute arose, to act as mediators between parties, and to make sure
that the Council was working from the most recent and accurate town maps. The
maps and surveys that Morris and Brewse provided were practical and useful, and
evolved as the town grew. As more settlers arrived and demanded their own plots
of land, Charles Morris and his surveys would become even more important to the
local administration. Unlike the Board of Trade, officials at Halifax had continual
access to the latest geographic and cartographic information.

                                      •••
By spring 1752, three years after John Brewse drew his sketch for the town, most
of the initial construction in Halifax required by the plan was complete. The Board
of Trade was anxious to bring an end to the growing settlement expenses, and
therefore instructed Cornwallis that since “the fortifications of Halifax are made
as far as the present plan extends,” perhaps he should terminate plans for any
new construction.145 Proposals to improve fortifications at the harbour were put
on hold, as were the perennial improvements to the battery on Georges Island, a
small bit of land in Halifax harbour. The Board suggested that Cornwallis continue
building only as his yearly budget allowed, and to employ whenever possible the
foreign Protestants who had travelled to Halifax on the condition that they would
work off the cost of their passage.146 Many German settlers had arrived in Halifax
but had been unable to establish a new settlement for fear of Indigenous attacks.
Cornwallis was unsuccessful in his settlement attempts, but the Board of Trade
assured Hopson that “we doubt not but that your humanity and prudence will
also suggest to you the means of alleviating the distress and disappointments of
the people themselves.”147 The Board had in its possession a map of a proposed
area of settlement at Musquodoboit, which “according to the plan and survey …
appears to be a very proper place.”148 Instead, however, the German settlers were
to be sent to Merligash, a picturesque harbour down the Atlantic coast southwest
from Halifax.
   Unlike Halifax, which was surveyed only after the settlers arrived, Merligash,
renamed Lunenburg, was scouted and mapped for settlement by Charles Morris,
who continued to serve imperial ends in Nova Scotia. Charles Lawrence was put
in charge of the settlement after he had established his reputation by founding
158                           Homelands and Empires


Fort Lawrence in 1750 in an attempt to remove the French from the Missaguash
River area on the isthmus.149 Lawrence relied heavily on Morris to make certain
that plots were laid out and distributed in a manner that would please the settlers.
Lawrence’s personal journal details Morris’s efforts. Over four hours in early June,
for example, Lawrence “fixed with Capt. Morris … the situation of the Town, and
also for the blockhouses for the defence of it.”150 Morris was capable enough to
realize that simply fixing boundary lines did not mark the end of settlement plan-
ning. The original instructions for the Lunenburg settlement stated that houses
should be kept 200 metres from the shore, but due to the inconsistent shoreline
it would “in Mr. Morris’s opinion have laid us infinite inconveniences.”151 There
were problems, especially with settlers arguing that their plot was too wet, or too
stony, or too hilly, and such complaints demanded new plots be surveyed and dis-
tributed to those whose land was inadequate.152 Settlers were growing impatient
over a lack of supplies, so Lawrence did what he could to appease those who were
upset about their land. He even managed to convince the settlers that creating a
commons – shared land to be used by all inhabitants – was more profitable than
smaller grants of individual plots.153
   Lawrence sent maps back to Hopson, but he often waited until they could pro-
vide a complete view of the settlement’s progress because incomplete maps could
not fully outline potential risks. Not wanting to rush the charting and surveying,
he informed Hopson, “it will be impractical to prepare the sketch of the peninsula,
town, & blockhouses, so as to send it away tomorrow. But by the next opportunity,
we shall certainly have it ready.”154 Lawrence’s military background also caused
him to emphasize Lunenburg’s need for defences. At times he worried that the
clean lines on a map could not represent the settlement’s dangerous position. He
wrote to Hopson and complained of the sketches that “it is impossible by these
means to point out the many ascents & descents, the covers and the various advan-
tages of ground” that provided cover and opportunity for an Indigenous attack.155
The local Mi’kmaq were angry that yet another settlement was being constructed
without their permission, a condition they believed was necessary for any expan-
sion to be “lawfully made” as stated in earlier treaties.156
   The Mi’kmaq grew increasingly upset about British expansion, and authori-
ties at London and Halifax sensed an imperial struggle looming on the horizon
that would require new fortifications to protect Halifax from both the French and
Indigenous forces. Commissioners of the Board of Trade were concerned that
their knowledge of the geography surrounding the Halifax region was still lim-
ited. Lieutenant Governor Charles Lawrence, who had replaced Hopson when eye
trouble forced the governor to return to England, became increasingly diligent in
sending reports on the local environment to London and was requested to send
over a plan locating the best areas for new blockhouses and batteries.157 Lawrence
wasted no time commissioning a new survey of the region, and by June 1754 he
had a map ready to send to London that outlined strategic areas, including water-
ways and popular overland routes, at which blockhouses could be placed to pre-
vent the Mi’kmaq from getting too close to Halifax. Although by 1751 the British
had established Fort Lawrence on the Isthmus of Chignecto and Fort Edward at
Minas Basin to defend against the Mi’kmaq during periods of sustained warfare,
it remained imperative to protect English settlements from surprise attacks.158
                                  A Pale on the Coast                               159


Blockhouses on the Shubenacadie River, which cuts into the interior of the penin-
sula from Cobequid Bay at the back of the Minas Basin, were first proposed in 1752
to establish trade with the Mi’kmaq in an attempt to win them over as allies.159
It was only after the short-lived 1752 treaty between Governor Hopson and Jean-
Baptiste Cope that the plan was revised with a more military purpose.
   In a 1753 report on the progress of British settlement in Nova Scotia, Charles
Morris ominously linked the danger from Mi’kmaw warriors to the Acadian pres-
ence at Chignecto. The “disturbances given by the Indian enemy” were, accord-
ing to the surveyor, the principal restriction to expanding British settlements.160
Moreover, the Mi’kmaq secured provisions from the French at Chignecto before
travelling down the Shubenacadie River by canoe en route to the English settle-
ments on the coast to “destroy and captivate the people.”161 A blockhouse on the
Shubenacadie would end this tactic and also cut off the Acadians – whose neu-
trality was constantly doubted – from the French at Louisbourg.162 Morris then
reanimated an old idea to open up Nova Scotia for British settlement: since the
Acadians both supported the Mi’kmaq and refused to swear an unconditional
oath of allegiance to the British, why not remove these “neutral French” from the
region altogether?163
   By this point, Lawrence was aware that he could not delay in sending surveys,
as he had at Lunenburg. The map that officials at Whitehall demanded was con-
sidered important enough to send even though it was incomplete. Lawrence noted
that the Shubenacadie River, the mouth of which was to be the site of a new fort,
“tho’ it is marked out and illuminated like the rest of the plan has not yet been
surveyed.”164 Lawrence probably knew about the river’s strategic position from
his military involvement in Nova Scotia, but he needed a detailed map to illustrate
its importance to the Board of Trade.165 Surveyors quickly created a more complete
map that detailed the strategic river, satisfying the Board of Trade’s desire to work
from the most recent surveys. In August, Lawrence wrote to the Board to empha-
size his desire to build a fort at the Shubenacadie. “I have just now obtained an
exact survey of this River,” Lawrence declared, “which I enclose your Lordships
… This further discovery of it has strongly confirmed me in my opinions of the
necessity of building a fort there.”166 The initial idea of constructing a fort required
a map to show the fort’s location. After a more careful survey of the area was
completed, Lawrence and the Board of Trade had an improved cartographic un-
derstanding and could coordinate their actions accordingly, even though Morris’s
proposal to expel the Acadians was excluded – for the time being (figure 4.10).
   The Board of Trade agreed with Lawrence, and its decision to support the lieu-
tenant governor was influenced by the maps he had commissioned and sent to
London. “We have attentively read and considered your observations of building
a Fort upon Cebben Accadie River, have also carefully examined the charts you
have transmitted, which mark its situation and advantages,” wrote the Board in
the fall of 1754, and the members concurred that the locations indicated on the
map would be the most strategic areas to fortify.167 These maps and reports pro-
vided the Board with the knowledge of geography that its members required to
administer the settlement from across the Atlantic. However, cartography provid-
ed spatial information that could anticipate an imperial presence in the region that
would be more difficult to secure than the maps suggested.

The founding of Halifax indicated to the French and the Mi’kmaq that Britain was
serious about transforming Nova Scotia from an imperial fiction into a British
province. While there was no guarantee that the settlement would survive, imperi-
al support was a huge step towards increasing Britain’s territorial sovereignty. Old
concerns and new tensions resulted from the settlement at Chebucto: French and
Indigenous peoples in the province questioned the limits of Acadian and British
authority within the peninsula; the Mi’kmaq in Nova Scotia continued their con-
flict with the British and launched new attacks; and all three sides prepared for a
war that would continue (British-Mi’kmaq) or begin again (British-French). Even
before Cornwallis and his fleet arrived at Chebucto, French officials were chastising
the English for their contempt towards previous treaties. In June of 1749, a French
official warned that they must act quickly to ward off new British establishments,
especially those planted outside the “ancient” Acadian boundaries mentioned in
the Treaty of Utrecht. The most ancient maps placed Acadia on the peninsula, so
French officials argued, which served as a perfect and natural boundary. Some
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              161


maps created in England since the Treaty of Utrecht had extended Acadia beyond
the isthmus, but such an interpretation could not change the agreement of 1713.168
   Priests and missionaries were equally upset about Britain’s attempts at extend-
ing their geographic control into disputed areas. In late August, Père Charlevoix
wrote to the minister of the Marine, Antoine-Louis Rouillé, outlining what he be-
lieved were Acadia’s boundaries. As before, Charlevoix relied on the presence of
Indigenous peoples to serve as a buffer zone. The English, however, were build-
ing on the Saint John River, which Charlevoix argued was never part of Acadia
and which was much closer to the Abenaki than previous settlements. Charlevoix
argued that France must continue to support Indigenous title to this region to pre-
vent the English from settling so close to Quebec.169 To the Abenaki in this region
were added the Acadians, who might also support French title. Abbé Le Loutre re-
ported in the fall of 1749 that these Acadians might form a militia to retain posses-
sion of the Saint John and other important rivers in the area. Such an action could
both console and animate the Acadians, most of whom, according to Le Loutre,
were ready to sacrifice for the glory of France.170 While some Acadians might have
fought for the French, in recent conflicts many had displayed their neutrality. The
farther Acadians lived from British settlements the more likely they were to re-
main independent and, possibly, pro-French.171 In all likelihood, geographic loca-
tion remained a factor in degrees of neutrality after 1710.
   Aside from Indigenous or Acadian support, the French would require more de-
tailed terrestrial and maritime information if they were to retake Acadia or limit
British expansion. Rouillé received letters from various officials and eager citizens
who believed the time had come to retake Acadia. M. Brissart, writing from Saint-
Malo and perhaps hunting for a patronage appointment, informed Rouillé that
the existing peace between France and Britain provided the perfect opportunity
for a surprise attack. He would even be willing to help organize such an endeav-
our, “but as I can find no maps to purchase of Canada, nor of the [St. Lawrence]
river, nor of Acadia (always a cause of boundary issues), if the court would send
me some it would be of great help.”172 Brissart suffered from a lack of geographic
evidence in Saint-Malo, yet there was no shortage of maps in the French ministry
of the Marine even though their accuracy was at times brought into question. By
1750, many of these maps were informing the discussions between British and
French representatives meeting in Paris to resolve the Acadian boundary dispute.
These maps helped illustrate what the French considered to be outrageous British
land claims. La Galissonière, the governor of New France who had been named a
commissary at the Acadian Boundary discussions, learned that the British were not
limiting their claims to the Saint John River area, but were instead still arguing for
the entire coast from New England to Beaubassin, as well as from Gaspé to Canso.
Like Charlevoix, La Galissonière argued that the Abenaki were France’s best allies,
but he used maps to demonstrate the British claims themselves. “The English base
their claims,” he argued, “on a map entitled L’Empire Anglois dans l’Amérique avec
les Conquete sur les Espagnols et les François by which they extend their Nova Scotia
to the southern coast of the St. Lawrence River almost to Quebec.”173 Such a claim
had to be balanced, and the French realized they needed persuasive, verifiable,
first-hand territorial descriptions.
162                            Homelands and Empires


   While British officials could rely on Charles Morris and his assistants to provide
timely and useful geographic reports and maps, French administrators were forced
to dispatch capable surveyors to the northeast to survey territory. Louis XV commis-
sioned two men to travel to Acadia, map the region, and issue geographic reports.
The trips of Louis Franquet and Joseph-Bernard de Chabert de Cogolin, demon-
strate the importance France placed in the 1750s on securing reliable maps and
charts. Wars already fought and those on the horizon, coupled with the boundary
commission’s focus on determining Acadia’s ancient limits, proved that the com-
petition over northeastern North America was about cartographic diplomacy as
much as military operations.
   Louis Franquet joined the French army at age twelve and served in various regi-
ments until he entered the engineer corps in 1720. He remained a member of the
engineer corps for thirty years, until 1750, when he was commissioned to travel
to Île Royale and report on the strength of French fortifications. Though he spent
several years in New France and wrote reports on the Canadians, the Acadians,
and various Indigenous groups, it was his work as an engineer that received the
most attention.174 Franquet’s trips to Île Royale and Île St Jean provided the French
government with detailed accounts of those regions and their fortifications, use-
ful information during the lull in British-French conflict. Franquet’s findings were
both strategic and cultural in nature, as travelling throughout the region provided
him with an opportunity to interact with its residents.175 Franquet and Chabert left
France together on La Mutine in the early summer of 1750.
   Though sent to investigate defences and report on military preparedness,
Franquet’s memoirs indicate an interest in geography, demography, and the
culture of New France’s residents. He noted that Île Madame and Petit-de-Grat
Island, two islands on the southeast coast of Île Royale with twenty inhabitants,
were likely one single body in the past but were now separated by a thin band of
water.176 Île Madame lay just beyond the Fronsac Passage (Gut of Canso), which
Franquet described as a narrow waterway that could be easily controlled by the
British.177 Franquet then visited Île St Jean and found himself in the middle of a de-
bate between two groups of residents who had decided to raise a church but could
not agree where it should be located. They saw Franquet as a representative of the
French government, even asking him to listen to their arguments and render a de-
cision.178 Like Charles Morris and John Brewse, France’s surveyors and engineers
often took on civic responsibilities.
   By combining his commissioned task (investigating forts and reporting on their
state) with an account of inhabitants and their desires, Franquet’s geographic
tracts helped French administrators understand the region better. Franquet in-
formed his superiors in France of the difficulties facing Acadian settlers and the
need to determine the region’s boundaries. He encountered a group of roughly
eighteen families at Baye Verte who had settled there temporarily. Franquet em-
phasized their situation as people between empires in an uncertain time. He not-
ed that they settled where they were only until Britain and France determined
the limits of Acadia. If their former lands fell into the possession of the English
and their present settlements remained with France, they would stay; if not, they
would likely go to Île St Jean or Île Royale.179 Franquet also provided reports on
Beauséjour and Île St Jean. “As for the fort of Beauséjour,” he wrote, “the map
                                 A Pale on the Coast                              163


attached here represents its exact shape.”180 It also included an explanation of its
construction and what needed to be done to make it capable of defending against a
cannon attack. Of Île St Jean, Franquet argued that the region was capable of more
agricultural production, enough to supply Île Royale within only a few years of
cultivation. The inhabitants would be much reassured of their security in case of
another rupture with England if France built a garrison, redoubts, and placed forts
at major ports. Ideally, according to Franquet, the island should be completely
independent from Île Royale.181
   Franquet’s fellow passenger on Le Mutine, Marquis de Chabert, was similarly
charged with reporting on conditions in the northeast. Specifically, Chabert was
dispatched to rectify the various maps and charts of the area. Chabert, at twenty-
five years old, was half Franquet’s age when the two sailed from France. Chabert
was the grandson of a French rear-admiral and the son of a French captain who had
been killed in battle. He entered the navy as a midshipman in 1741 and charts that
he drew during several trips to the Mediterranean caught the attention of the min-
ister of the Marine, who promoted him. In 1746, Chabert travelled to Acadia to cor-
rect French coastal charts. He mapped Chebucto Harbour and managed secretly to
map Annapolis Harbour and spy on British ships there. In 1750, after a brief period
of imprisonment (the British captured his ship off the coast of Spain in 1747) and
two years in Paris, Chabert was sent back to Acadia to continue his surveys.182 The
commission for his 1750 expedition coincided with the appointment to positions
of imperial importance of two men with an interest in maps and charts: Minister
Rouillé and La Galissonière. Named minister of the Marine in 1749, Rouillé con-
sidered maps “an essential part of navigation, which often determines the success
of the King’s forces, and always that of commerce and the safety of navigators.”183
Rouillé’s concerns were echoed by La Galissonière, recently selected as a represen-
tative to the Acadian boundary commission, who informed Chabert that he would
be dispatched to North America to continue his valuable work.
   This second trip to Acadia resulted in the 1753 publication of an account of his
voyage to North America. This work was important enough to the ministry of the
Marine that they purchased 200 copies to ensure its completion.184 Chabert began
his account: “There are few countries where it was as necessary to make astro-
nomical observations than in that part of North America that includes l’Acadie,
Île Royale, and Île Terre-Neuve; it should suffice, to convince doubters of this fact,
to cast an eye over the maps that have been used to this point, and to see how
little they resemble each other. In truth, they are established on estimations and
cannot find but little common ground.”185 Part of the reason for Chabert’s expe-
dition was to improve navigation for ships, too many of which were lost due to
mistaken charts that led them off course or into dangerous areas. It was for this
reason that newer maps created by the Dépôt de la Marine were based on journals
and commentaries provided by a number of officers and pilots. These maps were
further informed by observations taken at Quebec and Boston.186 As an area of
military and economic value, Acadia was understandably a region of heightened
cartographic interest (figure 4.11). Chabert spent two years in Paris working on the
surveys he had taken during his 1746 voyage to the northeast.
   Chabert’s memoir of the voyage combined descriptions of his various trips from
Louisbourg (where he was stationed) to the surrounding area. He detailed the

technical methods by which he derived his conclusions. Astronomical observa-

described the Fronsac passage as easily navigable by anyone who had seen it,
piloting almost any ship.187 In mapping Canso (figure 4.12), Chabert noted that he
took detailed remarks while circumnavigating the islands; for areas that he did not
visit, Chabert consulted the local inhabitants and followed their descriptions. He
was also able to compare charts received locally with those in the possession of the
Dépôt to determine how old maps could be altered with newer and more reliable
information.188 Essential to Chabert’s memoir were the maps he published, includ-
ing those of Canso, Île Royale, Chebucto Harbour, and Cape Sable. Some maps
were new and served to correct errors of older maps (Île Scatari near Louisbourg
was incorrectly positioned on Dépot maps twenty-two leagues further than its
actual location), while maps that Chabert prepared on his 1746 voyage were up-
dated (he added the town of Halifax to his 1746 map of Chebucto). Also included
were detailed astronomical observations for various places along the northeast-
ern coast. These measurements provided French administrators with updated
and specific materials about the location of key settlements and geographic fea-
tures. Combined with Franquet’s analysis of the region’s fortifications, France was
4.12 M de Chabert’s Plan du Port de Canseau, 1751. Chabert included depth soundings as well as the ruins of the Canso fort.
